Attempted Home Invasion

A brown skinned young man in white Tshirt removed the screen from our bathroom window, which was about 4 inches open at the time. I was working in my office and heard him, dropped what I was doing to go investigate, and scared him pretty badly. He was about to pull the window open further, but dropped the screen on the ground and bolted. I gave chase and ran after him barefoot as he leapt into a small, robin's egg blue, custom pick-up driven by another man with curly dark hair. They proceeded just fast enough to leave me gradually behind down Marin Ave, left onto Casino, left onto Yuba, and right on Shasta to turn right onto Amador, the service road to I-80, before I lost them. It was 12:46 when I got back into the apartment in time to answer a call from Lisa and beg-off temporarily in order to call 911. Despite our Richmond address they forwarded me to the San Pablo Police. Officers arrived just after 1:00. One went on to scout while the other took my statement, made a strenuous case for our being in San Pablo and not Richmond, dusted for prints in and out, found none and offered as much hope of other results, and then went on his way as Lisa was arriving home around 1:30 with Rosie, fertilizer, seedlings, and anti-snail measures.

cards.name: RQ 20111001
cards.content:
{{+date}}

[[Don McClure|Don]], [[Lisa WilliamsCraig|Peri]], [[Joanie Albee-Good|Phasia]], [[Joe Good|Cog]], [[Brandon WilliamsCraig|Graves]], [[Tim Schlaak|Tarkal]], [[Ted Greer|Torath]], [[Sivan Marcus|Clayton]], Brendan as Crazy, and Ryan as Gohan the Barbarian

 

Clay Fertility Sea 1604

Carmenian Adventures east of Esrolia

Half way through the first day: armored horses and riders coming - 5 knights and 12 retainers

Carmenians speak an hybrid of Sheshnellan and Hortlander (Carmenians are to Sheshella and Quebequa and to the French)

Front rider comes to us to ask our business and collect Duke Vidar's tax. Set fee or giving the Duke fist chance at the goods. 5w per wagon (10w) paid and we are lead to the road.

 

Pass villages w folks slightly more shesh some more Hortlander some more in between. Couple of kinds of temples to Storm/Lightbringers and churches to Invisible God (square w Infinity rune). Much higher quantity of metal on village militia etc. than in Prax. 1st town has an Inn and they speak Esrolian fluently in Stone's Throw. We prepare to stay at The Stone in the Boot inn and introduce the trolls as our night watchmen--therefter needing to leave immediately. The landlord is bummed to be losing our custom and people to eat his beef stew, so Graves performs a brief improvisation in which a stew is found to have troll inside provided humorous flavoring most harmlessly. The landlord guesses that we are traveling with a troll and, if we didn't have 17 armored guys there might be trouble. On the way out of town Duke Vidar's Man, Sir Flemming, puts down a small mutiny to continue with us. We come to a small farmhouse. We are allowed to camp in the barn around midnight. Part of the guards are guarding the other guards. Cog gets out of the cart and stretches his legs in the barn.

 

Wind Fertility Sea 1604

5am on our way on a five bison-a-breast road. Around sunset we arrive at the road to Nochett City (1.5days) and we camp 100ft. off the road while Cog stands guard with Tarkal, Graves, and finally Peri/Phasia. Third of the way through second watch four persons come out of invisibility as they are swinging at us. Graves puts a bolt 11 in A's 15 and takes 13 to his 12 of which 7 gets through, taking Graves to -1 at which point he falls. Everyone is waking up. Phasia Prot4 Cog and moves toward Graves, next round Prot4 Torath. Graves heal2 himself. Peri, hunting via Loiosh finds spell casters and begins to pursue, passing toward six more incoming bad guys--shooting them. Graves switches to broadsword and shield and activates his bladesharp doubling effect. The tide of battle begins to turn and the entire 12 flee before their battle magic drops.

 

We track the brigands for 1.5hrs to their lair. Graves detects magic to find that their perimeter is warded. Graves begins to cast Silences but Cog moves ahead early and trips a clatter string trap. Graves' Detect Life is blocked by a Ward spell.

Two sneak up on Phasia and Tarkal, are noticed, and Phasia fails a demoralize before asking "are you friendly, or are you going to die?" at which point they run away.

Graves goes wide left followed by Clayton, Peri goes wide right, as the others goe up the middle. Graves DetMgc to find the edge of the Ward and crouches behind his shield to dig up the rod. Battlemagic lights go on and Graves' shield Cracks, at which point he casts Insivibility and continues digging. Cog Jumps through the ward and into the middle of the palisade to begin laying about, and fonds 3 heavy xbows w two additional ready xbows and guys to be crankers. Four others are in plate armor and swilling 1 potion/rnd while the 4 others had insufficient time to don armor.

Peri puts two arc arrows into a guy's head and summons an ancestor to go munch oppositional souls, Torath runs thr Ward to crouch on palisade wall, Gohan arcs in twice and hides behind a tree, Cog is Fumbled to lose his mace, switches to maul. Graves uses DispMgc4mtx to kill uncovered square rock w rune corner of ward, takes damage, ward drops. Clayton charges, gets xbos bolt that blows off left leg.

Don Rule Clarification:if the damage does more than half of uyour weapon's hp, then the hp go down by one. Otherwise, more than hp, then the weapon breaks. Less than haf hp then no effect to weapon. Special parry means weapon takes no damage unless hit special and crit parry no damage unless attack was a critical.

Graves heal6mtx Clayton as he countermgc2 Cog who jumps back into the fray. Graves bounces a HvyXbo MultiMis3 off a plate armored guy. Everybody cleans up as Peri goes after an illusory magic caster. We go after her but the DspMgc6mtx makes his image disappear.

 

Clayton begins casting detect spells for treasure. Peri and Torath stay with him as Cog and Graves go for Tarkal and Phasia and the carts onto which we load our take: 4 sets bronze plate armor, 8 suits of chainmail, 10 broadsword, 4 greatswords, 2 bastard swords, 5 heavy Xbo, 100 bolts, 300ft rope, one handfull of gems worth about 4000, 942sp, 32wheels, 4lbs copper coin, 6 countermagic2 potions, 4 heal6 potions, remnants of caravans, wanted poster 1000sp dead or alive for ____ guy in plate armor, 5 jewelry pieces, gold w gems inserted, worth 12000 from rich people (some owned by specific familes - complicated to get a benefit from returning it - so we strip and break them down to their parts worth 6000), 2 bottles of wine, and 6 riding horses. Torath finds hollow log with generic tactical maps of the area, as well as one third of a treasure map! We need at least another third of the map to have any real context. A couple of villages in the area with what looks like drop points, of which Stone's Throw is one. Are they telling people which targets are worth hitting? Torath, Clayton, and Gohan calim the Carmenian (7pt) plate suits, the remaining one is siz 9,10,11. Clayton's chain takes its place in the group treasury. Torath kills one horse to pay his debt to a shaman who healed him. Cog eats it. The horse, not the Shaman.

 

Cog will hide in the deep woods with the lion and one cart. Torath and Graves obscure the tracks. In two weeks Cog will head for Nochett City if we have not returned. Everyone else will go to the town on the map that is not a drop point and is closest to Duke Vidar's palace.

 

Fire Fertility Sea 1604

The village: The people are insular/parochial while thinking of themselves as higher in culture than Esrolia. Storm Gods worshipped by peasants, but the upper class believes in the Invisible God and "Saint Orlanth". Conversations ensue about the ends of the world to the East and West.Carmenia is divided into Aristocracy, Tradesmen, Artisans, Peasants. The Duke is ten years old. The regent is decent--the previous Duke's brother. Taxes same, safe roads, no war. Lord of the area who treats the peasants like crap, without going out of his way to do so. Sherrif comes by and introduces himself, asking about us. We identify ourselves as merchants and ask who we might see about bounties. He goes with us. We show him the heads, armor, and jewels. He offers to introduce us to the Regent. We ride through the night and arrive at the castle around 3am, cross the drawbridge over the moat, and introduced to the commander of the watch who gives us two options: surrender weapons and stay in the hall or keep them and stay together in an adjecent building. Peri is recognized as a Rune Lord and given the best room. She accepts and invites Phasia to share it.

 

Wild Fertility Sea 1604

Morning, baths, breakfast, second breakfast, messenger announcing audience with Duke and responding to our request for a quick etiquette tutorial. In the Garden with Duke and Regent: Graves tells of the encounter with the bandits, Torath embellishes. His Lordship desperately wishes to meet the War Goat William. Graves fetches him and puts him through his paces, resulting in a 500sp offer for him which is declined respectfully. FYI His Lordship's father was assasinated during a hunting trip.

 

After the first day we are all visited by the Regent who asks for any details we might have omitted. We show him the maps and tell him of the Trolls, carefully. He epresses gratitude for our service and candor.

 

Water Stasis Sea 1604

Sir Flemming has been summoned and arrives and we are invited for the first time into the throne room. Gratitude is expressed and gifts are offered. We are to keep the moneys we find, given the 1000sp bounty, thanks for returning the jewelry (3,500sp value given us), provided with permission to keep armor (removing family filligree) or money. We keep the plate, after they do two days of work to remove the family marks, and they will escort us to the edge of all Carmenian lands.

FYI the duke has a retainer who goes to the northern border to fight against the trolls every year, even though this is the most Southern (and most tollerant) of the Dukedoms.

 

Graves and Tarkal go, with an armed patrol lead by Sir Flemming, to recover Cog. All of us head to the edge of Carmenia under escort by

Wind Stasis Sea 1604

cards.name: RQ 20111008
cards.content:
{{+date}}

[[Don McClure|Don]], [[Ted Greer|Torath]], [[Sivan Marcus|Clayton]] and then [[Sivan Marcus|Godfrey]], [[Lisa WilliamsCraig|Peri]], [[Joanie Albee-Good|Phasia]], [[Joe Good|Cog]], [[Brandon WilliamsCraig|Graves]], [[Tim Schlaak|Tarkal]], Brendan as Crazy, and Ryan as Gohan the Barbarian

 

{{RQ DMc group treasury|closed}}

 

Wind Stasis Sea 1604

All of us arrive at the edge of Hendreiki lands (Carmenia?) under escort. Edge of Hendreiki lands (one of six major Esrolian provinces).

After the Shadow Plateau (originall land of darkness gods where trolls interacted with other dark creatures on the surface) we will get to Nochett City. 100 grandmothers rule over the part of Esrolia (majority) in which Nochett City exists. Belentar united the six regions into modern Esrolia by convincing the grandmothers. The least favored god in Esrolia (after Lunar and Chaos) is Orlanth. The Orlathi temple is outside the walls in Nochett City. Hendreiki lands (a portion of the Hortlands) mainly a Storm pantheonic area, lots of fighters, organized violence. People in Hortlands must occasionally carry weapons to protect themselves in bad parts of town!

We pass trolls openly traveling in the road. A bit after two in the afternoon we...

We stop for the night at the Bent Horseshoe Inn where Ben charges us 14.5sp and completes the ritual to welcome Cog and Crazy to his darkenss. SCORE. Other travelers: merchants who don't look like us (like killers).

Torath tells  AWESOME battle tales (01%) into the night. We hear that Sir Ethelrest up north claims to have taken horses across Prax. (Went to escort Elejan across the waste.)

 

Three days to pass through Hendreiki lands while being warned constantly of Orlanthi bandits and the avoided by same if at all possible. The Shadow Lands are before us (four or five days to cross).

 

Freeze Movement Sea 1604

Even in the middle of the day the sun doesn't shine as brightly (mid day like half hour before dusk) in the Shadow Lands. 25% passing travelelrs ar Uz (trolls) and half of the humans wear darkness cult markings. Many Earth cultists pass. Cog and Crazy walk by day. Cog asks who the Mistress Race troll is at the Ligor Lidor temple at Nochett City. Not. Ratio of less Trollkin to trolls and Trollkin aren't armed in general. There is a Shadow Lands Mistress Race troll, however, in the Obsidian Castle in the Lead Hills.

Second day come over hill to find fight happening between 25 Trollkin (w bodies all over) vs 1 human and 4 Trolls (+1 troll down). All but Torath and Graves jump in. When the tide turns the Orlanthi Trollkin (7) teleport away before the rest are wiped up. The troll tells Cog of the Uz Kanath H'dar (Trollkin Rebellion). One quarter of the Trollkin in the Shadow Lands have begun worshipping other gods, rebelled, and demanded their own lands. The human is a Kigor Lidor worshipper putting in his five years.

 

There are no open inns or unbarricaded houses in Shadow Lands. All are ready for attack by Trollkin. We press on at maximum speed.

Impromptu recently widened road, huge amount supplies being moved south to north by contractors, masons, quarries opened near the base of the mountain to prepare to defend against the Lunar Empire. Once we reach government subsidized routes there is no chance of raids against us.

 

Wild Movement Sea 1604

Arrive at largest city we've ever seen, near the size of Old Pavis but fully built up and occupied. Takes a day to walk all the way across.

SE is docks with dozens of ships from various nations - dominated by (Greek Trireme) oared vessels from the Esrolian Royal Navy.

We also see Sheshnellan LEscalmi or Ralian cogs. Sacred Way (major central avenue) leads through the city and to Odaria (megopolis necropolis - Daka Fal holy site). North outside of main walls are the Storm Temples.

 

{{+Brandon notes|closed}}

 

Going to the Great Marketto. At 10 and 2pm Torath may find other "wild people" performing. A sorcerer's apprentice wants to sell his stall for 10sp so we set Clayton up in a stall to sell our stuff.

 

We go to visit Elejan's brother, Anadar el Nadir, in the Rich District. He feigns happiness after reading the letter from Elejan, then crumples and keeps it on his person, insisting that we stay the night. We are only offered a second cup of tea. Phasia intros the Lion and the potential sale to Rislin, and Anadar is "happy to help". Despite himself he is impressed by the Lion. He may know a second potential buyer. "Always more than happy to help my brother" find a safe place to store the lion. At dinner Anadar doesn't show up. Cog and Crazy guard the cart adn lion as usual. Torath spars with the guards (80%ish w lots of formal training, plate armor, and two-handed scimitars).

 

Peri goes to visit Anadar just after dinner. He is a third of the way through a bottle of hard liquor. When Peri prods gently he allows that his brother is "an ungrateful ass" but he doesn't want to talk about it. Turns out Elejan "tore down years of service for someone he has just met!" (Phasia) Peri notices a half burnt letter in the fire place. Later, he offers to have one of the guards escort her back to her room. She tells Phasia about the conflict.

 

God Movement Sea 1604

A note awaits Phasia in the morning: "Rislin is safe but more profit may be had from Polymous." We follow Phasia to Rislin's place. The trolls bear the lion. His estate is larger than a village and the guard livery includes plate armor. Walled area and second gate beyond which no weapons. Crazy and Graves leave weapons larger than a dagger and carry the lion for Phasia. Sumtuous estate, gaudy, makes rococo look minimalist, every surface is packed with curiosities so thick you can barely see individual stuff. We are lead to Main Hall (looks like a throne room) to find a person whose corpulence is almost unrivaled. Internally he is called Your Greatness. Phasia does a great job if the sales intro. Rislin calls servants to carry him forward. Much eval and bargain jockying ensues. We are invited to "lunch" with schmoozing while magical evaluation goes on in the background. He offers 65Ksp. Phasia compliments him for his humor and counters with 125Ksp. He must think about it and acknowledges that we might have others look at it.The others were given lunch while they waited and we emerge at 3pm.

{{+Prancing Posey|float:right}}

Torath heads for the Prancing Posey tavern wherein he was supposed to meet the Sheshnellan sorcerer, Godfrey. They hang out.

Cog went to Kigor Litor temple and asked about priestess of Obsidion Fortified Domicile. He leaves a contribution/tithe of 100sp.

 

Water Illusion Sea 1604

Receive note from Rislin inviting follow up meeting on Clay Illusion. Phasia will ask about for the best lead smith in the area. Torath fails to find an Issaries rune priest with rune magic to offer. Cog returns to traiing climbing with Peri. Graves visits The Bestiary and prices a monkey (1000sp) before researching the ruins of the Eurmal temple that practiced openly in Nochett City until it was raised and Eurmal worshippers banned. Strange markings may be found which indicate the god's ongoing presence. Graves follows them and discovers the ruins. Phasia seeks reasonable rooms for us for five days (5sp/night/room/2people) at the Prancing Posey.

 

Clay Illusion Sea 1604

Phasia returns to bargain with Rislin, who believes there may be another golden jresteli lion. He pays us 89Ksp for our lion, 2000sp of which must be spent in Pavis at the Lankhar Mai temple on research. If there is another he will pay 120Ksp (exclusive rights) to have it brought so he can own it. When we return to Pavis we must search for it. If it is destroyed he will pay 40Ksp for proof. We will take his gold to Anadar and get a letter of credit. Torath gives Clayton 500sp because he thinks he deserves it, for which Clayton makes him a gift of 3 Bladesharp4 potions.

 

Wind Illusion Sea 1604

Phasia waits until Anadar will see her and works on a relationship with him. He says she is not responsible for his brother's actions. She offers to take a letter back. He takes 45 minutes to write a Howler for her to take back.

 

First week post-Lion

Torath goes to an Issaries and trades a rune spell (command beast and summon animal for two points of absorpotion). He then happens on the barbarians. They do a horrible mummery of Barbarian cliches, making a mockery of Waha. Torath heckles them in Praxian until they end early. Peri uses one week to learn Spirit Speech up tp 5% at Odaria. An undead kingdom ruled over this area during chaos. Cog goes to lead smith for alternating bead decorations for horses as gift for a priestess (150sp). Tarkal wants to buy three composite bows (150sp each) to put in a preservative sack. Phasia buys one as well. Torath searches for semi-precious jade to take back for Meridian. Torath finds a butcher to work for (2sp/day) for a week.

Clayton sells our stuff. We get 40% of the value after his cut. Personal share 297sp 8c each.

9 suits of chainmail (incl. Clayton's 5pt chain)

10 broadsword

4 greatswords

2 bastard swords

4 heavy Xbo

Carmenian (7pt) plate suits size 9,10,11

We split Gems worth about 4000sp, Gold 32gp and Silver 5398sp from bandits

 

Torath sees the statue of a woman he recognizes (banged her in the forest) and find thereby her goddess shrine. He leaves an offering of food and water as he did before in the forest, feels great all of a sudden and, that evening at a tavern, he is propositioned by a woman who bangs him mercilessly and seems to look like the goddess. Phasia is summoned to see Qualik at the Issaries temple. He has been engaged by an admirer to provide training in Trade Talk for this entire week. Godfrey gets a check on Mystic Vision by peddling his skills this week. Tarkal visits the Lankar Mai Great Library (one of the largest in the world) and asks about Sankhor. Acolyte goes to a priest for a divination--turns out the knowledge just came into being. Tarkal tells a bit of the story and wonders if there is more. The priest takes notes and gives 5gp for the information. Tarkal gives three back as a donation and for that the priest admits that word of Sankhor has reached the ears of Lankar Mai. They offer to let him stay at the temple for the length of is stay in Nochettt City. Tarkal weaves a tale inserting Sankhor into Sheshnellan history, but the truth candle doesn't flicker and he puts his notes in a separate pile.

Mentioning Grebeard (was banished from Boldhome and sent to Pavis) gets a twitch from the priest. Greybeard was a member of a legendary band of Chaos fighter, but he was "wounded" to the point he was "not suitable" to live in civillized areas thereafter.

Graves recruits Trollkin for Crazy and then asks the group to wander casually through the Eurmal temple with him. Cog goes to Kigor Litor and asks to be made a Karg Son by the priestess. She brings in a Daka Fal priest to summon an ancestor to vouch. He does and she grants the request. The go through a big ceremony and Cog becomes a Rune Lord. They expect him to spend 90% of his time following the Kill the Red Bat Quest. He keeps the ancestor who vouched for him as an Allied Spirit.

Graves learns CounterMagic 2

 

End of Second Week

Touring the Eurmal Ruins. We go through a rough part of town. One of the kings during the second age formed the first open temple and a quarter of the city burned down during their first High Holy Day. Marble blocks, bronze sconces (still un-stripped unlucky to steal).

 

Enter, cool gestalt, find writing - nine (9) interchangeable pieces which form different meanings depending on how they are combined. No punctuation or capital letters. Only two ways

FYI In Shesh the words truth and lie, when flipped, are the same series of characters.

The sections say

EURMAL/OF EURMAL    DESTROYS/DIES/DEATH   AND THUS   HUMAKT/OF HUMAKT   THROUGH   THE WORLD   SOLVING/SAVING   IT IS TRUE/A LIE   THE MYSTERY

Graves begins putting them together:

And thus Eurmal saves the world

And thus Eurmal destroys the world

through solving the mystery humakt Is a lie and thus eurmal destroys the world

it is true humakt destroys and thus eurmal saves the world through the mystery

the world of eurmal humakt destroys through saving the mystery and thus it is true/false

it is a lie humakt destroys eurmal saving the world and thus the mystery

and thus eurmal destroys the world through humakt solving the mystery it is a lie

and thus it is a lie eurmal saves the world through destroy the mystery of humakt

the mystery is true/a lie through saving the world and thus humakt destroys eurmal

it is true eurmal destroys the mystery of humakt and thus saving the world

We all move into hero time. Godfrey is almost ripped apart but survives as his realty is eternally warped.

 

Future:

Next time Brandon's birthday game

Graves wants to seize any opportunity to practice Acting on the street.

cards.name: Living In Spin - Introduction
cards.content:
There are two introductions here, this one and the first chapter, “Posing
the Problem.” They serve somewhat different purposes. This one tells
how the inquiry of the book got started, offers a brief overview of its
argument, and gives some hints about where to start. Different readers
will bring quite different resources and questions to the book.
The inquiry here began by questioning what it means to be a historical
being, what it means to be part of a historical religion. Those
questions were posed for me by prior work in which biblical religion
(Christianity and rabbinic Judaism) became conspicuous in their focus
on history rather than nature or metaphysics. Start with history; nature
and philosophy come later. This book is accordingly a tentative and
cautious entry into the philosophy of historical religion.
To be a historical being means to act in the larger context of history,
and so the inquiry must needs begin with human action. I was
dissatisfied with traditional theories of action (in which an intention
causes a motion of some sort), and so turned to narrative instead.
The book does more than one thing: It is an inquiry into human action
on a non-Aristotelian basis; it is the working out of one Catholic
believer’s historical faith in philosophical terms; it is many philosophical
quarrels— at least; and it may be more.
Chapter 1 poses the problem; chapter 2 exhibits phenomena that
do not fit the Aristotelian model of intention-caused change; chapter 3
is necessary preliminaries before the inquiry can get started; chapter 4
acknowledges many philosophical debts; chapter 5 presents action on

the basis of narrative, in some of its plurality and ambiguity; chapter 6
xi

 

finishes that structure and applies it to the history of biblical religion;
chapter 7 applies the narrative structure of human action to the liturgy;
and chapter 8 deals with a few philosophical issues bypassed in the
main argument. The order developed logically as it appeared to me,
but it may not be entirely helpful for all readers.
Chapter 1 is for those who want a formal posing of the problem of
the book. Many will be able to skip it.
Those unpersuaded of the inadequacies of an Aristotelian approach
to action should probably start with chapter 2, and then proceed
as below. Chapter 2 is also an easy entry into human action on a
narrative basis.
Those who live in the Catholic sacramental system with little appetite
for technical philosophy should start with the brief remarks here
and go directly to chapter 7, coming back to chapters 5–6, and visit the
philosophical matter only if it holds any interest.
Those most interested in history should start with chapter 6.
Those most interested in narrative structure (from a philosopher’s
perspective, not literary theory, alas), should start with chapter 5.
Those interested in theology coming from physics should probably
start here also, for this chapter exhibits differences from a scientist’s
instinctive approach. Some preliminaries in chapter 3, especially sections
3.1 and 3.3, may help for those coming from naturalistic habits
of thought. Those sections show how the present inquiry goes well
beyond naturalism.
I beg the patience and forbearance of those coming from literary
theory, for there is no literary or narrative theory here. This is narrative
in the hermeneutical perspective of a retread from physics.
Those most interested in the philosophical antecedents should start
with chapter 4, which will testify against me how limited is my own
background.
Those coming from artificial intelligence, where the term distributed
ontology has an older home with a slightly different meaning,
should start with chapter 3. We belong to different disciplines (computer
science and Heideggerian phenomenology), with different discixii
plinary obligations, and so probably cannot everywhere agree, but the
disagreements may well be interesting. AI researchers have preceded
me in uncovering some of the phenomena here.
Two features of the preliminaries may be briefly summarized here,
for the many who find chapter 3 too dull (chapter 7 is where my own
heart is.). The term distributed ontology refers to the mode of being
of things that get their definition from the larger world around them,
things that cannot be conceptually isolated from the larger world. If
you can change what something is by changing something else far
from it, then it has a distributed ontology.
The term amended Dasein is taken from (or in opposition to) Heidegger.
Dasein is an ordinary German word that Heidegger borrowed
to denote the unique mode of being of human beings. He defined it as
the sort of being that has a stake in its own being; humans (and other
animals) do, rocks and spoons do not. The definition has a serious
problem: Human beings are not just the sort of beings that have an interest
in their own being and survival, they have interests in the being,
survival, opinions, and acts of other human beings — as others do in
their being also. That is the “amendment” to Heidegger’s definition,
and much of this book turns on making this correction.
The central points of the argument may be summarized briefly.
Narratability arises where there is contingency that affects someone’s
interests.
Narratability, rather than a told narrative, is what matters: We
sometimes spell out an act but more often do not, and don’t need to.
The relation between narrative and action is circular: Narrative
gives us what narrative has already shaped, not something that was
there before there was a narrative: for narrative selects from all the
motions of all the bodies in the world the motions that are part of,
relevant to, or illustrative of (because similar to) the act narrated.
What an act is can be changed by changing its circumstances: its
motions would be a different act in other circumstances. What an act

xiii

 

is depends on what you include, what you leave out, and how you
characterize what’s included.
For any motions in view, there are multiple narratives and multiple
acts: Many narratives can be told of particular motions, and so many
narratives, many acts “pass through” those motions. One true narrative
may be used to deflect attention from another, as in cover stories.
Trajectories are not the same thing as motions: A trajectory (e. g.)
solves a differential equation, and has no human meaning. A trajectory
is framed in the categories of some natural science, and is not a
narrative.
Motions are meaning-laden, and abstract from the particulars of
trajectories. It is the meaning that enables humans to discriminate
which trajectories qualify as a particular motion.
Acts can be transformed after the fact: Inasmuch as acts are defined
by larger narratives, later events, events later in those narratives,
can change what an act in view is.
Ambiguity of language entails ambiguity of action: It is language
that enables us to consider things not immediately present before us
now, and language has a selective function: it selects some things for
consideration, and omits others. That selective function is the root of
the ambiguity of language. Language both creates ambiguity (it opens
up for us many possible goals for an act) and to some extent enables
us to resolve ambiguity (it enables us to say which one was intended).
Language is a prerequisite for actor-narratable action because narrative
requires language. Non-linguistic animals exhibit only animal
behavior, not actor-narratable action. Acts of nature, of animals, and
of God are acts only by analogy to human actor-narratable action.
The ambiguity of language creates an ambiguity in the good, and
that ambiguity is one origin of sin, or one root of original sin: Language
enables an actor to discriminate between good and evil, to call
some things good and others evil, as in Genesis 2.17 and chapter 3.
We judge narratives and acts because we have a stake in them:
human beings have stakes in each other, not just in themselves (the
amended definition of Dasein, as noted above). We can ask what conxiv
tributes to human good, and despite a large liberty in answering, the
answers are open to responsible criticism. This rescues the circularity
of narrative and action from arbitrariness.
What lies beyond the motions of an act in immediate view can tell
us what this act is. When we say that what a thing is is constituted
by other things beyond it, those other things we call (here, at least)
foils. They may illuminate it by their similarity or difference (hence
borrowing the term foil from literary criticism); or they may be directly
relevant: consistent with some intentions and not others. When we are
not sure what an act is, not sure what someone was doing or intended,
we search for ontological foils that will resolve the ambiguity.
The turn to larger contexts is how we resolve the ambiguity of narratives
and acts: In the hermeneutical circle, we make sense of texts
and their parts as reciprocally related, and iterate between wholes and
parts until a stable reading is reached. As with texts, so with actions.
We draw on relevant larger contexts in order to make sense of actions.
The larger context may be history, nature, or some cosmological construct.
It is a confessional choice.
There are problems in the argument, many places where I myself
wish there were more detail or more depth, where I remain uneasy.
Fully developed, it would touch every area of the humanities, and doing
that is impossible in a single book. It is a cursory exploration at
many points, and so it is incomplete even in what it does touch. It is all
too often only a start. Yet it seemed better to publish it so that others
might improve it where I don’t see how to.
xv

cards.name: Living In Spin - Posing the Problem Ch 1
cards.content:
Human action happens, we easily think, when someone deliberates,
contemplates a goal, intends some changes to bring about that goal,
and then effects those changes, achieving the desired goal. Many acts
fit that pattern, but many more do not. People act without thinking
about what they are doing, or disagree about what someone was doing,
or decide later what they were doing earlier, or complain that someone’s
account is biased or leaves out important parts of the story. And
so we try to sort out what was going on, to get the story straight. What
happens in an act is not about the mechanics of intentions and motions
to bring about intended changes. It is about a narrative, and much
more belongs in a narrative than just an intention and some motions.
There are many questions. What it means to get a story straight is not
always obvious.
What matters in a story? And why? What must you include and
what can you leave out? What’s background and can be taken for
granted? What’s beyond background and doesn’t matter? What makes
the parts of a story fit together? How do you fit small events into larger
stories?
Looking at larger and larger contexts, what happens when you try
to fit all the events of a human life into one coherent whole? What
makes a human life be a coherent whole? What happens when you try
to get your life and other events to fit together, in one story? That may

1

 

2
change you. Both the story and the events it recounts can do things to
you: but what—and how? What can they do to you?
Philosophical thinking about human action usually begins and
ends where we began: with an act consisting of intention causing motions
to get to a goal. Superficial appearances notwithstanding, this is
not what we encounter in casual, colloquial, disputatious, legal, penitential,
casuistic, therapeutic, literary, historical, or biographical thinking
about human action. In literature and the movies, we are rarely
self-conscious in our thinking about action. Intention and cause don’t
always work as simply as the model of intention-as-cause assumes.
The main problem is that the model always already silently presupposes
some familiarity with the situation, some sense of what needs to
be included in the story. In a word, editing, and a narrative, at least
in token form, always come before we can speak of actions. When
the silent presupposition is exposed, that exposure calls for a different
philosophical approach. To say narratives are about actions is of limited
help. Paradoxically, actions will turn out to be about narratives
before narratives are about actions.
So what are narratives about? To turn the questioning about action
on its head, what does it mean to be a narratable thing, if that’s not too
strange a question? The present inquiry focuses on these questions.
The book will begin with colloquial usage, how ordinary people tell
stories, and then note some of the technical resources for the problem.
Then it will be possible to assemble the parts of an anatomy of narratable
things. Questions will arise as a consequence (though not always
with answers) and finally some applications.
Colloquial usage has become somewhat cynical. People know that
a story can be changed greatly by what is included or left out and by
how the included parts are characterized. The word for this is “spin.”
It may have originated in cynicism about politics, but it has propagated
to all of life, not just politics. We easily think we can can tell a story
without spin, in the sense that it is possible to include the right stuff
and ignore only what doesn’t matter. That is true enough, in a manner
of speaking, but it is very odd from a philosophical perspective. If

 

3
spin means choices about what to include, every story has some spin,
because every story reflects choices about what to include and what
to leave out. We have ways to criticize narratives and can sometimes
come to an agreement about whether a story has been well told or
not. It is possible to make sense of the disagreements that remain, as
we shall see eventually. Colloquial usage is onto something, and onto
something more than its cynicism would indicate. In spin, there is a
liberty in telling narratives, and though that liberty can be criticized as
responsible or not, it won’t go away.
Editing choices deal with the background, the “situation,” as we
might call it, the circumstantial facts. When a story is told economically,
the circumstances are left off-stage, not included in the narrative,
even though they do matter. Yet the background can quite transform
what’s happening on-stage, in the focus of the narrative. When we
tell a story, the narrator and the hearers make assumptions about what
is off-stage and, in particular, assume that the off-stage supports the
characterization of actions on-stage. Though it is left out, the off-stage
is essential to the on-stage.
This touches the principal contrast between the present approach
and the common approaches in Analytic philosophy,1 for Analytic philosophy
of action instinctively tries to isolate an act from its surroundings,
its off-stage. The way to recover the connections to the off-stage
is through narrative, by starting with narrative rather than with a few
elements of an “act”: deliberation, goal, choice, will, intent, etc. The
analytic instinct comes from the natural sciences, for there one seeks
cleanly to distinguish the phenomenon of interest from the rest of the
world — and rightly so: one could not function any other way in the
sciences. The sciences think in terms of systems, for that is what an
isolated portion of reality is. To view the world under the aspect of
nature is to construe the world with a systems ontology.
It is because the off-stage matters even when it is unseen that we
1 I upper-case “Analytic” because it functions as the proper name of a school of
philosophy, not as a generic adjective of method. Likewise “Continental” philosophy,
which has nothing to do with geography.

 

4

call the object of the present study a distributed ontology of human
action. What matters is distributed far beyond the immediate material
motions of the actor or what he changes in the world. Narrative is
the way to recover connections to the off-stage because it is in the
editing of narratives that we decide what to put on-stage and how to
evoke what is left out but there nevertheless. Narrative, like poetry and
unlike propositions, can evoke the off-stage, an entire world in a few
words. The present study is an ontology in this sense: We are asking
how acts be what they are, what constitutes them as what they are.
This is not a general treatise on Being as such, merely an inquiry into
how the concepts of narratable things work. It is also neither narrative
theory nor literary criticism. It’s just philosophy, and philosophy in the
service of goals in theology, as will become apparent in what follows.
Acts are about narratives before narratives are about acts because
to think of an act is always already to have at least a token of a narrative
in mind, an initial estimate of what was done. That token narrative
can be corrected—indeed, the “facts” may well demand that we do so
—but it is impossible to get started without an initial estimate. It is not
as if we survey all the circumstances and then, unprejudiced, produce
“objectively” an act that takes place in them. To survey all the circumstances
leads us to question which ones are pertinent. Hopefully, the
events themselves, the “facts,” will make a claim on us, making our
editing choices easy. That would be “objectivity”: nice, if you can get
it. Often, however, which facts are relevant depends on choices we
make, because the standards of relevance come from us. We know that
because people disagree about what counts as relevant. So our inquiry
will eventually turn to a quest for responsibility, when objectivity is
impossible and subjectivity an unsatisfying substitute for it. In a narrative
ontology of human action, editorial liberty and the claims of the
facts will always be reciprocally related.
The problem, then, is to start with the narratability of things and
explore what that narratability entails. How do narratable things work,
how do they be whatever it is that they are? The normal approach,
as noted at the beginning, is to start with the apparently basic compo

 

5
nents of the central examples of human actions. That strategy — call
it elementalism — though often tried, is not very promising. Unless
the hard cases are clearly treatable at the outset, they may never be
reached from the easy cases. It will emerge as the inquiry proceeds
that some narratable things are what we normally call human actions,
and some others are actions at least by analogy.
Let me say a little bit in a moment about the features of narratability
but first indicate something of the motive and larger context of the
inquiry, how it got started. Just to tell the story, as I began years ago to
sort out biblical criticism, biblical religion among other religions, and
the modern predicament in theology, two or three centuries of scholarship,
especially the last, have made it clear that biblical religion is a
historical religion. That leads to a question: If we are to understand
historical religion, what then does it mean to be a historical being?
What does it mean to put human lives and human actions in a historical
context? To understand historical religion (or better, just living in
history), we will have to understand how human actions fit into history,
how human actions are constituted. The goal is to understand living
in history, and the starting point is the constitution of human action.
Both are about narrative.
The structure of the argument, then, in brief preview: It is a hypothetical
inquiry. In our search beyond analytic approaches, let us place
only the most minimal limitations on what can be narrated. Assume
merely that action happens when some contingency affects someone’s
interests and is narratable. Narratives can be told in many ways, in
many styles. The act, the actor, and the events will unfold from the
narrative. What would follow from this starting point? The present inquiry
is an exploration of that question, asking what its consequences
are. More features of human action can be seen on this approach than
by starting with an act isolated from the world, typically though not
only as an intention causing a change.
New puzzles will arise, largely from the ambiguities and openness
inherent in narratability (hence the choice of the title word “spin” as
the flag-word for the inquiry). These ambiguities might seem disas

 

6
trous to those in search of certainty. It will turn out that the ambiguities
of narratability that get transferred to the ontology of human action
are not so much the problem as the condition for a solution. We live
with spin, whether we like it or not, whether we acknowledge it or not.
The task is to understand how to live well in spin. Some suggestions,
however exploratory and preliminary, can be found.
Look at some concrete features of action through the eyes of narrative:
Narratives are open and revisable, and so also is anything that
depends on narratives. If actions are about narratives as much as narratives
are about actions, then actions can, to an extent yet to be explored,
be revised. Narratives depend on the off-stage as much as the
on-stage. The off-stage is what is left out of the narrative, the “situation,”
the world that is presupposed by the narrative. When we tell a
story, we presuppose that everything off-stage supports the characterization
of events on-stage; this assumption is quite precarious, as we
shall see. The off-stage includes the future of the events in question.
An act can get its meaning from what comes after it as much as its own
time and what came before it.
An act gets its being from the narratability of its events. We don’t
always spell out narratives, nor need we. But if you ask about an act,
as if the act could get its being merely from the the natural motions of
all the particles and bodies in the world, that assumption may be met
with questions: Which ones? Which motions? Which bodies? And
Why? The answers to those questions always already presuppose at
least a token of a narrative, often not spelled out. Those tokens can
be turned into a real narrative and then examined and corrected. But
a proto-narrative is there before you can think of an act, because it is
present in the first thinking of the act. This inquiry explores what it
would mean to make that priority not just incidental but ontological.
An act gets its being from its narratability.
Four observations can be made at this point, and they will be repeated
as the inquiry unfolds:
(1) One and the same act can be narrated in multiple
(and possibly conflicting) ways;

 

7
(2) One and the same set of motions
can be fitted into many acts;
many narratives and so many acts
“pass through” somebody’s motions on-stage;
(3) What is happening on-stage
is constituted in part by what is happening off-stage;
(4) Some things about an act (but not all)
can be revised after the fact.
To these we may add the observation that if action presupposes
narratability, it also presupposes language, or language-capability, at
least in principle, in the actor: we are speaking of zÄon logikìn, Aristotle’s
phrase, usually translated as the rational animal. Better would
be the linguistic animal.
One of the core commitments that is not obvious in the brief summary
above is that acts get their being from their larger context; this
is familiar from the hermeneutical circle. Parts and wholes get their
being reciprocally from each other. The whole is ultimately the larger
context in history. The problem of larger context, at the scale of human
lives, leads to the question of coherence of a human life: what does it
take for a human life to be a coherent whole? Coherence of a human
life is another way of asking about a person’s basic life orientation
(i. e., religion).
This exploration of the concepts of action and history will, accordingly,
be a work of the philosophical theology of a historical religion.
It is emphatically not a work of literary theory: the author is
not a literature scholar. Philosophical theology has known narrative
for a long time, but in its own limited way: it occasionally notes biblical
narratives (with little interest in narrative for its own sake), and
moves quickly to philosophical concerns abstracted from biblical narratives.
The present study keeps one foot in that tradition while the
other has become self-conscious about narrative. However modest,
this is a philosopher’s perspective. It is also not a work in philosophy
of history, though it will digress more into philosophy of history than
into literary theory. History is the larger context of action, and theolo

 

8
gians tend to be more conscious of history than of literature (a purely
accidental reason, but it’s the best I can do.).
There are several immediate consequences of a narrative approach.
Narratives depend on choices that the narrator and hearers (and before
them, the actors) make. The openness of choice raises the question of
responsibility: what is the right way to choose? This will not be solved
by either objectivity or subjectivity; some other kind of responsibility
is needed. H. Richard Niebuhr’s answer was that these are confessional
commitments, and Alasdair MacIntyre unraveled how to criticize
them in what his readers have called “tradition-bound rationality.”
Eventually, in an inquiry beyond the limits of this one, narratives and
the choices in them would come up against what are called boundary
situations, unanswerable questions, or as the problem is more familiarly
known, transcendence.
With this much attention to ambiguity, uncertainty, and choice,
the question of truth will inevitably arise. To deny truth (which some
might otherwise suspect) would be performatively incoherent. We do
have ways of settling questions about what so-and-so was doing on
such-and-such an occasion, at least some of the time, even if we have
no single method for doing so. (I am not aware of any single general
method, and there are arguments against the possibility of one.) One
might say that the physical particulars of all the actions are objectively
true and useful—if we know them. That is true, I suppose, as far as it
goes, but it doesn’t go very far, and all the interesting questions arise
when appeal to material particulars alone is insufficient. The question
“which ones?” always arises, and its answers come from editing and
human interests, not from naturalistic considerations.
Let me moot here an approximation of truth in narrative. We shall
return to it in what follows. It does not solve the problem of truth
so much as restate it, though it should ward off objections that there
is no truth here, and the restatement will enable further inquiry. A
true narrative spells out correctly and fairly the interests of all interested
parties, the intended goals of the actions, the effective goals of
the actions (not necessarily the same as the intended goals), and the

 

9
real consequences of the actions, as seen thus far. One could put it another
way: a true narrative includes what matters and leaves out what
doesn’t matter. (But what does it mean to matter, for whom, and why?)
We will eventually observe that a true narrative is adjudicated in community,
and it can be revised in the light of later events. That, perhaps,
is why truth in narrative will cause such anxiety. From this beginning
will come some applications. We will be able to contrast this view of
action with the mainstream view, which simply takes an act to be a
change caused by an intention.
We will be able to make a few observations about the lives of those
who would affirm living in a historical world. In a word, biblical religion
is the sort of basic life orientation that takes human life as historical
and affirms human life in this historical world, in full view of
all its pain and suffering. We shall be interested in biblical religion in
its Christian form, which seems to me to have more perplexities than
does rabbinic Judaism.
Let me give some idea of how the problem arose in the literature.
Biblical scholarship of the last two centuries has made it amply clear
that biblical religion is a species of historical religion. The contrast
with nature religions appears in Mircea Eliade’s Cosmos and History
and again in Merold Westphal’s God, Guilt, and Death. In nature religions,
human action in some sense follows from its rootedness in
nature. In historical religions, human action is free in the sense that its
narration is not determined by nature, and human actors accordingly
have a degree of responsibility that they do not on naturalistic considerations
alone. The task posed by this literature is one of finding a philosophical
account of what it means to live in history, to be a historical
being. Martin Heidegger and Søren Kierkegaard offer a starting point
but not enough about narrative to get us very far. The philosophical resources
that did enable progress were for me accidental and contingent
(themes often to be repeated in what follows), and so the present study
inherits that contingent character. It engages only selected thinkers. I
am painfully aware of the limitations of my own reading, a product
of both contemporary fashion and accidents. The present study is ac

 

10
cordingly tentative and exploratory. Those with other resources will
be able to add more than what is here. The last needs emphasis: What
follows is an anatomy, the skeleton, if you will, of a distributed ontology
of human action, but there is no claim here that all the bones
are present and accounted for. Others, who find missing features of
this anatomy of human action, may well have good cause to revise this
account of action.
Alasdair MacIntyre, the first of the principal sources, had to deal
with narratability in the course of his own thinking about ethics. Herbert
Fingarette found in narratability the key to unraveling the puzzles
of self-deception. Hans-Georg Gadamer’s Truth and Method, though
not a general organon of the human sciences, gave us essential features
of the interpretation of narratives. Paul Ricoeur gave me more philosophical
reflection on narratability than any other single source. Other
writers appear in supporting roles.
Chapter 2 gives some colloquial and literary evidence for a distributed
ontology of human action. Chapter 3 works through a number
of essential ideas that need to be amended before they become usable.
Chapter 4 reviews the technical breakthroughs that made the present
inquiry possible. Chapter 5 outlines the basic features of human action.
Chapter 6 expands that initial sketch and focuses on the problem
of meaning and motions, with some examples from biblical history.
Chapter 7 will develop the notion of foils off-stage that transform acts
in focal view, “on-stage.”
Human action touches every area of the humanities and many beyond
the humanities, and we shall occasionally trespass into topics adjacent
to action, but for the most part, to keep this study manageable,
I shall try resolutely to stay within very limited bounds. In particular,
action must figure large in any philosophical or theological anthropology,
yet there will be no complete anthropology here. That means that
narrative, prominent in recent literature on the self, and even in some
of our sources, will not be developed into a theory of the self. Only
action is here, not a theory of the self, even though we touch the self
in questions of coherence of acts and lives (section 7.4).

 

11
The project sounds like it is a theory. It isn’t really. The distributed
ontology of human action that follows is more like a feature-list than
a theory, and doubtless not a complete one, either. It is some of what
follows if you approach human action starting from its narratability
rather than from a theory about intentions causing changes.

Law Enforcement systems, LLC

PO BOX 1348

Long Island City, NY 11101-0348

 

RE violation T1105675749

 

To whom it may concern,

 

We moved in March from Berkeley to Richmond and attempted to change our address three times via the FasTrak website. It still showed our old address when I spoke to Luctricia (badge #9163) on October 18th, 2011. I let her know that we had a mail theft issue which got resolved but created a mail forwarding issue when we moved. That finally got resolved recently, and October 18th we received your collections notice for $75, if paid by Oct 17th. Luctricia was very helpful, updated our information on her end, and let us know that she would send me an account profile that we might send on to you to document that we had a FasTrak account at the time of violation T1105675749. She assured me that upon seeing it you would remove the toll evasion notice from our record. Regarding three items that might cause confusion, at the time of the violation our vehicle had not been converted from its Oregon registration/plate (596DCA) to California (6RER906). In addition, I displayed our Fastrak as usual while going through the toll plaza only to find out later that it didn't work due to a mechanical failure of some kind. I investigated and FasTrak replaced it, so that we were using it again by June 15th, never knowing that a fine had been attached. Finally, the FasTrak account is in my wife, Lisa's, name but you will see that the addresses on the account and on the citation are identical. Thanks to Luctricia, all our information is now up-to-date.

Please confirm receipt of this letter and its attached account profile, and the removal of the toll evasion listed as violation T1105675749 from the record.

Sincerely,

Brandon and Lisa Williamscraig

[[Don McClure|Don]], [[Ted Greer|Torath]], [[Sivan Marcus|Clayton]] and then [[Sivan Marcus|Godfrey]], [[Lisa WilliamsCraig|Peri]], [[Joanie Albee-Good|Phasia]], [[Joe Good|Cog]], [[Brandon WilliamsCraig|Graves]], [[Tim Schlaak|Tarkal]].

 

{{RQ DMc group treasury|closed}}

 

God time

 

Cog sees (and thereby co-creates) a pitched battle

Graves decides it is a mummers' show and ritual recreation of an historical battle and assumes the guise of one of the winning side's warriors, announcing that it is all over, with victory to Us, and declaring a feast. They slap Graves on the back and mill around, but at a distance undead/demons are chasing down and carving up humans (native Esrolians from a previous age) and the things they are carrying are not practical items. Graves rallies the actors and the party to charge the bad guys who melt away but are replaced by an equal number of non-fleeing bad guys. Phasia orates such that all the humans run with us back toward the temple, and Graves pulls a turkey out of his bag, throwing it at the demons and demanding that they not touch the Turkeys of Goodness which grant immmortality. The turkeys multiply for every bad guy and continue to do so such that no bad guys can do anything but continue eating without being able to stop. Cog holds the line against demons, crushing one. Torath explodes one's head with an arrow between the eyes. Phasia lightwalls to protect the humans. Peri makes arrow skewers of three demons closest to the incoming people. Graves causes the heads of the dead to pop off, grabs two and, popping his own off, juggles three, one of which Peri shoots for good measure. Graves puts the wrong one back on his neck, before realizing his error and swapping back to his own.

 

Torath asks for guidance and a guy crawls up, saying: "Nontraya the Taker and waster attacked and is trying to take Ernalda at he temple of Esry," and dies. He then rises once more says "and you must help her!" before dying again. Torath sees a spire in the distance and pauses to make sure there are no demons disguised as humans, spots one doing so, and slits its throat. Graves becomes invisible and the group goes forth, tracking and sneaking. Graves becomes visible to track, hide in cover, and move silently with everybody else.

 

Travel montage. Arrive at the spire. Also a farmhouse. Woman standing out the side looking at spire. Late 20's early 30's priestess of Ernalda. Graves offers to help and attempts seduction. She slaps him, knocking off his head. He is sad. Enfangin (the woman) is on a hero quest to be Ernalda. She needs to die and be carried in a funeral procession. Nontraya (rides a great horned wolf) will send more undead talokens to see that she is in fact dead, give up, and leave the land, at which point she will need to come back to life. Her resurrection assistant has got lost. We discuss various costs and benefits of working together, since her hero quest is wobbly, due at least in part to our cunning interventions hereabouts. Graves imbues William with size and strength to make him a full sized mount (like the horned wolf) so the possibility of impersonation exists. Anything that gets Nontraya out of these lands is a WIN.

 

Graves will Find The Way to the missing resurrection companion, and invites Tarkal. Everyone else will defend the area until we get back. Traps and ambushes are set. Graves mounts William and goes with Tarkal back towards the city, only to find incredibly vicious but well sated demons sleeping in a circle around a very nervous guy. Following our instructions to sneak toward us he steps on and breaks a stick, waking the demons, who attack him. Graves makes him invisible, and shoots demons, while Tarkal turns into a bladesharped whirling instrument of death. Turns out the intended resurrection companion died saving this guy. He mistakes Graves (vis a vie William) for Nontraya and asks for a gold piece as a test. Given. Graves asks for it back now that the issue is settled. Battle ensues. Graves attempts to get him to calm down by only parrying but Torath spear whacks him to the ground, thereby defeating him on the hero plane (and getting his final chip) after which the hapless dude fades away!

 

We go back and discuss the various ways to help Enfangin finish her hero quest successfully so all clerics in the Nochett City environs may have their resurrection spells restored for the coming year! After MUCH understandable reluctance, Peri agrees to cast and thereby loose her one resurrection spell, since Cog would have to D.I. to achieve the same effect, thereby bringing his deity into her hero quest which would be problematic. In return Peri insists that Enfangin guarantee Trolls will be resurrected for a year and a day anyway. Enfangin agrees.

 

We will be her bearers, following the river to where Esry is. She lies down on the bed and dies. We carry her. Procession people begin to join us. After a while Graves notices humans dressed as demons among the other real demons lurking nearby. Two demons and one of the disguised human come down to look at our procession. The human in demon form suggests burning her just to be sure. Graves weeps hugely (and Acts successfully). Torath threatens the guy not to desecrate the body and Peri sais that, as a Daka Fal, she must insist that burning not happen because her ancestors would be unable to encounter her in her pure form.  The guy says, "Daka  Fal, huh?", nods with satisfaction, and departs. Tarkal makes a spot hidden and sees nothing weird. We experience misgivings.

 

Graves dumps her body of the table when we are alone, makes her invisible, and takes her place. Torath takes over and gently puts her body aside. Cog is guarding Graves. Peri fakes resurrecting Graves who gasps theatrically and comes back to life. Suddenly something odd happens with the wand, but we're not sure what. We all look at it and then get back to business. Peri fades back and surreptitiously "resurrects the annoying chick." Cog does something all concealy. The aforementioned human disguised as a demon appears to Cancel Magic vs Resurrection. Peri has Loiosh summon an ancestor, his wife Rawtsa, and attack DemonHuman. Four scimitar wiedling henchmen appear to attack. Peri enters a contest of wills with the Lunar? sorceror while Graves continues to pretend to be dead. Graves stands up to Lie about the success of Peri's resurrection, re-rolls twice to hit the Pow v Pow roll. The sorceror says "It is broken", and breaks a small figurine of Ernalda before vaporizing with his henchmen. Ernalda priestess Enfangin wakes up. We all fade back into the temple of Ernalda.

 

Benefits from the Hero Quest. All checks skills or pow are auto. Peri now may buy Resurrection rune spells for two instead of three points. When Graves buys Detach Limb, he may pray on wild day to bring back any number of points. Phasia may cast light walls at two instead of four points. Torath can use hide in cover against pow/#people to hide a bunch of people. Cog's Crush is 10% higher chance.

 

Three or four guards are dispatching the last of some spy/assassins. Some initiates are dead. Weapons are levelled at us but we are given bona fides by Enfangin and all is well. The two other guys in her circle have poisoned arrows in them. The temple authorities take over and we are escorted to an area of isolation with food and wine while they talk things over. A woman walks in and sits to give "greetings" in Trade Talk. What were we doing in their major annual hero quest? We are two days outside Nochett City on the way to the megalopolis necropolis. Trolls may resurrect for a year and a day. Peri is owed big too and may choose between 2000gp cash or book to read (the Hephenoros Text - written in the Second Age - outlining many of the rules for Hero Questing). We will take the night to discuss and decide. Esry has 8 temples (Temple of Treasures allows worship of any god). Even Eurmal? Yes but within the next five days. This temple is with man others within a five mile diameter called The Sacred Ring (4 miniature armies guard + the villages around). Peri opts for cash and they bring us chests of silver to be transferred into gold whenever we like. 

 

Phasia will stay at temple of Esry 12 weeks and train Trade talk to 90%. Isaries looks down and smiles. Also gives 10% in ceremony. After the invocations, Phasia feels a harmony with Issaries, the world, and her (now Rune Priest) magic returns upon praying. Her Charisma goes up by 1. Allied Spirit Int12 and Pow14 put in her staff.

Tarkal trains his Dex up a point.

Many people from this area are headed North towards the border.

Graves performs on the street for 8 weeks up to 75% Acting, and then pays for professional training by _________ (?) 1,600/wk (4800sp) up to 90% by week 11. Then he goes to the Temple of Treasures alone, is charged 1 silver penny but asked for a 4000sp deposit to be returned if there is no damage. Don flips a coin and Eurmal says no for this season. (Eurmal info in Trickster Cult in Runequest Companion or Pavis Pack). Peri purchases iron plate (5700sp). Cog buys 15 pigs to give to Phasia. Trains strength and DispelMgc4 and Healing6.

Stay two more weeks.

 

Torath finds Found Child temple at Temple of Riches and prays for one week. Second week seeks temple by describing Nochett City shrine etc. Green Daughter (GD) plants and people defending themselves against evil, and fought and died fighting against dog men killed in the Secnd Age in the mountains east of here. (We fought them skiing on the way here.) Third week spent praying to Green Daughter for guidance at shrine - vision one night: village looks like to the north feels like Sartar near place with white walls w people there praying for salvation from governor of town. Leaves the next day. The border is fully militarized and the Esrolians are trying to wall off the whole country. He promises to kill Lunars and come back. At border welcomed by Lunars. Introduced to cultural attache who gives the usual schpiel. Pays 100L to kill a horse and hands over battle axe and plate armor in exchange for paper of ownership. Goes on to White Wall, which is part of the Lunar Empire but does not recognize that yet (under siege). Travels on the main road for a week, which turns out to be incredibly safe. Feels right compared to the dream. Communes and fasts. Next day tracks to farming village of 8-9 houses off the road. Talk to children at edge of town in Sartarite, and then picks a farm. There IS a huge problem. Governor is taxing unfairly and randomly and taking daughters. Borrows axe and heads for nicest house. Takes "governor" to see his horse, kills same by cutting off head, presents paper receipt to make Lunar approval (of all his actions) entirely clear. Discusses various wrongs done peasants and threatens demise should same continue. Reports to peasants. Returns axe. Departs.

 

Entire party waits an entire additional season in Nochett City environs so Graves can have another shot at Rune status. Graves binds three more allied spirits with Peri's help and returns to the temple. Brandon calls heads on five coin flips in a row, all of which come up tails, before quitting with a loss from 21 Pow down to 16. Lisa proposes a mercy intervention and the party supports Graves in going off to the temple ruins for an impromptu restoration of its power and One More Try. Graves has posters made trumpetting Disturbed Graves and His War Goat Performing Unnatural Axe, hires urchins to talk it up, and buys much beer to offer for free for those interested. A few foreign sailors who don't know better are convinced, drink a lot of the beer, unwittingly take part in the Eurmal Restoration Ceremony and Brandon finally rolls an 08 to make the ceremony a success and become a Rune Priest.

cards.name: FOR CHILDREN’S CLASS
cards.content:
3 Period Lesson  (basic mind process)

 

“This is….”

“Show me…”

“What is….”

 

When having demonstrated ---“You will feel it here and here”---touching, tracing on body; adjusting body when needed to correct sensation.

 

Practice in 2 groups; change sides; start from  the opposite direction, etc.  Then with all sitting in a line to watch demonstrate again calling attention to a specific point.

 

(For 2nd Plane children) “A question to ask yourself.  Am I doing this the best that I can?  not the best that Clothilda  can or that Daren can, but the best that I can , right now?”

 

At appropriate time:  “Aren’t we lucky (blessed, glad, happy)

to have bodies that can do so many things.”

 

Consider:  Start with standing in circle calling each child’s name for them to sit-without-using-hands.

 

 (Sitting on heels, hand clap, bowing are very important – try asking if they can feel their heels, or where their eyes go when they bow, or if the clap sounds loud or soft to them)

 

Ritualize call to circle

 

Try:  5 min. verbal instruction, 10 min demos, 30 min. practice, 15 min free play  (run, jump, obstacle course).

Stand facing partner arms at sides.  Roll front to front, back to back while standing.

 

Corny Dog  (roll child in rug, put condiments on and eat him up)

 

Pease Porridge Hot --- one doesn’t get to do a backward roll until the end of the 2nd verse.

 

Yd. stick or long pole – walk the length heel/toe and back as closely as you can before jumping over and backward, then zigzag two feet together.

cards.name: MNv PxPx TRS Elementary
cards.content:
Make sure the mats are down and the water and cups are ready before going to get the kids at 4.

 

Coming to the dojo space from the play yard, the kids bring their energy down while removing their shoes in the foyer outside the dojo.

The shoes are placed neatly against the wall in the foyer before bowing at the door and entering the dojo one at a time.

 

Rather than running wild at first, each will go from the door to the bowing line where an adult waits, being sent back if they have trouble holding their center. When all are assembled share 2 bows and 4 claps to get everyone acting in concert, followed by "I will use aikido to help and not to hurt."

 

Brief stretching: focus on whole body/system moving together at once, rather than on isolations.

You!  Point   Collapse

You!  Point   Backroll "I'm back!"

Leading to backward and then forward ukemi, standing with heels and then toes at the edge of the mats. If space is hard to come by, count off into 1s and 2s so alternating bodies roll at different times.

 

Helicopter and bio break

 

Tai Sabaki-based Drills:

Use the three part learning strategy of Observation, Demonstration, and Inquiry: This is ___.  Show me ___. What is ___?

Example:  Say and show "This is I'm Listening, or Tenkan".  Go around asking "Please show me I'm Listening, or Tenkan". Return later to each child to ask "What is I'm Listening, or Tenkan?" and give feedback/encouragement.

 

Assign partners, so each child with the most difficulty focusing has a partner who is more self-controlled, rather than allowing them to choose. Add one or (at most) two new drill(s) each week.

{{MNv Drills+Basic Movements|closed}}

Helicopter and bio break

 

If there is time repeat anything that needed a second going over.

Circle

Questions?

Bow out.

Put shoes on while behaving moderately, as there are others nearby with work in progress.

Return kids to classrooms, walking in a line between an adult leading and an adult following.
