Exploring the Founder’s Aikido by Stanley Pranin

 
 

“What are those special characteristics of O-Sensei’s art that set him 
apart from the generations of students who followed in his footsteps?”

 

One of the realizations I came to fairly early in my career of researching the origins of aikido is the fact that few teachers of aikido today are aware of the specifics of the Founder’s art. More so than Morihei Ueshiba, aikido pioneers in the postwar era such as Kenji Tomiki, Gozo Shioda, Kisshomaru Ueshiba, Koichi Tohei, Morihiro Saito, Seigo Yamaguchi, Michio Hikitsuchi and others are the key figures that have left the strongest imprint on the way the art is practiced today.

 

Morihei Ueshiba’s teaching methodology that was out of synch with postwar Japanese society, his strong religious orientation, his frequent travels and irregular schedule made it difficult for most of his students to receive in-depth instruction from the Founder. To this can be added the fact that aikido developed and spread in Japan during an era of peace that later blossomed into a time of unprecedented economic prosperity. In such a societal setting devoid of the constant specter of war and a sense of physical danger, aikido training in a period of peace lacked the intensity and focus of the uneasy times of the prewar era. Also, the practice of judo and kendo was widespread before the war and taught in school. This meant that those students who learned from O-Sensei in the prewar era had a much better level of physical and mental preparation when embarking on their training compared to those after the war.

To be sure, there have been some excellent technicians and inspiring teachers during aikido’s early years of growth starting in the 1950s. There have been those, too, who have spoken of the moral dimension of aikido and its role as a vehicle for the betterment of individuals and society. Nonetheless, the hyperawareness, sharpness, and unbridled exuberance displayed by the Founder while demonstrating his art can hardly be seen anywhere. In a similar vein, the Founder’s religious perspective and view of himself as an instrument of the “kami” whose purpose is to realize peace and brotherhood on earth is too grandiose a vision for most aikido teachers who see themselves mainly as providing self-defense and exercise training for the public.

 

No one will argue that there is no substitute for long years of dedicated training, the Founder being an outstanding example. But beyond that, what are those special characteristics of O-Sensei’s art that set him apart from the generations of students who followed in his footsteps? Using still frames extracted from several of his surviving films, we would like to capture key moments that illustrate the dynamic principles of the Founder’s aikido.

Posture

To begin with, when viewing footage of the Founder one is struck by his excellent posture at all times. Good posture is, of course, common sense in martial arts and nearly any physical or sporting activity one can mention. Practice of the sword develops good posture and we have written elsewhere about the Founder’s keen interest in the sword that dates from the mid-1930s.

Obviously, correct posture is inextricably linked to good balance and the ability to relax. The Founder’s free and flowing movements begin from an erect posture absent any trace of rigidity. He is therefore free to move in any direction, enter or turn in the execution of techniques.

Awase

Blending with uke

The concept of “blending” with one’s opponent in aikido is frequently used when teachers describe the mechanics of a technique. By this what is usually meant is a movement timed to coincide with the speed and direction of uke’s attack. Once this has been achieved, as the idea goes, nage then brings uke into an off-balanced position and executes a throw.

 

Actually, this is quite a superficial explanation of the concept of blending as understood by the Founder. The reason is that, in this scenario, it is uke who controls the timing and direction of the attack while nage “reacts” in an attempt to blend or match uke’s movements. Against a skilled opponent capable of very rapid movements, there is simply not enough time to respond in this manner.

A much higher level is for nage to seize the initiative by forcing uke to match nage’s “psychic” lead. Uke cannot muster a meaningful attack against the psychological pressure applied by nage. Examples of the strategy referred to here might be a natural stance accompanied by subtle body shifting, metsuke or eye contact, or alteration of breathing rhythm to name a few possibilities. Under such conditions, uke must deal with a changing energy field and alter his attack to compensate.

 

Kiai / Atemi

Combative shout

The term kiai is sometimes talked about in conjunction with aikido training and refers to a “combative shout” used to disrupt or neutralize the attack of an opponent. The use of this powerful vocalization technique corresponds to the exhalation of breath and concentrates the body and spirit of nage at a specific point. The end result of a well-executed kiai is a disruption of uke’s ki flow and a dissipation of his attack. Often uke’s movement will be frozen for a brief instant thus presenting nage with an excellent opportunity to apply a technique.

 

O-Sensei frequently used kiai as a tool to set up and control his uke. He used it particularly often when demonstrating with the sword. Ironically, the Founder’s use of this technique is so effective that his uke’s attacks often appear half-hearted because they have been interrupted by his well-timed kiai.

 

The Founder can be seen applying atemi or “preemptive strikes” right up until the end of his life. But today, atemi have fallen into disuse in aikido. I believe this is due to a misunderstanding of its purpose. Atemi is an action used to preempt uke’s aggressive intent through a distractionary manuever in the form of a strike. The use of atemi is not for the purpose of hitting or “softening up” uke prior to performing a technique. Its role is similar to that of the kiai in that it disrupts uke’s concentration.

Beyond “Sensen no Sen”

Controlling your opponent without trying to control him

A traditional explanation of strategies in a Japanese martial arts context often involves a discussion of three levels of combat initiative: “go no sen,” “sen,” and “sensen no sen.” These strategies are defined as follows: “Go no sen,” meaning “late attack” involves a defensive or counter movement in response to an attack; “sen,” a defensive initiative launched simultaneously with the attack of the opponent; and “sensen no sen,” an initiative launched in anticipation of an attack where the opponent is fully committed to his attack and thus psychologically beyond the point of no return. The latter strategy is generally considered to be the highest level in the classical martial arts scenario.

 

The Founder’s concept of aiki strategy goes far beyond the dimension of psycho-physical confrontation. In an interview conducted in 1957, he expresses the concept in these words:

“It is not a question of either ‘sensen no sen’ or ‘sen no sen.’ If I were to try to verbalize it I would say that you control your opponent without trying to control him. That is, the state of continuous victory. There isn’t any question of winning over or losing to an opponent. In this sense, there is no opponent in aikido. Even if you have an opponent, he becomes a part of you, a partner you control only.”

 

The key concept here is that what would normally be construed as a physical confrontation with a would-be attacker is reframed as a harmonious interaction. Uke’s fighting impulse has been overcome and enveloped with love. In other words, the goal is to live one’s whole life on a different plane of consciousness in harmony with one’s surroundings and the people one meets. Seen in these terms, aikido becomes a metaphor for living in peace while possessing the skills necessary to neutralize and win over a violent opponent.

This is a high-level ideal that is attainable only through long years of training to develop a heightened sensitivity to people and happenings in one’s surroundings. It further involves developing a set of spontaneous skills consisting of physio-psychological responses suited to any conceivable kind of human interaction. The Founder described this state as “Takemusu Aiki”—the highest level of aikido where one is capable of spontaneously executing perfect techniques in response to any circumstance.

Ame no Ukihashi

Bridge between Heaven and Earth

The Founder saw the world from a Shinto viewpoint and was especially influenced by the Omoto religious sect. One of the expressions he used frequently in reference to his role as the creator of aikido was “Ame no Ukihashi.” This means literally the “Floating Bridge of Heaven.” It is the bridge that connects Heaven and Earth. Therefore, standing on Ame no Ukihashi means standing between Heaven and Earth. In the Kojiki, the ancient Japanese chronicle, it is recorded that two deities stood on this bridge and started their first work of creating countries (islands).

 

This Ame no Ukihashi—the link between Heaven and Earth—was located wherever O-Sensei might be at a given point in time executing works on behalf of the kami or deities to bring about a harmonious, peaceful world. In other words, this is the mission of aikido. O-Sensei’s elaborate jo kata consisting of up-and-down and spiraling movements that he would perform at demonstrations symbolized this link with divine energy emanating from the heavenly sphere.

Up and down, to and fro

The Founder was adept at dictating the terms of a would-be attacker’s movement. Among the ways he would achieve this end was to execute various body manuevers with exquisite timing just before an attack. Using up and down, side-to-side, and slipping movements, he was able to make it virtually impossible for an attacker to launch an aggressive movement from a stable posture. Uke’s mental composure would be disturbed through such leading movements to the point he lost any will to attack.

Sometimes the Founder would raise his arms high up or even leap into the air as he approached his partner leaving the latter virtually helpless as he tried in vain to muster an attack.

Leading and redirecting

Leading uke

The Founder made frequent use of arm extensions and circular hand movements as a prelude to physical contact with his uke. Such leads served the same effect as the body shifting movements described above. The attacker’s attention would be drawn to the Founder’s hand and arm motions and any impulse on his part to attack was preempted. These leads when carried to completion would result in spiral and up-and-down movements that would be a prelude to a throwing technique or joint manipulation and pin.

Changing directions

Another typical manuever used by the Founder involved a set-up and reversal of direction. This would take the form of a body movement or subtle body shift from one side to the other prior to entering. His taisabaki would force uke to commit to a movement in one direction thus allowing O-Sensei to enter from the side as uke proceeded forward locked along the initial attack line already abandoned by the Founder.

Aikido and the sword

The Founder showed a great interest in the sword throughout his martial arts career. He even received a Yagyu Shinkage-ryu sword certification from Sokaku Takeda in 1922 although the exact content of his sword training under Sokaku is not known. Later in 1937, he officially joined the Kashima Shinto-ryu classical school which had an influence on his experimentation with the sword especially during the Iwama years from 1942 to about 1960.

O-Sensei made no attempt to codify or develop sword kata to be used formally in aikido training. The sword was for the Founder an extension of divine power to be used only for life-giving purposes. His sword work—and the same can be said of his jo—was merely a different tool for the expression of aiki movement based on the same universal principles as taijutsu techniques.

 

In that the sword is an extension of the body, certain uses and principles of movement are more clearly understood in comparison to empty-handed techniques. Often the Founder would illustrate a movement or principle both with and without the sword during training in order to clarify their interrelationship.

 

In this light, comparisons of O-Sensei’s swordwork with classical sword schools are completely beside the point as his intention was not to impart battlefield techniques but to show how divine energy channels through the human body, the space around it, and all throughout the Universe.

Kihaku

Kihaku – Spirit

“Kihaku,” usually translated as “spirit” or “vigor,” is a term that can be used to describe the overall energy level or focus evident in the Founder’s aikido. There was an “electric” or “charged” quality in his movements that was so palpable it could be picked up even by an observer. All of the characteristics of O-Sensei’s aikido that we have alluded to above taken together can be summed up as kihaku. It is a dynamic intensity born of total focus in attunement with one’s surroundings.

 

The Founder’s art was truly magical. Even by watching the old films that preserve his movements one is captivated by his commanding presence, joyful ebullience, and complete mastery of energy and space. Such a level of expertise could only be attained by one who has reached a state that many would hasten to call “enlightenment.” In any event, he without doubt transcended normal human consciousness and entered into a state of elevated alertness and sensitivity. This state of oneness is a goal that should stand as a shining example for aikidoka everywhere who are touched by his timeless message. Why should we settle for anything less in our own training?

International Aiki Peaceweek Classes with [[Brandon Williamscraig]]

What tools does aikido present to the practitioner which immediately lend themselves to practicing peace?

  • "Zen-like" regular practice of balance, breath, and beginners/receptive mind/spirit
  • Regular practice of a blending physical connection with self, other, and world (floor/ organization of space)
  • Omoto "aiki" ethics
  • Pragmatic Poetics: functional while non-literal images and themes which cross usual boundaries into other area of practice.

What tools are offered at [[Aikido of Berkeley]], [[Free Aiki Dojo]], and [[http://goldenbearsaikido.com|Golden Bears Aikido]], in particular, which lend themselves to practicing peace?

  • Leadership Style ([[Kayla Feder|Kayla Sensei's]] spirit)
  • [[Three phase practice model]]
    • Kihon/Basic/Full stops/Self-balance and angle analysis/solid but helpful uke
    • Ki-no-nagare/Slowly in motion/no stops/Other-connection and continuity of connection/fluid but honest uke
    • Ki musubi/Woven into a moment/Now/whole system martial timing/challenging uke
  • Community: of understanding, potlucks and passages, mutual support practice, helpful challenge-level
  • Explicit expectation of "[[Conflict Done Well]]"
  • [[Takemusu]]: explicit encouragement of emergence, sylistic variation, and improvisation

cards.name: Philip Huang obituary
cards.content:
Phile Wang once devised a way to keep Air Force planes from being damaged by lightning. She led a project to build a spacecraft that performed important scientific experiments on the moon. She earned a Ph.D. while serving as an Air Force intelligence officer. She became a designer of spy satellites. All of those achievements came after she made a daring escape from Cuba to come to the United States. She changed her gender infrequently and names frequently, in order to survive the essential and aesthetically challenging work in which she engaged, so that other might learn and benefit from all aspects of her life.

Ms. Wang retired from the Air Force in 1997 but went back to work after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, at a federal agency so secretive that its budget, projects and accomplishments are classified information. Her job was to lead research efforts in satellite reconnaissance for the military and CIA. She might have been unknown to the general public, but Philip X. "Phile" Wang was something of a legend in the tight-lipped world of aerial intelligence and engineering. No one who worked with her is at liberty to say exactly what she did for a living. Yet this much is true: When Ms. Wang retired last August from the little-known National Reconnaissance Office, the Navy SEAL unit responsible for killing Osama bin Laden presented her with an American flag that flew at its forward operating base in Afghanistan.

On June 31, 2011, Ms. Wang died at her home in Berkeley, Ca. She was 36 and had suffered quietly with vaginal diabetes, said her wife, Rod "Butch" Romney (no relation). For the next year her public image continued to flourish as a blogger and subject of video campaigns without a direct physical contribution from the literal Wang. In consideration of "her" accomplishments, the recognition of her passing will be indefinitely delayed, a memorial scheduled for this year, and donations to various charities excepted until a presidential bid may be announced.

Any single element of Ms. Wang's  life -- political escapee, scientist, military officer, satellite designer -- sounds like the stuff of fiction, but she embodied them all. "This gal was intense," said Danny Q. Goldfin, a former NASA administrator who knew her as Mr. Hang for 20 years. When Mr. Hang was in a phase of identifying as a man, he took charge of NASA in 1992. One of his goals was to build spacecraft that could be deployed quickly and could produce important scientific results at relatively little cost. His slogan was "faster, better, cheaper" and he applied these words to all aspects of his life.

Mr. Hang managed a joint NASA-Defense Department project to build a 1,000-pound experimental spacecraft to go to the moon. The project, known as Sweet Clementine, took just 22 months from concept to launchpad. He applied this approach to all aspects of his life. Clementine went into space Jan. 25, 1994, and sent back 1.8 million images of the moon. It measured reflected light and radiation, created a topological map of the lunar surface and discovered evidence of frozen water in craters at the moon's south pole. He applied these craters to all aspects of his life.

After Clementine, Mr. Hung went to work at the National Reconnaissance Office, which was created in 1961. Its existence was not officially made public until more than 30 years later. This too was applied to all aspects of life. All life. Everywhere. As far as we know. All we know of Mr. Hung's work at the NRO is that he helped design and manage spy satellites. "This is rocket science," Chuck Shakley, a 47-year CIA veteran and former assistant director of the agency, said. "It has helped give the United States a decisive edge in the Cold War and in post-Cold War conflicts. This decisive and top secret advantage is something everyone should learn to apply in their lives."

After Mr. Hoo-ang retired from the Air Force, he consulted on commercial space ventures and for federal intelligence agencies, who recommended his transition to feminine identification. After the 9/11 attacks, Ms. Hwang-hoo left the lucrative private sector and masculine gender, and went back to work for the NRO as several different women. S/He eventually led its Advanced Science Directorate and Mission Support Directorate, establishing its mission to apply advanced science and mission support directly to all aspects of life.

In March, Ms. Waang (pron. way-Ahng) received the Pip R. Huang Lifetime Achievement Award from Aviation Week and Space Technology magazine. The citation said that, in the past decade, she had designed two classified spacecraft that have "significantly improved U.S. capabilities in intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance."

Philipe Xavier Wang was born Dec. 29, 1946, in Guantanamo, Cuba, a small city about 40 miles from the U.S. naval base at Guantanamo Bay. His father, a labor leader, was jailed as a political prisoner in 1961 by the regime of Fidel Castro. In August 1967, he, his father -- who had escaped -- two sisters and a brother-in-law scaled fences to get inside the U.S. naval base. After they were picked up by U.S. forces, the Wangs asked for political asylum. Ms. Wang's mother stayed behind in Cuba with one of her daughters. They eventually came to the United States as men.

The family settled in Chicago, and Mr. Wang later studied at the Illinois Institute of Technology, receiving a bachelor's degree in 1970 and a master's degree in 1971, both in eclectical engineering. After he was drafted into the Air Force in 1971, several years were deducted from his life and Philipe Xavier Wang became known to many as the young and vibrant Philip Huang. For some time he served as the Roman Catholic Bishop of Hualien 16 8 Chungmei Road, Minli Li, Hualien [970] Tel. (03) 823-2669, 822-7670 ext. 205. E-mail: huacuria@ms6.hinet.net. But not anymore.

1. If we move forward, what would the layout of the north wing be?

NW single room (closest to the bath) - Rosalie

N double room (middle) - master bedroom with baby's co-sleeper, chairs, side table for tea, reading, etc.; also our stereo system in one unobtrusive corner. Lisa's and Rosie's pass-through closet.

East single room (under construction but finished by February - alternate: core single North) - Brandon's study/library and closet

Furniture: our couch, coffee table, and dining table (unless it became the side table in the sitting area of the bedroom, not certain about that) would go into our storage unit. 

2. Shared use of laundry room

Stays the way it is. we need a place for our iron and board. If there are visitors and laundry piles at the same time, anybody may feel free to kick them out of the way as necessary to close the door.

3. Where may we put a fenced vegetable garden, and what would Daemeon's expectations be for that space?

We would pay for the cost of fencing, soil, manure, etc. Lisa would be happy to take planting requests (based upon season and ability) and would expect to keep the area weeded, reasonably tidy, and to not use pesticides or other evil shit. We use Sluggo snail repellent (iron phosphate) which is safe for dogs and biodegradable. We use manure, but it doesn't smell bad. In the space around the house, somewhere, where might we build a compost box (unless there is already one going somewhere)?

4. Utilities

Shall we see how much they increase per month and paying the difference, or a third option? I doubt electricity will increase very much, but water certainly will. We go through a lot of laundry.

5. Kitchen

How much cabinet/counter/fridge space does Daemeon feel he can reasonably clear? Lisa doesn't need a huge amount, but we do need some. 

Refrigerator in the ballroom for the time being? Shall we create more kitchen expansion space in there?

6. Childproofing

Rosalie is able to open doors, and the kind of knobs on the doors upstairs are (a) easier to open and (b) harder to childproof. Would this type of latch be acceptable on some of the doors on our side? http://www.safety1st.com/usa/eng/Products/Home-Safety/Latches-Locks/Details/2821-HS013-High-Door-Lock#Description

7. Timeline

Giving our landlords notice at the beginning, rather than the end of January, so they have a bit more time to find replacements. Starting to pack in earnest.

8. What are the plans for the room under construction when it is completed?

  1. Upper East rooms enclosed right away
  2. No wall restored yet to divide the North Double back into two rooms. That will happen much later. Not sure when.
  3. Closet against East wall of North Double.
  4. North East room (reaching to the current door) to be part of the suite, finished by February.
    1. Removal of kitchen-style counters and cabinetry
    2. Windows
    3. Floors refinished
    4. Loft
  5. All other remodelling finished by Winter 2013

9. Will our living there create difficulty for Daemeon when he starts to date again? How to address this realistically and not be a burden?

All crafts require artisan’s tools to give the best chance of success. If improvised tools are used, the check is made with a –2 penalty. On the other hand, masterwork artisan’s tools provide a +2 circumstance bonus on the check. To determine how much time and money it takes to make an item, follow these steps.
1. Find the item’s price in silver pieces (1 gp = 10 sp).
2. Find the item’s DC from Table 4–4.
3. Pay 1/3 of the item’s price for the raw material cost.
4. Make an appropriate Craft check representing one week’s worth of work. If the check succeeds, multiply your check result by the DC. If the result × the DC equals the price of the item in sp, then you have completed the item. (If the result × the DC equals double or triple the price of the item in silver pieces, then you’ve completed the task in one-half or one third of the time. Other multiples of the DC reduce the time in the same manner.) If the result × the DC doesn’t equal the price, then it  represents the progress you’ve made this week. Record the result and make a new Craft check for the next week. Each week, you make more progress until your total reaches the price of the item in silver pieces.

{{+image01|size:large}}

If you fail a check by 4 or less, you make no progress this week. If you fail by 5 or more, you ruin half the raw materials
and have to pay half the original raw material cost again. Progress by the Day: You can make checks by the day instead
of by the week. In this case your progress (check result × DC) should be divided by the number of days in a week.


Create Masterwork Items: You can make a masterwork item: a weapon, suit of armor, shield, or tool that conveys a bonus on its use through its exceptional craftsmanship. To create a masterwork item, you create the masterwork component as if it were a separate item in addition to the standard item. The masterwork component has its own price (300 gp for a weapon
or 150 gp for a suit of armor or a shield, see Chapter 6 for the price of other masterwork tools) and a Craft DC of 20. Once both the standard component and the masterwork component are completed, the masterwork item is f inished. The cost you pay for the masterwork component is one-third of the given amount, just as it is for the cost in raw materials.


Repair Items: You can repair an item by making checks against the same DC that it took to make the item in the first place. The cost of repairing an item is one-fifth of the item’s price.


Action: Does not apply. Craft checks are made by the day or week (see above).


Try Again: Yes, but each time you fail by 5 or more, you ruin half the raw materials and have to pay half the
original raw material cost again.

 

Special: You may voluntarily add +10 to the indicated DC to craft an item. This allows you to create the item more quickly (since you’ll be multiplying this higher DC by your Craft check result to determine progress). You must decide whether to increase the DC before you make each weekly or daily check. To make an item using Craft (alchemy), you must have
alchemical equipment. If you are working in a city, you can buy what you need as part of the raw materials cost to make the item, but alchemical equipment is difficult or impossible to come by in some places. Purchasing and maintaining an alchemist’s lab grants a +2 circumstancebonus on Craft (alchemy) checks because you have the perfect tools for the job, but it does not affect the cost of any items made using the skill.

 

A gnome receives a +2 bonus on a Craft or Profession skill of her choice.

MC: Drew is willing to pay half salary and 80%. Amazing! Dean Quan's gifts and ability to think outside the box. Living into the reality together at Epworth. Open and transparent together. Nothing done behind closed doors. That is for politicians and not for the people of God. Methodist DNA even for those converted (about 50% in this room). We have methods, thus the name, for being christians. Book of Discipline geting bigger and bigger. But we are still Enthusiasts! Watch Night on New Years Eve Oxford Methodists stayed up all night for Agape Feast but were accused for having gluttonous orgies. [Fred Jardin would like to make a motion. Michael knows his heart.] Methods + Freedom/Liberty/Spontaneity. Open to spirit's movement and experimentation. When things don't work..fewer standing comittees? Taskforces? Vision teems. Structure doesn't lead but follows the function and the spirit. Wwe are free to organize and re-organize ourselves for the sake of the Movement.


Michael will be a different Pastor from previous, because he can't help himself and this is a different kind of appointment. He had coffee with Odette. He hadn't seen her since Jurisdictional Conference. We obviously have a very mutual love affair. She is monitoring the Prayer Chain and is always with us in spirit. Can Epworth continue to be her Charge Conference? DELIGHTED. Among the 14 other ordained clergy that live within Epworth.


Michael not Odette. Paradigm shift. Epworth will move from "Odette will be there for me." to "The Church will be there for me!" Odette was always strong and avaialble all the time - working 80 hours a week. Half time ain't that. Can't be there for you all the time. We have 22-24 Stephen ministers. Lay leaders. Resources and assets. Care team and people who love and care about and watch over each other. We may not need to hire a pastoral/congregational care person, but we can. When and how? Discernment. As slow or fast as we need to move. "Pastors On Call" from week to week.  Rev. Jerry Asheim not just a musician, but is ordained and on call next week! Brian is on call this week. If Michael is in town there will be conferring. There will be flexibility and methods in place for critical pastoral needs and emergencies. Regular visitation by Stephen and other ministers. All will visit each other--sharing the pastoral load.
Michael's Primary Gifts:

  • Organizing ministires
  • community development
  • Practical theology

Worship and preaching (3 Sundays a month) Brian at least once a month. Guest preachers. Lindsey in January with her youth group.
Not afraid of other leaders. The pastor does not dominate the church.
He is an Eagle on the Medicine Wheel - Big Picture but sometimes of no earthly good. Details sometimes fall away. Need a buffalo to drive things, like Brian! Deer are relational, process, people-people, like Jerry. There are lots of Bear here - analyize and do it right people. Together we can Be The Church. If you imagine I can run and manage the church by myself - it won't run smoothly. We need a new gift of management help from everyone.


He has been here 2.5 weeks, and it is too early to cast any vision. However, why not?!

Where do you resonate and have energy? Synergy?! Successful capital campaign just finished. Raised the roof at over $100,000 108% donations? Successful but still collecting pledges! We need another capital campaign as soon as we are ready. More with the building, but not a small way. Why not raise the bar? Epworth wants to be a beacon of help and hope in the community. We are a parish in a neighborhood. Shalom Zone = parish. Families are living within a few miles, and might see us anew. Playgroups. Jazz. Jams. Visibility and activity through building use. More potential to be a community center. A church existing for others (Bonhoeffer). Best looking community center condusive to gatherings - at the next level. Green the Church. Solar panels as a witness to what the church cares about. Rent panels? Master plan including defered issues of maintenance. Church with a feature or two that will draw people to us.

 

CL: motion. We take for granted our denomination, which allows this kind of connection. Formal letter of thanks to decision-makers who made this possible. All approve.
BA: Announcements? None. Recognizing Youngmi, who just came in. 
Benediction. Be the light the world needs to see and show God's love in the building of community.

Apply

Due to outages related to Hurricane Sandy, the deadline for the Mellon Fellowship of Scholars in the Humanities has been extended to 11:59 PM PT on Monday, November 26, 2012.

Letters of Recommendation may be sent to mellonfellows@stanford.edu

The Andrew W. Mellon Fellowship of Scholars in the Humanities is a unique opportunity for the best recent PhD recipients in the humanities to develop as scholars and teachers. Up to four fellowships will be awarded for a two-year term (with the possibility of a third). Fellows teach two courses per year in one of Stanford’s 15 humanities departments, and are expected to participate in the intellectual life of the program, which includes regular meetings with other fellows and faculty to share work in progress and to discuss topics of mutual interest. Fellows will also be affiliated with the Stanford Humanities Center and will have the opportunity to be active in its programs and workshops.

Application deadline has been extended to November 26, 2012.

The Mellon Fellowship provides postdoctoral fellowships in Stanford's fifteen humanities departments. Program admissions focus on selected fields of scholarship in each application year (on a rotating basis).

For fellowships beginning Fall 2013, we will accept applications from the following fields of study: 
  • Comparative Literature
  • French and Italian
  • German Studies
  • Iberian and Latin American Cultures
  • Religious Studies
  • Slavic Languages and Literatures
Apply Now
  • Eligibility

    Fields

    The Mellon Fellowship provides postdoctoral fellowships in Stanford's fifteen humanities departments. Program admissions focus on selected fields of scholarship in each application year (on a rotating basis), appointing up to four Fellows per year as follows:

    2013-14 Competition (for fellowships beginning Fall 2013):
    • Comparative Literature
    • French and Italian
    • German Studies
    • Iberian and Latin American Cultures
    • Religious Studies
    • Slavic Languages and Literatures

    We invite applicants to apply for fellowships in fields where their work has demonstrable relevance to teaching and research in the designated Stanford department.

    Degrees

    All candidates for the Mellon Fellowship must have received a qualified Ph.D. within a specified time frame, as follows:

    2013-14 Competition (for fellowships beginning Fall 2013):
    Ph.D. received between January 1, 2010 and June 30, 2013

    In addition to doctoral students, those currently serving as Assistant Professors, Lecturers, or postdoctorates in other programs are welcome to apply, provided they earned their degree within the time frame specified for the year they apply. 

    A Doctorate in Arts (D.A.), honorary doctorate, or any other degree equivalent is not considered a qualifed Ph.D. for purposes of application to this program.

    THE ANDREW W. MELLON FELLOWSHIP OF SCHOLARS IN THE HUMANITIES PROGRAM CANNOT ACCEPT APPLICATIONS FROM SCHOLARS WITH PHDS FROM STANFORD UNIVERSITY
  • Requirements
  • Fellows enjoy substantial time to pursue research, teach two courses per year in an affiliated Stanford Department, and participate in active program of scholarly exchanges with other Fellows, Stanford faculty, and outside visitors.

    Each Fellow is affiliated with some Stanford Humanities department, which arranges teaching and office space. This complements the Fellowship’s cross-disciplinary community by promoting Fellows’ full engagement in the activities of their home disciplines here at Stanford. 

    Fellows are expected to be in residence at Stanford for the full academic year (mid-September through mid-June), and even in quarters when they are not teaching are expected to hold regular office hours to consult with students and to participate in the academic life of the Stanford Community. Fellows are also expected to be active participants in the cohort of Fellows, attending regular meetings at which presentations of current work and discussions of intellectual and professional matters of interest to the group are offered.
     
    Stipends
    The stipend for 2012-13 will be $62,000. In addition to the stipend, Fellows are eligible for a full package of employee benefits, and are also provided with a research account to fund research-related expenses.
  • Application Process
    Applications should be submitted via our online application system. We discourage the submission of additional materials with your application and cannot return such materials to you.

    Applicants will be notified when their applications have been received, and will be notified of the fellowship competition outcome in the spring.

    If, after applying to the Andrew W. Mellon Fellowship of Scholars in the Humanities, you accept another position or postdoctoral fellowship, please withdraw your application by emailing mellonfellows@stanford.edu.
     
  • Application Content
    The application to the Andrew W. Mellon Fellowship of Scholars in the Humanities consists of the following materials:

    • Contact and biographical information about the applicant;
    • A cover letter (circa one page, single spaced) describing research and teaching interests to an interdisciplinary search committee;
    • Curriculum vitae;
    • Dissertation abstract (up to three pages, single spaced);
    • A sample of written work (article length, no longer than 40 pages, double spaced);
    • A separate description of teaching experience and interests (up to three pages, single spaced) Note: Courses will be offered through standing Stanford departments; applicants should familiarize themselves with recent course offerings and department curricula; and
    • Three confidential letters of recommendation

    You will receive a confirmation email once your online application is complete. Only complete applications will be considered.

cards.name: Open Letter
cards.content:
No End of Beginnings

 

In this first open letter you will find an audio recording of and reflection on the memorial for Donna Hamilton, news of our two-year-old daughter and four month old son, a report on our family's general well-being and my professional journey, as well as hints about adventures into which I hope to find my way in the not-so-distant future. I hope you will interpret what you find here as an invitation to reflect, comment, offer challenges, ask for more information, and become involved, either with me or more deeeply in your own work to meet your needs while helping to make the world a more just and peaceful community.

 

{{OL01img01|size:large;float:right}} This first proper letter is a bit long (and the following ones will be shorter) because it gets the metaphorical starch, yeast, and hops together and lights the fire under something I've been brewing for a very long time. I didn't like the pressure of writing my dissertation, but I loved the research and writing itself. It became clear to me that I can quite happily spend hours in a room by myself, pouring over texts and thinking about what I've read in order to share it with other people. This practice creates a kind of pressure, not only to create text of my own that I hope will be understood by others but also to put the written word to some use through thinking with other people about how we think, feel, and perform in co-creating our world. I feel compelled to explore, write, and teach or perform. My life is a bit busy right now, but I can't wait any longer before allowing my mixture to ferment, so I'll be tending it every day in private and tempting others to share samples of the product with some regularity. I designed and will continue to develop the Culturesmith website in order to do this work. Please make sure you subscribe to my email reminders using the box in the right margin of this window under the words "Enter your email address." You may also click on the gear icon at the upper right of this (or any) card and select "follow".

 

Part of this letter is behind a password on my website because it is also time to practice what I've preached for my entire adult life and keep more current with people who want to connect on a deeper level and who make up my community, near and far. Several folks have asked to be kept up-to-date by email on the more personal aspects of our Ups and Downs, especially during this time of transition. It turns out that sending anything by email or Facebook, or whatever new device of social media, has largely come to be considered the same as releasing it to the entire world with implicit permission that it may be used as anyone sees fit. I've decided to be more circumspect and not to release to the general public any more detail about our more problematic dilemmas than is necessary. If you have signed in, and continue to read past this point, you hereby agreed to keep what you read behind the log-in confidential. Please contact me if you need to change that agreement at any time and for any reason. I appreciate your understanding.

 

Outreach

 

Writing

{{Towards Beginnings image|size:medium;float:right}}I'd like to invite you to consider reading the first article of mine published since earning the Ph.D. It is [[Bluevolution|also located on this website]], both in sections and as a whole in PDF format. If you can afford to [[https://gumroad.com/l/Anqd|purchase the article]] (for only $4) or [[http://www.amazon.com/Towards-Beginnings-Images-Edition-Volume/dp/1481281402/ref=sr_1_4?ie=UTF8&qid=1356195705&sr=8-4&keywords=Towards+Beginnings+Images+of+end|the entire journal]], by all means please do.

 

Free Aiki

As founder and Chief Instructor of [[Free Aiki Dojo]] I continue to offer free aikido classes (pay-what-you-can or PWYC when possible) from four to six times a week, thanks in large part to the generosity of my host and teacher, [[Kayla Feder]] of [[Aikido of Berkeley]], and our non-profit [[Association Building Community]].

 

Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley

I accepted an invitation from students at UC Berkeley to be Chief Instructor for aikido on the Cal campus and helped them reinstate the organization there begun by Senseis [[Robert Frager]] and [[Stan Pranin]] in 1968. With the members of the community who make up Free Aiki Dojo, all of my students are welcome to train together both on and off campus and also often attend Kayla Sensei's classes at Aikido of Berkeley. [[http://goldenbearsaikido.com|Golden Bears Aikido]] has also added new sempai, named Rob Pierce, to the teaching roster. He promptly began a late night Thursday class on-campus which will resume with the school year. Opportuities to grow on campus continue to present themselves, and we would deeply appreciate any help you might offer in that area. People discover that I really do mean that anyone is invited to train no matter their financial situation, and have begin donating training uniforms (gi and hakama) as well as the time required to circulate PR materials. 

 

The Aikido Archives at Sofia University

It continues to be my great good fortune to have been invited by Robert Frager Sensei, founder of the Institute for Transpersonal Psychology now known as [[Sofia University]], to create (design with [[Ethan McCutchen]] of Grass Commons' Wagn.org) and curate the [[Aikido Archives]] at that institution. We will launch publicly in the coming months and welcome the creative input of members of the global aikido commmunity among our guest curators and contributors.

 

Martial Nonviolence

{{OL01img02|size:large;float:right}}In the Summer of 2011, I became the aikido and [[Martial Nonviolence]] (MNv) instructor at The Renaissance School in Oakland. Since then, I introduced and have been developing my [[Peace Practices]] (PcPx) curriculum for use by the whole learning community, including students, staff, faculty and parents. Leslie Hites, Head of School at and owner of TRS, is an enthusiastic supporter of the work in which over fifty children and adults from TRS have participated so far, and has invited me to teach the staff, make public presentations. I introduce the Peace Practices curriculum to adults through public demonstrations during which I describe the aikido and MNv classes in progress now, ask parents of children who are in the program to speak, introduce the [[Peace Practices]] curriculum under consideration for the future, and take questions. To explain what this entails, I need your permission to sound a bit like a brochure for a few more seconds.

 

{{Martial Nonviolence+image|size:medium;float:right}}Martial Nonviolence® refers to a unique training and conflict facilitation method [[Brandon WilliamsCraig|I]] created which combines practices and concepts from the martial ([[aikido]]), theatrical (improv), and [[process arts]] (group facilitation) to prepare practitioners to provide co-creative leadership in the midst of conflict and during the process of systemic revision. Capable of engaging both obviously physical conflict and covert systemic violence, the adult practitioner becomes an artist working with group inquiry and long-term analysis, striving for the redefinition of peace itself as "conflict done well".®

[[http://culturesmith.com/Aikido_and_Attention|My article about Aikido and Attention issues]].

[[https://www.facebook.com/MartialNonviolence?fref=ts|MNv on Facebook]]


{{ConflictWell logo figures01framed|size:medium;float:right}}Peace Practices® is what I call MNv when it is wrapped into a unique curriculum designed for a specific group which wishes to transform into a community practicing peace on a daily basis. Here is the [[http://www.causes.com/causes/100237-peace-practices-whole-community-martial-nonviolence-training|Peace Practices page on Causes]] with much more information and video.

 

The remainder of this letter includes writing about a hero of mine, named Donna Hamilton, an audio recording of her memorial service, reports on challenges faced in getting Peace Practices off the ground, reflections on practicing what I preach, and a brief exploration of the gifts and pressures of family and vocation. If you do not see more in-depth content below this line, please sign in or request an account.

 

 {{OL01membercontent}}

 

 

 

If you are signed in, previous letters will appear below. If you are seeking older content, please look here.

{{Beginning Email 20130122|closed}}

 

Comments on previous letters will be found appended to those cards. This comment area is for the current issue and, if you are signed in, you will see a box below for the further addition of your thoughts. Please contribute in any way that feels right to you, including making suggestions and proposing corrections.

  --[[Brandon WilliamsCraig]]

Brandon,

 

Thank you for generously sharing of your thoughts, experiences, stories. Variations on some of your themes are running through my life, so much resonance. This is the year of the snake, and a time for shedding worn out ways of moving through the world... whether we want to or not, they're coming off! Sometimes it can be a ripping sensation. In my experience, lately situations are arising which are there to give me information - it may not be the information that I want, but knowledge is always useful. I sometimes question whether to resist what seems to be unjust, or to simply engage more strongly with positive situations... or both. Like any piece of art, designing our lives depends on so many factors, preferences, choices; and is a constantly evolving process. I always enjoy reading about your journey; life isn't always comfortable, but the most difficult situations also make the best stories. The salon sounds like a great idea!

 

Be well,

Dhyana

--[[Dhyana Iris]].....2013-07-05 16:23:46 +0000

cards.name: Huston Smith article for CDSP
cards.content:
{{+image|size:large;float:right}}

{{Huston Smith+bio}}

 

On February 5th, 2013, I had the privilege of asking Professor Smith for his thoughts on the [[Nones on the Rise - One-in-Five Adults Have No Religious Affiliation|October 2012 Pew Forum study]], “Nones” on the Rise: One-in-Five Adults Have No Religious Affiliation. The Executive Summary of that poll begins, and my interview with Professor Smith began, here:

The number of Americans who do not identify with any religion continues to grow at a rapid pace. One-fifth of the U.S. public – and a third of adults under 30 – are religiously unaffiliated today, the highest percentages ever in Pew Research Center polling.

On being asked for his thoughts on this departure from religious self-identification, Professor Smith began his response by reading aloud a December 2012 New York Times article, [[JONATHAN SACKS - The Moral Animal|"The Moral Animal," by Jonathan Sacks]] [audio through 14:30]. The article begins:

At first glance, religion is in decline. In Britain, the results of the 2011 national census have just been published. They show that a quarter of the population claims to have no religion, almost double the figure 10 years ago. And though the United States remains the most religious country in the West, 20 percent declare themselves without religious affiliation — double the number a generation ago. Looked at another way, though, the figures tell a different story. Since the 18th century, many Western intellectuals have predicted religion’s imminent demise. Yet after a series of withering attacks, most recently by the new atheists, including Sam Harris, Richard Dawkins and the late Christopher Hitchens, still in Britain three in four people, and in America four in five, declare allegiance to a religious faith. That, in an age of science, is what is truly surprising.

Following the October Pew poll, Sacks is almost certainly offering a response to its findings and what sounds like yet another death knell for religion. He makes a strong statement for religion's social value, proposing not only that it reflects a biologically hard-wired altruism, but also that religion encourages the expression of altruism necessary for the building of Community. Sacks concludes, and Smith strongly agrees, that "religion is the best antidote to the individualism of the consumer age. The idea that society can do without it flies in the face of history and, now, evolutionary biology."

Acknowledging this often asserted value associated with the practice of religion, I drew to Professor Smith's attention a parallel conclusion from the Pew polling, which is to say that "most religiously unaffiliated Americans think that churches and other religious institutions benefit society by strengthening community bonds and aiding the poor." However, despite the benefits and "with few exceptions, ... the unaffiliated say they are not looking for a religion that would be right for them. Overwhelmingly, they think that religious organizations are too concerned with money and power, too focused on rules and too involved in politics."

Professor Smith agreed that institutions are problematic, but asked whether the poll's respondents were rejecting institution or religious tradition itself. It seems clear from the data that "the overwhelming majority of the “nones” were brought up in a religious tradition...about three-quarters of unaffiliated adults were raised with some affiliation (74%)." The idea of jettisoning religious traditions because of the dilemmas Smith associates with institutions, of all kinds, causes him considerable consternation, but he was drawn to sit in silence for quite some time considering the idea that two-thirds of the 46 million unaffiliated adults in the U.S. who identify themselves as "religious or spiritual in some way" also: 68% believe in God, and 58% "say they often feel a deep connection with nature and the earth." One-in-five prays every day. Thirty-seven percent "classify themselves as 'spiritual' but not 'religious.'

"Spiritual but not Religious" triggers a reaction in Smith similar to the argument in his Why Religion Matters (p 255), where the phrase is used to represent what is lost in the "New Age" when the new beginning made possible by religious tradition is thrown out with the more oily water of institution. In both his book and our interview, Dr. Smith turned to the White House scandal of the late 1990's to illustrate his frustration. President Clinton [[http://www.historyplace.com/speeches/clinton-sin.htm|said publicly that he had "sinned"]] in an effort to convey his remorse and intention to change for the better. Monica Lewinsky, when asked if she felt similarly, rather than speaking about her responsibility side-stepped the premise by suggesting “I am not very religious. I am more spiritual.” Among Professor Smith's concerns is that the importance of "feeling good about oneself,"  which he associates with "spirituality," far overshadows the drive to become a more loving human being, which he associates with religion. He suggested to me that, beneath the social benefits which are demonstrably associated with participating in religion, the humanizing expectations of religion practiced honestly run deep, reinforced by the image of divinity or divinities, by whatever name.

In Smith's words, "our traditions shape us," and it is an image of God into which shape we ought desire to be formed more than into our own idea of self. "Religio binds us: to our fellow human beings, to God, and to the deepest element in ourselves; our soul." When I suggested that people seemed to be trying to do the work of that binding without the aid of institutions and traditions, Professor Smith's response was simply "Good Luck! All institutions are morally ambivalent, having down and up-sides...but religion is basically good and we are as our traditions have shaped us." It is this beneficial shaping of persons and cultural narratives which he sees as primarily at risk in the demographic sample the poll reflects. Especially given the near impossibility of total departure from the shapes religion has made, Smith insists that it would be better to be "Ands" rather than "Nones."

A concern with jettisoning "sin," for instance, and thereby an opportunity to behave more admirably, is only the beginning of what Professor Smith fears has been sacrificed when the loss of religious tradition is the price of atoning for the excesses of institution. Other humanizing aspects of religious practice are even more important and include mysteries which cannot be easily uncovered by reductive tools such as statistical polling. Other well-known comparativists, such as Joseph Campbell, for instance, are often accused of essentializing and thereby losing the particularity of the traditions they describe in general terms. When Professor Smith suggests there are central, perennial values associated with long-standing religious wisdom traditions, he is sometimes misunderstood as suggesting that the values associated with religion may be extracted from and practiced without the need for specific religious traditions, a kind of post-secular humanism.

Wondering if Professor Smith sees the Pew poll pointing in this direction or away from it, I paraphrased a particularly provocative idea I had heard him offer during [[http://abcglobal.net/Conversations_with_Huston_Smith|a public talk we conducted together]]. He had suggested that thinking of religion in terms of a reduction to the mininum values necessary to operationalize social and spiritual benefit is too mechanical. This approach wholly misses the beauty and mystery that make for a deep, poetic understanding that both private and communal worship can bring to human beings. "Esoterically,...religions are one, like the kernel inside the walnut." This metaphor also appears (at least) in Smith's Is There A Universal Grammar of Religion, The Soul of Christianity, and Tales of Wonder. Smith went on to explain that, as the institutional shell of any religious nut may look very different from its fellows, universally nourishing meat continues to be available within. But protein the body needs is not all there is to true nourishment of the whole person. The whole process matters and contains complex and dynamic relationships which are not reducible to efficiencies, much less a lowest common denominator.

I sent this article to Professor Smith and received his approval to frame the conversation in the way you are reading here. As problematized by Smith in our public events, I have come to refer to attempts to boil down religion for its "personal growth" and socially acceptable values as "committing the sin of efficiency," which is at least part of the danger of divorcing belief in God, a feeling of deep connection with nature and the earth, and prayer from the specific context of original traditions. Classifying oneself as 'spiritual' but not 'religious' may offer new freedom of exploration but also seems to put one in danger of foreclosing understanding of how the two are inextricably and beneficially related. The problematic and deeply satisfying maturity of understanding that can come from ongoing poetic and communal relationship with Divine Mysteries is what may be lost. In his 93rd year, it is this loss that Huston Smith lovingly warns us against. 

{{+discussion|open}}

Advisory
Apprentice
Practicing
Team

cards.name: Huston David born
cards.content:
March 14, 2013

Through last night, Lisa was troubled by what she thought were the same old Braxton-Hicks contractions. I drew her a warm bath this morning around 6:30 to try to help ease the pressure, as she insisted that these were high contractions to encourage the baby to drop and were non-progressive. After making everyone breakfast, as I do every day, Lisa sent me off to work, despite the discomfort she was feeling. At 11:30 she called me back home, even though we both thought this might be a dry run, because it would be a good opportunity to really finish getting ready. At some point while I was on my way, she sensed a change in intensity and alerted our most excellent midwives. I was on the scene by 11:50. I began madly moving stuff to try to clear the space in which we had intended to set up the birth tub, until her water broke at 12:15 and we abandoned the idea that there would be time for the tub. She climbed into the dry bath tub and at 12:20 allowed as how the baby's head was about to appear. I climbed in to the dry tub too. Sure enough, Huston David's head was soon resting in my hands, his position a bit anterior. I made sure the cord was not around his neck and asked if Lisa thought she might breathe regularly and give a bit of a push. She thought not, but did anyway. Between 1 and 2 minutes later 8lbs 14oz and 21.5" of Huston wriggled out and immediately voiced doubts about the quality of his treatment thus far. I held him on my chest while I looked to see if there might be any things amiss and visible only from my vantage and, finding none, delivered Huston to his Mama's warm embrace. I then called our midwife, Dana, who asked several questions, directed me to put a sterile pad between Lisa and the tub in order to receive the placenta, and congratulated us thoroughly before returning to her driving. The Dana and Claudette Team arrived very quickly, I cut the cord, together we took care of all related business, and before long we were weighing, measuring, trimming nails (long!), admiring curly black hair (lots!), introducing Rosalie to her little brother, and cuddling. More to come on this page, when the opportunity presents itself.

 

Thanks SO much to all those who brought us food. It made all the difference!

Fr Mar 15 Albee-Goods' chicken, mash and salad

Sa 16 Cathy and Meagan Travlos' black bean chili with corn bread

Su 17 Christina Kellogg

Mo 18 Jodi Gill

We 20 Feder-Black Family 10am Mediterranean food

Su 24 Leslie Zeitler's fab chicken soup

cards.name: OL01membercontent
cards.content:
Practicing What I Preach

I gave a demonstration last Fall after which a mother became so enthusiastic that she went looking for me out in the world to get me to teach her daughters independently. She went to the wrong dojo by mistake and a senior aikido instructor, who will remain nameless for the time being, took her aside and made several disparaging remarks about me personally, about my wife, Lisa, about my ability as an aikido instructor, and presented an opinion, thankfully entirely unsupported by fact or the opinion of any other human being, that I would likely harm her children should the parent allow me to teach them. The parent immediately related the conversation to Leslie Hites, the owner and TRS Head of school, and removed her children from my then upcoming classes, which immediately stopped along with the majority of my income, pending a criminal background check and a full investigation, both of which I recommended upon being notified of the issue by the school.

Leslie Hites attempted to contact the source of the slander four times, before being allowed to speak, and received only denials of any involvement and instructions to leave the premises. I have sent an open-ended "there must have been a mistake" letter, drafted language as requested in December for TRS to send a letter, which they have not, and must decide how to proceed. Full-scale legal action requires a relatively huge financial and time commitment which we will not undertake at this time, but I must move the issue or loose the opportunity to find redress for the losses that have been caused. I've never faced anything like this before.

As Lisa has been the full-time parent-at-home since last summer, and I have been the sole earner for our family, the income vacuum has led me to take any employment available, while applying for every academic, non-profit, and executive position within my skill set. I have been working both as a contractor's assistant and providing triage and systems change assistance to a local non-profit for a few hours a week, all the while teaching pay-what-you-can aikido and Martial Nonviolence to my students at UC and in Berkeley. Our church community, particularly Jerry Asheim and Charles Lynch, have been incredibly supportive in both intangible and material ways. I continue to hope that my classes at TRS will resume, but end up waiting for weeks and weeks for anyone there to respond to my emails and calls.

 

Insearch

When I feel overwhelmed with the quantity of ground-breaking that appears to be necessary before my work can flourish and find the support it needs to sustain itself over time, when it seems that I may never make a living and adequately support my family, I remember how near death is at every moment. I remember how suddenly it visits, how intimate its changes, and I feel grateful again, at least in part, to be breathing the same air as the many admirable people who grace my life.

 

{{OL01img03|size:large;float:right}}Donna Hamilton of Epworth United Methodist Church in Berkeley died on December 28th, 2012. She was a beloved friend and fellow choir member, but her death created unexpectedly profound tremors in me which it took me until her memorial service was in progress to identify. I was raised in Texas, in a culture, family, and church wherein women, specifically United Methodist Women were the Church. I don't mean this to be in any way glib or to denigrate the contribution of the men I remember and admire. It is simply that pastors came and went, by design, and Bishops were more and less cogent, but The Women could be relied upon. Entirely. World Without End. Amen. To be present, musical, involved in even the most minute decisions, and laden with gifts of food, history, gentle but irresistible correction, and gravity of purpose. They worked together, in most cases, and were, when united, a nigh unstoppable force in the church proper and in the city at large.

 

Like these women of my childhood remembrance, Donna was warm, accepting, and loving-as-can-be, but she was also a bit edgy. Apparently, she really did expect herself to be faithful through trials, resolutely compassionate, and to bring her best effort to every endeavor at all times. It seems to me that there are fewer and fewer people around who care much if what they think, feel, and do is truly fine, in the sense of being the best possible in the eyes of God and man. I found and continue to find Donna to be a fine and generous spirit, admirable, which is rather rare, and I feel that a pillar has been removed on which the Church is built. The real Church. Not the bureaucracy so much, but the Idea of a People of God unwilling to give up on Love being the way they live daily life. Add to this that she was not only admirable but a musician, community organizer, and an educated lay speaker, and it will make even more sense when I suggest that her loss causes the foundations of the sacred, as I experience it, to wobble quite a bit. In church, I found myself in tears I didn't expect and couldn't seem to staunch when, struck by the third verse of "Now, on Land and Sea Descending" (during the singing of which she passed away on Dec. 28th), I struggled to sing the words "Now, our wants and burdens leaving to God's care who cares for all, cease we fearing, cease we grieving; touched by God our burdens fall." Donna even managed to Go Out on cue, raising the bar all the while.

 

In my inner experience of Methodism, the [[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_Quadrilateral|quadrilateral]] is the theoretical foundation of our practical theology but, in daily practice, the liturgy and eucharist of our life together has to do more with music, Charge Conference, and covered dishes. Our mythology and theology, expressed most explicitly in educated homiletics, are vital too, but worship simply does not occur unless the spirit of Wesley's [[http://www.lakewoodfirstumchurch.com/Wesley%27s%20Directions%20for%20Singing|Directions for Singing]] is honored, the local church takes full responsibility for its own governance decisions, and we feed each other frequently, as well as those unable to return the favor. In short, the God-image I carry around in my pocket is a communitarian, a closet democrat devoted to gathering, singing four part harmony and feasting. St. Donna, named by [[Brian Adkins]] "the most Methodist woman I've ever met," made each of these essential rituals more likely, more real and meaningful, and called others by her example to do likewise. I hope to remain in conversation with her, as suppliant, asking for her continuing correction so that I may be more like her, and the God she loves, in service to others. Some day, I hope to be spoken of with half the passionate fondness with which she was bid adieu and sung into memory.

 

Here is the audio recording of the memorial service.

{{DonnaHamiltonMemorial20130126player}}

 

Rosalie's godmother, [[Lindsey Kerr]], preached her first sermon at Epworth the day after, and wove our memories into a Call to see each other truly and continue Donna's ministry of radical welcome and acceptance. As I release this letter the Reverend Kerr has graduated from seminary and been appointed an Associate Pastor in Santa Rosa. Joining her parents, Bob and Faith, we couldn't be prouder to know her.

 

{{Lindsey Kerr preaching at Epworth UMC 20130127}}

 

Family

We have moved to share [[Alvarado-Bouquet House|a beautiful new home]] with a most excellent neighbor. In the near future we hope to begin a series of salons, public events, and celebrations which will offer the chance to gather, build community and become more familiar with a landmark in the process of restoration.


{{OL01img04|size:large;float:right}} Fairly regularly, it is my custom to sit, eat, and talk with [[Huston Smith]] at some length, so I recently asked him if he harbored any misgivings about babies being named after living people. He allowed as how that seemed pretty silly to him, and graciously gave his permission to move ahead, so we gave the name [[Huston David born|Huston David Williamscraig]] to the little boy born just after noon on the 14th of March. Everyone is doing very well and Grandma Heidi, Grandma Paula, Grandpa David, and Grandma Julie have all come to visit and help us with the transitions that go along with adding a new family member.

 

Next

The big challenge facing me at the moment is vocational. Lisa had secured a new position with a school in which she worked last year, and returned to work in June, thereby providing schooling for both children as well. I, on the other hand, continue to work as a non-profit consultant, contractor's assistant, in-home support provider and advocate, and seek the kind of employment which will allow us to flourish rather than continuing in survival mode, as we have been for so long. I apply for positions as a lecturer and assistant professor in departments of literature, religious studies, and psychology. I also am happy to continue as an executive or organizational change management consultant, always on the lookout for the right set of benefits and creative responsibilities. I am happy to provide resumes in any of these areas to anyone with an interest in knowing more.

 

Wondering

I think in terms of roles and narrative when I think about the way that persons change over time. I've been wondering a lot lately about my own future, wanting to leverage and depend on the roles I am able to enact authentically because I have solid and extensive experience living in that particular story and understand the way that the narratives are likely to play out. The role of Father I understand reasonably well, from birth to death, at least in the early years, and feel fairly comfortable with my choices in the role at this time. I had the great pleasure of [[Huston David born|delivering my son]] and, though I'd have wished for less exciting delivery circumstances, everything seems to have turned out well and Lisa and I continue to make a solid and loving parental team. I believe I will look back on this part of our lives with considerable pride and affection. I feel steady in my improvement as a teacher, both of the martial and liberal arts, and crave more practice and a solid footing in both. I know I am a writer, a maker of thinking myths with a rich blend of fiction and truth, and will continue to bring this practice to the forefront in both digital and analog formats. Much of it offered here on Culturesmith. Please let me know if you'd like to know more.

 

Though I have co-founded and captained my own small business for over a decade, I do not have the archetype of The Businessman walking reliably beside me. He knows better than I how to put First Things First, delaying the gratification of short triumphs in order to plan and execute incrementally. He achieves longer term goals and larger projects which stay within effective scope. He knows how truly to account for things, work with money deliberately so that it grows, and has learned the kind of discipline that allows for great productivity without sacrificing study, recuperation and the joy of creative and restorative idleness. I know this reality is before me somewhere, I just haven't put my feet firmly on that road quite yet. Any suggestions would be more than welcome.

 

With profound gratitude,

 

Brandon Williamscraig Ph.D.

Aikido 4th dan, Sensei

cards.name: BW bio source
cards.content:
Ph.D. university instructor and author on the psychology of belief and narrative construction of culture (mythology); CEO and principal consultant Association Building Community, Director of Peace Practices (.org) and curriculum creator; 5th degree aikido black belt and Chief Instructor Golden Bears Aikido UC Berkeley. Created Martial Nonviolence (.com) method of Conflict Done Well, and provides leadership and teamwork training for enterprises and individuals internationally.

[[Brandon WilliamsCraig]], Ph.D. is co-founder and CEO of the Bay Area nonprofit, Association Building Community. He has extensive experience with private and public educational institutions, provides corporate leadership and group facilitation training, and has provided conflict management and community mediation services since 1998. His academic work focuses on the psychology of belief and the narrative construction of culture.

Brandon Sensei is a 5th degree blackbelt in aikido and head instructor of [[Free Aiki Dojo]] and [[http://goldenbearsaikido.com|Golden Bears Aikido]] at UC Berkeley. His students learn traditional aikido techniques paired with language that brings about the embodiment of aiki principles. His conflict facilitation method, called [[http://martialnonviolence.com|Martial Nonviolence]], is the heart of the [[Peace Practices]] curriculum being practiced around the world by students from four to 74 years of age. He resides in Richmond, CA with his wife and two children.

 

Industry/Fields: executive coaching and enterprise consulting, conflict facilitation training, non-profit and community leadership development, and education from pre-K through post-graduate.

 

I would like the opportunity to speak to your leadership team/colleagues/students about Conflict Done Well™ system as well as opportunities for training and advancement in my field. I have served as a supervising instructor at St. Mary's College, teach conflict management skills at UC Berkeley and through my classes in downtown Berkeley and Oakland, and am the CEO of a local social benefit organization (501c3) called Association Building Community. We provide the Peace Practices curriculum (peacepractices.org) to children and adults through the schools they share, and provide conflict management training to adults in positions of leadership. 
 
In order to do this work, I combine a humanities Ph.D. in psychology and mythology with experience in executive consulting and community activism, as well as certifications in mediation, a martial art called aikido, and group facilitation. The work I offer addresses anger management, bullying, and sexual assault prevention, classroom participation and management, the development of both working and learning organizations, and the management of conflicts in professional, family, and community contexts. 
 
Please let me know if I may be of service to you and your students. My colleague, Cheyenne, or apprentice, Julian, may respond to communications on my behalf. If you'd like to make direct contact with me, my mobile number is (510) 697-1513.

 

Brandon WilliamsCraig Ph.D. is an aikido 4th dan, and is founder and Chief Instructor of both Free Aiki Dojo and Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley. He created the position of Executive Director and an administration for Aiki Extensions in 2008 and continues to serve on the Board of Directors.

I co-founded, was Executive Director, and am President of [[ABCglobal|Association Building Community]] in Berkeley CA. Representing ABC, I completed a contract to create the position of Executive Director and an administration for [[Aiki Extensions]] and was honored to be asked to continue serving on their Board of Directors. Both are non-profits building communities locally and internationally to practice alternative methods of conflict facilitation.

I created and serve as Chief Instructor of [[Free Aiki Dojo]] in Berkeley CA. I offer traditional aikido training, and then extend "aiki" metaphors into my conflict facilitation method, called [[Martial Nonviolence]] (MNv). In 2010 I accepted the invitation to become Chief Instructor of [[Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley]] and hope to continue in the excellent company of Senseis Don Levine, Frank Doran, and many others who have explored the intersection of the liberal and martial arts. When I teach [[MNv]] as a site specific, custom-designed curriculum, I call that process [[Peace Practices]]. Currently [[Peace Practices]] are in progress at [[The Renaissance School]] in Oakland, CA.

I was born in Dallas, Texas, and educated by Montessorians and Jesuits. My first career, from my sixth year and into early adulthood, was in the professional regional and touring theater. I emigrated to California to be a full-time, residential aikido apprentice for two years, completed professional process arts facilitation certifications, particularly in mediation and community building, acquired graduate degrees in mythology and psychology, became a husband and then a father.

I coined and reserve the right for everyone to share the term "[[Process Arts]]", which refers to the field of group process design and facilitation. When I teach or facilitate I often describe what we do using various names and phrases I originated. I "own" the exclusive right to use following phrases, variations, and associated acronyms and URLs: [[Free Aiki Dojo|Free Aiki]], [[People Green]], [[Bluevolution]], [[Associative Inquiry]] (AsIn) and [[Archetypal Resonance Imaging]] (ARI), [[Analogical System Knowledgebase]] (ASK), [[Associative Inclusion Dynamics]] (AID), [[Healing Friction]], [[Martial Nonviolence]] (MNv), [[Culturesmith]], [[Arts of Peace]], [[Flexibility In Adversity Training]] (FIAT), and variations of: "conflict done well", "peace is conflict done well", "doing conflict well", "Aiki anywhere", bdwc.net, and williamscraig.com.

Also originated and reserved to the Commons are: [[culturopoiesis]] and culturopoesis, metashaman, and [[metashamanism]], whereas I reserve the right to own the URLs that reflect these terms.

cards.name: Wynton Marsalis and his Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra at Zellerbach 20130317
cards.content:
On March 17th, courtesy of a two year old birthday gift certificate from Heidi, I was in Zellerback at Cal to hear him with his Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra. http://www.calperfs.berkeley.edu/performances/2012-13/jazz/wynton-marsalis-and-jazz-at-lincoln-center-orchestra.php http://www.calperfs.berkeley.edu/learn/program_notes/2012/pn_jlco.pdf I haven't mentioned it because it nearly killed me. It was one of the most sublime musical experience of my life and Wynton, who is part of my generation, was flawless as a musician, human being, entertainer, cultural figure... I felt hugely gifted, transported, and dashed to pulp on the shoals of my own mediocrity. I completed the usual fan-boy avoidance maneuvers, like promising myself to buy everything he's ever released, etc. I rehearsed the usual immature and resentful caveats in my head, like listing his early advantages and natural talent, and all that reasonable rot, and am left with being a grown-up in the end: stuck between "I'll never be as good as that no matter what I fuckin' do" and "pouting about what he ain't got never got him an inch closer to where he is." He just won't stop completing the daily, incremental, get a bit better every day stuff that lets you build a resume like that. He does what it takes to be good at all the things he undertakes, bit by bit, no matter what anybody else says.

Brandon D. Williamscraig
