(510) 697-1513

Monday, April 29, 2013

Sara Thacker J.D.  LL.M.

Director & Ombudsperson

Staff Ombuds Office, UC Berkeley

 

Ms. Thacker,

 

I would like very much to work for you as an Associate Ombudsperson at UC Berkeley. I have over thirteen years of experience working through conflict in academic and management environments, and am comfortable engaging with an extremely diverse range of individuals and groups at all organizational levels. I continue to assist clients in constructively managing conflicts in highly sensitive and complex situations, as well as providing feedback to officers and managers, proposing preventative measures to address systemic issues, and making recommendations for both interventions and long-term change. My primary area of interest and process involves discerning and articulating the potential consequences associated with "what we chose not to know" by investigating the culture of educational institutions, businesses, divisions, and project teams. I work to uncover limiting assumptions and distinguish them from individual needs and desires in order to push beyond self-justification in search of sustainable responses to conflict.

 

Whether my client is an individual or group, I hope to help them articulate an ongoing range of options from within their own experience with the conflicts at hand. Rather than offering answers, I model candid but safe discussion, looking to open lines of communication and suggest resources. I am regularly asked to offer ongoing interpersonal communication skills and conflict coaching with a special focus in class, race, and cross-cultural issues. I frequently conduct shuttle diplomacy of an informal but confidential nature to avoid litigation and set goals for personal development. I design trainings and created a unique curriculum for the children and adults at a local private school to include conflict training in their daily learning together in order to address bullying and deal with normalizing conflict by treating it as a learning opportunity. Toward this end, I have studied the process arts since I obtained my mediation certification in 1997, practice and teach a non-violent martial art, called aikido, and have cultivated a professional practice utilizing  alternative dispute resolution techniques. I would now like to develop my experience mediating work-related conflicts by serving as an organizational ombudsperson.  I love to learn and work with both students and adults; I truly value public education, and hope for a chance to contribute to the Staff Ombuds program you have built. I hope to meet with you, as face-to-face is the only place to get a sense of what it might be like to include me in your team. Please contact me so we may set up a time.

 

With gratitude,

 

Brandon Williamscraig


5739 McBryde Ave. Richmond, CA 94805

brandon@williamscraig.com

(510) 697-1513

o   Identify what holds them back by deconstructing hard to face differences

cards.content:
Anniversary card for Lisa 2013

{{20130605+BW+Correspondence+image|float:right;size:large}}

I savor the sweetness of being with you.

The poesies that spring from you

make my life delightful;

they are gifts for which I will never be able to express enough thanks.

You seem mostly unaware of standing, sometimes, between me and darkness,

a glittery spirit

showing your true colors with integrity.

Children see you.

I rehearse peacock fantasies:

Nobility, Holiness, Guidance, Protection and Watchfulness--

Rejuvenation and self-esteem.

Shuttling from blah and blue to a swaying display evoking all that is fine and beautiful,

it is a pleasure to see you walking tall and proud in your colors!

Like Hera did, you create in me peacock eyes from Argus' whose hundred sights prick the night sky of experience without daylight's denial that the dark is the background before which all our beautiful opportunities to hope are made to shine.

You shine.

Deliciously.

Administrator
Francisco Pontual
David Williams
Cheyenne Barr

cards.name: Aiki Extensions 2013 Conference offering
cards.content:
Aiki Extensions 2013 Conference offering

 

Ideography

Please stretch and warm up to move a bit as I begin with a brief introduction to the world in which this work is imagined.

Ask questions at any time.

For those who haven't met me yet...

Free Aiki Dojo and Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley. Frager and Pranin 1968.

ABC (AE Exec Dir. in 2008 > Board). Sofia has contracted with ABC for me to be the Curator of the Aikido Archives, about which I'd love to tell you more later. Please ask.

ABC offers work with the process skills people need to build sustainable communities, which is to say doing conflict well.

 

You've used "green" products which have lower ecological impacts, and ABC might even offer a sustainable relationship proactices certificate some day, perhaps call it PeopleGreen.

Some object that what we are really suggesting is a certification for being a good person...Sure. People do it all the time when they ask about others behavior and track record.

What metric or standard could one possibly apply to a person or group of people in order to certify them as PeopleGreen?

Demonstrated sustainable relationship practices, in particular measuring and building conflict capacity, resilience under stress, and the repeated experience of facilitating Conflict Done Well.

 

Relationship skills could be cultivated through psychotherapy, for instance, and put into broad practice through social justice training and public service or compassionate team building and business management.

One can study NVC for basic peace-making language skills, but the body is most often left unprepared to host this entire process, to stay the course and continue to make good choices under the extreme stress and threat of conflict.

"Continuing to make good choices under stress?" = Martial Arts, but which?

 

More specifically, Aikido, designed from the ground up to habituate the body to nonviolent responses rather than violent reactions. But is that enough? I call the shift I am talking about "Aikido 2.0," because the vast majority of dojos do not prepare students for the use of language, which will actually be the environment within which conflict skills are most freqently deployed. There is much talk about how aikido brings one to contemplate peace, but no direct application of the lessons learned from martial arts of every kind. If you want to be ready for violence, practice specific basics in a community dedicated to that purpose, until your conflict skills become more subtle and effective.

Writ large - Karate phenom Ed Parker, TKD became huge, also Brazillian Jujutsu, next Aikido 2.0

"Aiki-Extensions is the 21st Century iteration of how O'Sensei envisioned Aikido's role in global peace. AE is in direct lineage to his vision and it is thus playing out what his vision projected in a world marked by transforming technologies and new epidemics of strife." - Richard Strozzi-Heckler

To move this into the world of the concrete, I created Martial Nonviolence (aikido+theater+facilitation) and deployed it as a community specific curriculum, called Peace Practices, most recently at The Renaissance School in Oakland and at UC Berkeley, but we are looking at more potential sites in the near future.

It goes something like this:

 

Pedagogy

For adults, primary attention to how you move, Tai Sabaki, or body management, is used to situate the work most fundamentally in the body.

 

exercise

 

Then we habituate a three part process, with the first layer of which many of you may be familiar:

  • BASIC kihon (ME) Shift in mechanism (What) Behavior
  • IN MOTION ki no nagare (YOU) Shift in quality (How) Thought and Language
  • AT ONCE ki musubi (US) Shift in consciousness (Who) (imagination/visualization) Character or Role

exercise

 

Then adding language

{{MNv Drills+Basic Movements}}

Moving from a set basic script to variations in motion, to actual verbal conflicts, to shifting back and forth between verbal and physical to sharpen both physical self-defense (which often overlooks the necessity of the language that frequently bookends violence) and the use of language, visualization, and imagination to work throug conflict.

 

Role Plays?

 

Kids and Adults in community

 

?The connection with Montessori and the three-part lesson?

  1. Receiving
  2. Responding/Identifying
  3. Reproducing (Offerings and Testing)

Earning and Growing

 

Modest Ask:

In the tradition of our Founder, who redefined the Way of War as love in service, let us ask to change what happens in every dojo to let aikido be its whole self and truly pursue its mission.

"Aiki-Extensions is the 21st Century iteration of how O'Sensei envisioned Aikido's role in global peace. AE is in direct lineage to his vision and it is thus playing out what his vision projected in a world marked by transforming technologies and new epidemics of strife." - Richard Strozzi-Heckler

Aikido 2.0 launches today.

cards.name: BW w Chris Thorsen 20131114_1000-1145pst
cards.content:
Mission: Generate Revenue, 100k gross income, doing what I love and can feel proud of offering at a professional level of mastery.
Means: writing, work with organizations, leader support, conferences and travel, in order to build visibility and potential for cultural impact.
Operating Goals for next year and prioritization to be playing at the global level by age 50.
Develop through writing and cultivating a reputation for CDW, process arts and community development education in Peace Practices such that I gain enough renown to influence culture at a high level: UN, national governments, etc.
Parallel Tracks: valuable but possibly too many possible winners in a cluster diffusing power. Missing the core track and priorities. Closing monitoring required and letting go of something to go with others.
Projection: not much money to be made in education unless long rise or scoring a healthy grant

CT: Carnegie grant after a year of teaching haiku in Bay Are schools. A "Consultant in Creativity" gets paid twice as much as he who shares haiku with children.

Flip the elevator speech: I help people work together while advising C-level executives as a coach. I also help non-profits and academic institutions.

Loose Survey of corporate aiki consulting work resulting in actual income
Crum 3-7000/day depending on group size. Heckler even more.
Thorsen $3-7k per day of consulting, down to $2,500 if engagement contracts over time. $5k-10k for a big room and people brought in, depending on how many and scope of expectations + what/who one must bring.

TRAINING
Avg corp trainer 1,000-1,500/day. Heckler is the only one to really succeed at this. Has to do with filling seats (good to have infrastructure, staff, institute)

CONSULTING
CT has limited perspective with training. Primary focus has been "crack consulting," doing coaching and teamwork in organizations, in search of an observable impact and leverage in deepening relationship.
Innovation and fast growth have been the through-lines in CT career. OD strategic relationships, senior teams, executive coaching

LEADERSHIP & MASTERY
More in the realms of Crum, Heckler, and Palmer. Also possible to create engagements with leadership cohorts in organizations  and for non-profits that themselves draw cohorts from other organizations.

PRESENTATIONS & SEMINARS
The two feed each other. Some coaching comes as a result of presentations.
An important tool to augmenting OD w aikido seminars inside organizational client environments.

What is my unique offering?
Crum Heckler Palmer emphasis is on training side. If they consult, it tends to be a coaching/consulting of an individual.

They also work w groups of people, developing their skills. The focus is also on, for example, developing coaches, bodyworkers, etc. but not including in their curriculum both marketing and sales. Work as strategic adviser in C-suites and with teams seems less common. Maybe Lance Giroux. Aiki consulting practicioner seldom play a role as strategic consultants to organizations, except Heckler within the military and consulting on high performance.

 

CT more along the lines (like ABC?) of: senior leaders and their teams posit vision/mission/culture/strategy/system of accountability/development system and working the often missed critical function of conducting sophisticated discourse.


My skills and history are not replicated Out There. This is not reflected in my elevator speech.

Executive coaching should play a role augmenting the role of Strategic Adviser.
My chops in both process and systems awareness are not replicated by senior colleagues in aiki consulting. This is an edge in consulting orgs and leaders. Emphasize both sides of that coin: reading environments and assessing the state of organizations in the world, and their potential... Flesh out OD role, not just executive coaching. Read the field of a community and advise on that specific community's strengths and weaknesses, holes, how filled in, Org Dev.
It is one thing to advise a leader in their leadership (Conflict Done Well). It is another level of capability to help a leader(s) assess process capability and flow in an organization. Build the process arts emphasis on facilitation.

 

Story: CT acted as adviser to COO who took over operations and released CEO to tech innovation and sales. Rebuilt neglected infrastructure until involving senior team as never before. CT sensed org, what is in place and not. See Enterprise Covenant: what is in place and not. Had vision and mission, but CEO had generated strategy by thinking it up and telling everyone what it was. Created 3 yr (these days long term) strategy through quarterly retreat for Senior Team. Op Strat for year. Set of commitments and individual SLT level for Q-objectives toward fulfillment in layers.
SLT meeting participation by phone. Coached individuals in teams in between. Started tighter teams and stayed in touch with them. Sat w C-levels and VC primary owners at the Board Level. Reported on conflicts raw from the beginning. Original CEO visionary intuitive had to hand the company off to a bean-counter, and it drove him nuts.

OD side has carried CT revenues for decades, and has supported his leadership training work with various executives.
CT 30 yrs ago vision:

Horizontal axis - get this core embodiment knowledge training and education access to the whole world

Vertical axis - work w leaders, gaining jurisdiction w higher and higher until causing culture.

Much more personally limited to vertical than the horizontal axes.

Palmer Heckler and Crum took the horiz - developing trainings, but got drawn into Exec Coaching axis, rather than volume.

In the car on the way home from church we experienced a developmental leap in Rosie. The question: what to do about lunch? Lisa suggests we go home. Rosie pipes up from the back seat "I want to go out for lunch." What does she want? "French fries!" I ask "How shall we decide? How about if everyone says a bit more and then we make a decision together?" This receives universal approval. {{+image|size:large;float:right}}

Lisa is feeling poorly and might not be able to finish a burger, fries, etc. which are not very good re-heated. She also notes that we have already purchased food of precisely that kind which is in the refrigerator. On being asked to say more about going out, Rosie says that "it feels good" and she likes it better. I note that these are all very good reasons. Silence follows. I start the framing process which will illustrate, it seems to me, that Mama has identified the slightly more weighty reasons, when Rosie interrupts with "Mama? Why don't we take you home, and then we can go out to lunch?" We laughed loud and long, celebrated Rosie for being both clever and hilarious (almost always a winner), and went out for burgers and fries, which everyone finished handily. I love my family.  -- [[Brandon WilliamsCraig]]

[[Brandon WilliamsCraig|Brandon]] writing.

Everyone introduced themselves and we welcomed

[[Daemeon Reiydelle]]

[[Jennifer Diaz-Zamora]]

[[Laurent Colvin]]

[[Martin Taber]]

[[Michael Mansfield]]

[[Sergio Diaz-Zamora]]

I suggested that the metaphor "[[soul]]" might be near the core of this group's work, having to do with depth (soul music, food, soulfullness, etc.) and the way in which human beings make meaning from imagining, sense, and experience. Soul is the founding principle of psychology (psyche=soul+logic or modus operandi), and [[mytho-psychology|mythologies and psychologies]] are very similar in the way's that life imagined as  "inner" is written onto a world imagined as "outer" and narratives of Outside and Inside start to mirror each other. I handed out [[Rebecca Mead - Particle Follies - New Yorker|an article from the New Yorker]].

 

Signposts of this mirroring may be the metaphors we live by (tip of the hat to [[George Lakoff]]), the [[archetypal]] complexes (Mother, Power, Food, Birth, and Death) which mark one, and one's thinking and feeling as Human. Perhaps it is the working with these big ideas (who to identify as heroes, how to govern ourselves, eat, come into the world and out of it) that brings us into some understanding of each other and makes [[Community]] possible.

We spoke of choosing our rituals with care, and soul in mind: eating, checking-in, reading, thinking, and speaking together.

 

We noted that it is not only possible but likely that we use the same words and mean different things and ideas.

 

We spoke of the roles appearing in the room, as things got framed in the perspective of The Business Person, for instance, The Teacher, the Craftsman, the Tradesman, etc.

 

Then we chewed on what we might do with these ideas and turned over several subject areas which might be if interest to us:

  1.  HEALTH & ADVERTISING: Flu, Public Health, Media, Advertising, messaging, For Profit Health Insurance Companies, "Single Payer", Who Gets Paid?, more...
  2. GLOBALIZATION & SOURCING: "Sourcing" (knowing where and how, and from whom your products come), Raw Materials, Food, Coffee, Extractive Industries (mining, growing, logging, etc.), Jewelry, Environment, International, Local, Globalization, Labor, Wage Economies of Scale, Distribution of Wealth, Equity, Americanism.
  3. REALITY ACCESS & CONTROL: Legality and social obligation, Spin, Exposure to Risk, Fiction, Reality, Message Control, Actuality, Truth and Story, Narrator-based Realities, Photoshop(tm), Sectional Realities, Integrity, Transparency of Presentation, Manipulation, Voluntary and Involuntary Suspension of Disbelief, Dissociation, Russian Olympic Reality.

and we opted to treat GLOBALIZATION & SOURCING next session, Sunday, March 9th, from 5-8pm

 

I agreed to provide these notes, subscribe everyone to the same email group, and keep us connected.

Daemeon offered to provide food and drink at his own expense.

 

I asked for donations in the form of a monthly contribution to Association Building Community via this link:

http://abcglobal.net/Community_Roundtables

 

Martin agreed to send an email developing GLOBALIZATION & SOURCING further.

cards.name: Journal
cards.content:
13 Nov 2021

I'm listening...Front foot pivots while back foot swings round.

I'm behind you...front foot slides in then back foot swings round.

• In the dojo, studio, or during your research, what theme(s) became apparent to you this week? Did you choose a particular technique from class and experiment?
  • Please record any specific comparisons and relevant thoughts you noticed, including feelings, emotions, ideas for improvement, your sense of discovery...
  • Is this inquiry still on its agreed upon track, growing more likely to hit the mark, while avoiding overwhelm by cool ideas that end up sounding far flung and general?
  • Does this inquiry continue to feel organic/authentic?

{{+One|closed}}{{+Two|closed}}{{+Three|closed}}{{+Four|closed}}{{+Five|closed}}{{+Six|closed}}{{+Seven|closed}}{{+Eight|closed}}{{+Nine|closed}}{{+Ten|closed}}

In Bill Levine’s article “Aikido and Creative Expression in Music”, he talks about his experience using music as a form of expression and how aikido has played a large role in influencing his creative development.  As a dancer, I completely share his discoveries.  He says, “The embodied wisdom and awareness gained from the practice of aikido flowed naturally, almost inevitably, into my artistic process as a pianist and composer.”  Although I have only been practicing aikido for a year and a half, I might as well have written that statement myself substituting “pianist and composer” for “dancer and teacher”.   I do not like to imagine dance without aikido now.  Aikido has helped me find my center in a different way.  It encourages me to be aware of my surroundings.  It has quickened my reaction time.  And very importantly, it has helped me to remain present.  When I practice aikido I am only practicing aikido.  When I dance, I am sometimes eating lunch in my mind.  But with a new respect for the importance of staying present, now when I dance, I am only dancing.

 

I was particularly struck by the two contrasting intentions that Levine claims are expressed through the creative process.  Ego-oriented intention can be compared to most organized dance, which is choreographed.  Spiritual or sacred intention seems to relate more to improvisation or the process of originating choreography.  Through spiritual intention, Levine implies that we become a conduit for the energy of the art.  He feels that the two intentions do not overlap.  Maybe not in music, but in dance, however, I believe we can still have aspects of the ego-oriented intention and still channel the spiritual intention.  As dancers, once a series of steps has seeped into our muscle memories we have two choices.  We can execute the moves as given to us in a “copy and paste” sort of manner, or we can do what I consider to be our job as professional artists: make the movements our own.  When we allow ourselves to put our own artistic footprints on the choreography, we then channel the sacred intention.  The same is true in aikido.  Maybe we have practiced a technique thousands of times.  But the moment we are able to take the technique and make it work, we can then play with our own martial artistic licensing and figure out how to improve it to suit our own bodies. 

 

Levine says, “I am asking what is beneficial for the artist.  What is the function of one’s artistic intention?” YES what IS it?  For the sake of this journal entry, I would like to say that one of the many intentions of an artist is simply self-expression.  Sometimes the expression is ego-oriented, sometimes it is spiritual.  Nonetheless, it is an expression.  In my interviews, I asked dancer Jennifer Goodman how she feels dance is as a form of self-expression and her response was beautiful.  “Not being so socially outgoing in a talkative way, through the movement is when I feel like I’m expressing myself and moving my body and feeling free.  If you don’t feel like you can speak things, just get in and dance and move your body and there’s that expression.  It just feels free.  It feels good.  You can let go of issues in your life, getting your mind somewhere else.  It makes me feel more outgoing especially if I am dancing a character role.  I get to take on the expressions of the character… It feels so good to move your body.  It is like singing with my body.  It is like my body is singing with the music.”  Aikidoist Wendy Guyer has similar feelings regarding aikido as a form of self-expression.  She says, “It becomes like a form of dialogue.  I feel like every aikido practice is a form of conversation with your partner and conversation with yourself.  It is very expressive.  I like it because it is all about the energy that is happening between myself and my partner and also drawing from the energy of what has been going on in my day and in a larger world.  I think aikido expresses a lot.  What am I expressing?  It is definitely emotional.  Whatever kind of day and who ever you are you are bringing that onto the mat and you are interacting with another human being so you are expressing yourself emotionally… The more you practice aikido the more you make it your own and the more your own personality and style… it becomes more an expression of you and less like trying to copy the teacher.  You are using the teacher’s ideas to express yourself and playing with another person’s ideas, but you are really making them your own.  As I progress, my aikido becomes more an expression of who I am and allows me to explore different parts of myself that might not find expression in other parts of my day.  And in a very clear way- I can express the loving parts of myself and also the more aggressive parts of myself and they are all fair game to explore in a non-threatening way.  It’s expressive in ways we probably don’t even realize as well.”

 

Levine: “Aikido enables the body to viscerally appreciate the nature of conflict and harmony, a polar tension important in every art.” ABSOLUTELY.  I have a visceral reaction to this statement, but am having trouble putting analysis onto paper.  Big surprise.  My weakness is being able to express myself through the boundaries of written words.  This is why I dance.  And practice aikido.  I’ll have to meditate on this one.

 

This week I have been thinking a lot about my center or hara.  Finding ones center, in my opinion, is a lifelong practice.  It is interesting to me that I find my center much easier as a dancer, a dance teacher, and Pilates trainer than as an aikidoist.  I hope my experience with finding my center in all of these other movement based activities will help me locate my center more often while practicing aikido.  I am sure my center of balance is stronger than other beginners, however, since I am hyper-aware of my body I tend to feel as if I am constantly searching for balanced alignment.  Practicing jo waza helps me to feel more aligned with aikido movements.  After today’s practice, I named the jo, “centering stick”.  I can’t believe I haven’t thought of that name before!  We worked on both ai hanmi and gyaku hanmi shihonage techniques and when we changed back to open hand practice I found that my movements were smoother, more connected, and controlled around my own center.

 

Levine talks about the importance of being centered.  He realizes that he cannot play optimally unless he finds his center.  “I would realize I was off when I forced ideas, expressing overly emotional and inappropriately loud music… Non-centered artistic expression becomes stressful and I play wrong notes.”  This speaks to my discoveries of the importance of balance.  Jennifer Goodman says, “When I was younger I would try to just force holding a balance.  Now I understand it’s just finding a balance, a center, so it becomes more just being, allowing.  Letting your body just stack in a line.  You can find that alignment finding counterbalance.  I think a lot of balance is internal and mental.  If I had to visualize it I would say it is from the crown of your head through the center of your body out through your tailbone, your base sacral area.  When I am balanced it is easy.  It is not forced.”  Similarly, Wendy Guyer states, “Balance is central to aikido- not only physical balance but emotional balance. Physical balance is essential to every technique.  I step back and I think, ‘Wow, I am a woman and I am sometimes throwing these very big dudes around.’ It takes incredible balance and correct technique in order to do something like that because I am not using brute strength.  My goal is to take my partner’s balance and in order to do that you have to be very in balance yourself.  You have to intuitively feel where your balance point is and where their balance point is.”  In both aikido and dance we need to have balance in order to execute proper technique, keep those surrounding us safe, and to allow ourselves to be malleable: quick on our feet and ready for our next movement. 

 

If I do not feel centered it is impossible to take my partner’s balance.  So along with finding my own center this week, I was also able to experiment a bit with taking my partner off balance.  With the jo, twisting and drawing down forces uke off balance and towards me. I am then able to redirect the energy of that imbalance into a throw.  Removing the jo, I absolutely love the idea that sometimes it is just as simple as allowing the weight of my arms to alter uke’s balance.  We can’t always fight hard to accomplish something.  Sometimes we must just allow, as Goodman mentioned.  The act of allowing is an art in itself and we practice it in both aikido and dance.  Port de bras, or carriage of the arms, in dance helps my arm movements in aikido.  While dancing, we have fluid and flowing, yet controlled and weighted movements of our arms.  We allow our arms to move through space in the fashion that best suits the goal of whatever we happen to be dancing.  This notion assists my arm movements while practicing aikido and, ultimately, is one of the things that helps me find my center.

 

Also this week, I realized something else important involving stability and centering.  During our warm ups that include funekugi undo, ikyo undo, and tenkan, I notice that I ground myself using the same techniques and feelings as when I prepare for pirouettes or jumps while dancing.  I push energy through my legs and DOWN into the floor, pressing my heels into floor to feel that rebound heel/glute connection.  In turn, I can control my pelvis moving through space.  Because every action has an equal and opposite reaction, I feel the feedback pushing up from the ground under my back heel all the way up to my center, which propels my movement, yet simultaneously keeps me stabile. I love experimenting with this connection, but find it challenging to feel while working with a partner.  Undoubtedly, however, this is another great thing to work on that will ultimately help keep me grounded.

 

Oftentimes, in a dance audition or performance, I will repeat several mantras to myself based on what my needs are in that particular moment.  Many times, however, this mantra is “if you relax, you’ll float”.  It is nearly impossible to have a tense body and brain and be able to perform at my best.  In these situations, I need to take a moment and concentrate on breathing and releasing tension and stress so that I may either book the job or finish the show.  I have begun taking this mantra onto the mat and I feel it is very helpful.  If I am relaxed, not only am I better prepared to move, but I can complete aikido techniques with proper ease and effortlessness.  It is a lot more difficult to attack someone that is floating, wouldn’t you think?  And as uke, this relaxed approach allows me to safely follow nage and blend with the energy of her movements.  Levine seems to have the same experience playing piano.  “I discovered through aikido… a central secret to piano technique: relax… The trick is to blend with the piano, as in aikido we blend with training partners… Through relaxation and expansion, based on aikido principles, I began to create music that flowed like a river.”  Relaxation fits right into the category I mentioned earlier: the art of allowing.  What a relief when we actually allow it all happen.

 

{{+Seeley Eval|closed}}

cards.name: BW verification of ABC employment for TalentWise
Understand and respond to hurtful teasing
cards.content:
Meghan Williams Keepin
September 28 at 8:55pm ·

Alright you smart and thoughtful adults! How to help a 5 year old understand and respond to hurtful teasing? Elijah came to me saying that peer said "that he looks like a girl and acts like a girl and the proof is his long hair. And that he's small." He said that he said that he is a boy with long hair and that he's small for his age. And that what hurt his feelings was that she went on saying that he is actually a girl over and over in a really mean way even though now she knew. How to explain "acting like a girl" as an insult? Ugh. Or teasing. Got any good ideas? Any pithy, peaceful responses to offer him? Kim JordanNaomi Keepin,Micah,Brandon WilliamsCraigMichele GuannelAutumn Barnett?


  • Kimber Davis Sad
     
  • Alex Gramps telling her calmly that there's nothing wrong with acting like a girl or being a girl, but that he is a boy and is going to be a boy no matter what she thinks or says? And then ignoring her. How tough for him!

  • Pamela Elliott Smith Well.. I would point out the strengths of women.. & say it's actually a compliment from a small minded person .. Beauty & strength are in both genders. To demean either gender for any reason is a sign of a closed mind. Period.

  • Chris Walton I don't think there's much point to trying to explain that "girl" is meant as an insult; Elijah was upset by not being acknowledged for who he is. It seems like enough to say that the other kid was rude and unfriendly, and that no one likes a rude kid. Maybe that's even a useful response: "You're wrong and rude."

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Alex Gramps, we talked about that your hair does not make you a girl or a boy and that it's "silly" to say otherwise, he said very clearly to me that she was saying that he is acting like a girl, and that is the mean thing.
     
  • Chris Walton "I guess you don't know enough boys."

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Oo, Chris Walton, sharp response, I did say that what was rude was not listening to his clear request to call him "he". Regardless of the boy/girl part.
     
  • Meghan Williams Keepin Ha!
     
  • Meghan Williams Keepin Val said "tell him you're going to tell his big brother!" Eli said "I could just drop a bucket of water on her head."

  • Michele Guannel I don't have an answer at the moment, but I like the comments above and what you did! This reminds me of a reaction to my 2+-year-old son at our apt complex's playground. There were a couple of boys playing there (maybe 3, 4 years old), with some typical "boy" stuff like play swords. At first they started playing with Milo and sharing their toys. But then his shorts got wet from rain on the slide, so my husband changed his pants - and the boys saw Milo's pink underwear ('cause that's the way we roll). They asked him if he was a girl and then took their toys back. Another time, some girls asked if Milo was a girl because he was wearing a pinkish orange shirt and then looked very confused. Regardless of how gender-neutral we raise our kids, there is no way to avoid others' perceptions and damn those perceptions start so young!!
     
  • Sarah DeSilvey steps- 1) solidify the fact that long hair in no way implies gender. Show him pictures of Sikhs and Rastafarians and John Lennon and all the hair bands of the 80s and 90s because part of her presumed power is that he is different and she is signaling it out and in fact he is not alone at all. 2) point out that the real insult lies in anyone assuming gender by appearances. A tomboy or young butch girl might be just as hurt to be told their gender when it is only something we really know within. 3) do a little commentary on how sad it is that being a girl is assumed a point of weakness and show him pictures of Joan of Arc and Anne Frank and Serena Williams and all the girl punk bands of the 70-now. The key is not to have the comeback it is to know within how absurd her argument is and to have confidence in his own self just the way he is. Once he knows this even a simple "that's silly" and a cheek turning will suffice. Though he could create a PowerPoint on the above issues and slay her with logic if he likes.

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Yes, Michele Guannel, I've been amazed watching all my boys and the very narrow allowances of their peers for gender rules. Often kids will be really upset by having guessed wrong about my boys being girls and then won't want to play with them anymore.
     
  • Meghan Williams Keepin So lovely, Sarah DeSilvey! Val is very into Prince, Freddie Mercury, etc. and has read extensively about Vikings with long braids and other long haired warriors. Eli has been included in all this...I think the gender non-conforming piece is sufficiently in our family "norm". Maybe I'm too concerned about him being able to socially handle the teasing. I think he, in himself, is actually quite secure. I worry about the progression of teasing that can happen...he is a very sensitive little soul and with an intense emotional life. I'm frequently trying support him in managing that in the outside world.

  • Chris Walton Unpleasant as it is, there's no avoiding teasing by other kids. I've focused on affirming Gregory's feelings and trying to help him figure when to ignore it, find an ally, talk back, or get an adult involved. It's amazing how many toxic features of our culture we have to help our kids recognize, adapt to, and resist.

  • Kim Jordan I echo Sarah DeSilvey's steps. But I disagree with Chris Walton in that there IS a way to interrupt and confront teasing by other kids. Tools can be taught, ally behavior can be encouraged, kids can be peer pressured to be kind instead of cruel. (It's a pipe dream, but it is POSSIBLE!) Also, I suggest looking into Outright Vermont's Gender Creative Kids program as a resource for Eli to talk with his peers about gender norms. Also, I wonder how his school and teachers talk with students about diversity, gender, how they present their identities, how to connect with people who look different, etc? What is the school climate like? What activities do they utilize to dialogue with the kids about this stuff in age-appropriate ways? Check out Teaching Tolerance magazine and website. It's got INCREDIBLE resources about anti-bias education and how to build empathy skills in all types of learners.

  • Autumn Barnett "Cool, I like the way girls act.

  • Autumn Barnett ... except when they're not being nice to me by teasing me."

  • Naomi Keepin Oh, dear, this is tough. Perhaps I'll have a better answer for you in the morning after my auntie-anger subsides. I do agree with you, Meghan, that the issue here is how to help our sweet boy deal with the meanness and teasing of others, as he does seem rather solid in his own identity expression, and gender non-conformity is more "normal" than not in this family. I'm reminded of Val, some years ago, informing a child at the playground who mistook him for a girl "I'm a boy--you can tell by my long hair", or Elijah telling me recently "at first I didn't know Micah was a she, but then I found out she was a she and I was like 'okay let's play legos'"...but the meanness of others...I'm still trying to wrap my head around that one.

  • Kimber Davis Naomi that's cute what Elijah told you....

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Thanks Kim Jordan, and Thanks all!

  • Kimber Davis Give him a hug for me! He's adorable!

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Chris Walton, I'm liking this suggestion: recognize, adapt to, resist. Sounds like you have really thought this out for Gregory. I appreciate all the ideas! Having a supportive community is so helpful.

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Kimber Davis, he is adorable! Quite a character.

  • Pamela Elliott Smith Also hair in any length.. Is not gender specific ...

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Oh Auntie Naomi Keepin, I know, It's painful to think of him being singled out for teasing at this little age. Both the boys have asked me some version of "why won't people just take me as I am?" and it's a hard conversation to have. It's hard to explain the particular meanness that is leveled at those who are not trying to fit in, or those who have decided that the cost is too high. And I do like those stories, very sweet

  • Meghan Williams Keepin The 5 year old's opinion of all this teasing nonsense...

  • Marcus Allen Gramps Have him tell her that her words are ugly words, not true words.

  • Beth Doyle Bean Meghan - so many thoughtful responses. Elijah's response was oh so perfect, but it doesn't help the hurt feelings. One thing I begin with when something like this happens - and yes, at 12 and 13 it still happens - is to let them know that kids who tease do not necessarily feel good about themselves and they lash out at others to make them feel sad, too. I am sure your kids don't need lessons in empathy, but to flip it this way sometimes helps.....at least a little. "The teasing is not about me, but about them being unhappy".

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Yes, Beth Doyle Bean, I think that empathy is a great response. One of the things I said to him right after was that what she said probably had nothing to do with him or how he really is, but that she was upset and sad inside herself and that it "bubbled out" and got on him. Ugh. I'm just hoping that he will keep telling me what happens so we can talk about it. Thanks for chiming in on this, it's so helpful to hear other parents opinions who are farther down this path.
     
  • Deb Loring Oh boy, this has got to be so hard to deal with. With dogs, all I have to ever say is, yeah, sorry, I know, my dogs are assholes. Yeah, it's their fault. Really. I'm really sorry. This, well, this kind of challenge would be really tough - I feel for you both!

  • Michele Guannel This thread has tons of great info for future use. Thanks, everybody!! It is wonderful to know of so many caring parents out there...

  • Paula Craig First I get it straight by saying, "She was saying things that hurt your feelings ? (or 'were angry' or 'were mean') ? "Well, did you say things to hurt her feelings ? "You didn't ?" " Well, then it is not your problem. You are only responsible for what comes out of your mouth, not what comes out of somebody else's. Some people say crazy things. If she does it again, just say, "That's your problem." sotto voce : " I think she doesn't understand."

  • Meghan Williams Keepin Michele Guannel, isn't is great to hear thoughtful and kind responses? Encouraging.
     
  • Meghan Williams Keepin Paula Craig, it certainly is liberating to remember where the problem lies! I know I fall into reflexive apologizing too much myself....good thing to remember to help Elijah not to do that.
     
  • Brandon WilliamsCraig I love these responses and feel warmer and more hopeful reading them all!

  • Brandon WilliamsCraig I hope that my children will be peaceful by being both martial (addressing conflict directly by practicing with fellow learners techniques that work) and nonviolent (practiced opting-out of individual and group domination, especially including revenge, in order to work toward helping everyone get what they believe they need). If peace is then a martial art of nonviolence (see http://martialnonviolence.com), it must be trained using the body and words together in situations precisely like this. The reality is often that, especially when someone is cruel, one doesn't know what to say or do.

    I believe that it is essential to begin stating explicitly and regularly at the earliest possible moment in a child's life that doing conflict well is an essential skill to be practiced often, and that keeping one's center balanced and moving out of the way of "attack" is the core physical and emotional discipline in times of stress. The next essential piece always involves speaking the truth, at least to oneself if the truth would escalate tensions.

    Some developmentally appropriate steps and words which create good conflict habits, which I have been refining through practice for several years now, go something like this: "I feel hurt by what you were saying/doing. When that happens I have a hard time knowing what to do. Would you like to take turns listening to each other now or should we be apart and try again later?" Next steps might include: "Should we ask for help? What do you need? Let's go together. Tell me more." All the while, the attention is on "how shall we do this together?" rather than "how can I make you stop/leave me alone/improve yourself," etc. because that simply invites the next attack. Whenever "they" come after you, they should know that they will be received in a way that makes further attack irrelevant if not impossible. Practice is required to deploy the art of changing the rules to co-create a world that works well for everyone involved in a way that remains ever open to hearing from others what that might be.
     
    MartialNonviolence.com
    MNv is a method created by Brandon WilliamsCraig to combine the strengths of improv, martial arts, and process arts (facilitation) to work for peace.
    martialnonviolence.com

From February to May 2015, as part of her undergraduate work with [[St. Mary's College]], [[Meredith Ann Seeley]] conducting a comparative inquiry into aspects of dance and aikido. Though the liberal, performing, and martial arts have many shared elements, this study involves a research focus refined by the following factors:

  • Aikido themes are universal but any style practiced is one of many possible styles. Meredith's experience (since summer of 2013) is with the Midwest Aikido Center (USAF) founded by Tohei Sensei. She has attended seminars with Yokota Shihan, Vu Ha Sensei, Andy Sato Shihan, Bernath Shihan, Yamada, and Seki.
  • Dance takes many different forms. This study primarily considers ballet and modern, with brief comparative forays into other areas.
  • The study is experiential and fulfills undergraduate requirements, and so does not attempt an exhaustive review of literature. The resources included in the study are listed as Works Cited.

cards.name: Example Sequence Peace Practices PRINTS
cards.content:
Martial Nonviolence™ for Peace Practices™

 

Change (shoes to bare feet and optional gi/top)

Enter Dojo walking all in a line (with a bow at the door) until being seated, in line in seiza, being still and silent while waiting.

Bowing in

Stretching and Breathing

Cycle through the following movements, asking that everyone truly listen silently, breathe more than they need, and follow--doing together with their body what you are doing with yours. Following the numbered stretches, please find movements marked with * which may be inserted as necessary and helpful to keep the deshi engaged and focused.

  1. "Reach up" for the ceiling or sky while taking in more air than I feel I need.

  2. "And back," blowing out until all your air is gone while stretching backward broadly before standing up again.

  3. "As far forward as you can" with toes closer than heels, reaching hands in an arc towards the floor, with straight legs but unlocked knees, to bring the nose toward the knees.

  4. "Bend knees" to recover the vertical line.

  5. Repeat 1 and 2.

  6. From mid back, pretend to "reach your arms around a tree", bending your knees as much as possible as though you might pull this tree up by its roots.
  7. Repeat #1 "and drop"your arms.

  8. Split "feet far apart", hinging forward at the waist and dropping weight in the center while reaching "arms far apart" to the sides to "fly like an airplane".

  9. “Make a bridge” (in yoga "Downward Facing Dog"): forming a bridge with the body, pushing away from the hands so the butt rises as the chest moves toward the floor, and bringing the heels down at the same time.

  10. “Knees down for Dog and Cat”, bringing the belly down (and wagging the tail) while the nose moves up, and then peering at the belly while arching the back.

  11. “Snake” whose hips are on the mat while he turns fully to right and left "slithering", looking behind and hissing.

  12. “Swimming Frog” whose knees pull up to each side and whose feet touch, while another stretch to the mid-section and groin are in progress.

  13. "Pull your toes where you can see them wiggle" for a seated hip stretch, pulling the souls of the feet together in front, "and lean forward" then pressing down on the knees evenly while leaning the shoulders forward with no back bend, as though to "sniff a flower just out of reach".

  14. Core lift the "hands up" into the air and press them together, then lift and press the "feet up" and together. "Balance on your bottom".

  15. "Pedal" the feet and then "backward", reversing directions, extending from center through extremities rather than clinching muscle to isolate bits.

  16. "Straighten your legs" together and "let them down" onto the floor to "push your heels and pull your toes."

  17. Pull the feet through to "seiza" and then reach to twist and "look behind" on one and then "on the other side."

  18. Flip under and "squish your toes", so that weight rests on the balls of  the feet and body weight stretches the toes. Rock the heels back and forth to squish the toes evenly.

  19. Sit upright on the toes in "[[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiza#Kiza|kiza]]," and rock the "knees off the mat" while holding the head and upper body erect, balancing on the balls of the feet "like a bird perching on a branch".

  20. Moving the arms up and down to the side, "fly up" to standing and slowly back "down" to perching [several times]. End standing.

  21. Trap the shoulder by all "pointing" with the same arm at the same wall and then taking that same arm "across" to point at the opposite wall. Then bring the free arm up to form a cross and "pull"/stretch the shoulder while keeping the lower body still and the knees over the toes.

  22. "Point behind and pull" the arm of the shoulder already stretched behind the head, across and down. Then "lean" far over in the direction you are pulling. "Until your hands go OUT" away from the body "and you go round and round" rotating into reaching circles, "like" your upper body were "the hands of a clock". "Stop at the top", reaching up, "and drop".

  23. Repeat O and P on the other side of the body

  24. "Shake your face", then "shoulders", then the "hands", "and feet".

  25. Allowing the head and feet to remain unmoved, "roll your hips" around in a widening circle in one direction, "and on the other side".

  26. "Reach up" for the ceiling or sky while taking in more air than I feel I need, "and drop".

  27. "Hop like a frog" in place.

* "Spinning to the right" and "to the left" with hands down, out, or up.

 All content © Brandon Williamscraig - contact via ABCglobal.net

 

Sneaking and Ki-ai

Moving Together and Apart

Hanmi and Tai Sabaki

Dodging and hopping over the bokken

"I'm going!" Mae ukemi to hop

Ushiro ukemi to hop "I'm back!"

Shiko "All together."

Tae no henko (body only) - "You are wrong!" (words only) "I'm listening." - both body and words

Katatedori kotegaeshi (body only, no kuzushi until elementary) - "Me first!" (words only) "Let's go together." - both body and words (no kuzushi until elementary)

Shomenuchi Irimi(nage) (body only, no kuzushi until elementary) - "It's your fault!" (words only) "Tell me more." - both body and words (no kuzushi until elementary)

Game

  • Freezetag
  • Helisockter (Jump the Shot)
  • Creature-in-the-grass

Sit in line in seiza, being still and silent while waiting

Bowing out

Leaving together in a line, bowing to the mat before exiting

Changing back into shoes, jackets, etc.

 

NOTES

Please remember that Primary aged children do not test but may look forward to rank and colored belts as they reach toward the Elementary classroom.

If your body is not in shape, for instance to roll well or shikko, please have the most ready student demonstrate with your direction so that others may observe and follow.

Plan it in advance in order to choose, for instance, which tai sabaki to offer in order to introduce the technique of the day. Make sure to go through the attendance process several times before trying to do it in front of kids.
 
Stick to the script and your plan, unless the children would clearly benefit from a detour. Try not to just wing it with whatever comes to mind. Honor with repetition the rituals the group has established and ask the locals to help lead, sometimes varying the order within sequences based on students' choice.

Don Levine Eulogy by Jamie Leno Zimron
cards.content:
We have all lost a dear and irreplaceable friend, colleague, and leader in Don Levine's recent passing. I was grateful to be asked to share about Professor Don Sensei's aikido and AE work at the funeral last week. The service was a beautiful gathering and reflection of the loving communities Don created and nurtured so well. As people expressed their experiences with and appreciations for him, through words and stories and soul-stirring music, a tapestry of tribute was weaved that spoke and sung from the hearts of everyone who was graced by this great and wonderful man. 
In love and gratitude as together we keep on training and moving along the path.
Jamie
 
 
Professor [[Don Levine]] Sensei Celebration of Life
 
The founder of Aikido, Morihei Uyeshiba O'Sensei, saw his Martial Art of Peace as 'medicine for a sick world.' Tho Don didn't begin training until he was 48 years old, his whole being - mind, body, heart and soul - resonated immediately and completely with the great master's teachings. Don relished Aikido, both intellectually and interactively, every moment even to his dying days. 
 
Through his vast vision and tireless efforts, Don Levine has given what O'Sensei directly charged us with: infusing the world itself with more Aikido and Ai-Ki. He not only articulated but formed the actual not-for-profit organization - Aiki Extensions - to allow conscious application of Aikido principles and practices into every facet of life. We, his students and colleagues, all have him (and O'Sensei) to thank for perhaps the most meaningful part of our training and our lives.
 
Don himself was a divine extension of AiKi on earth. In his own inimitable ways, he was filled to overflowing with AI / love, and with KI, life-energy. Indeed he was the embodiment of living life & love. For this and so many reasons his absence leaves a huge hole. He will be sorely missed.
 
Assuming Don is hovering here to hear what we're all saying about him, I think he'd be nodding along that being a Sensei is a lot like being a rabbi on the mat, dressed up in Japanese dogi and hakama rather than talit and yarmulke, and sermonizing through somatics. Aiki Extensions is a complete embodiment of what were Don Sensei's Jewish social action genes and penchant for doing full-time Tikkun Olam - Repair of The World. 
 
Not only that. Don was a master of chutzpah! While many people scarcely dream, his visions were grand and he always took audacious action. It just seemed obvious to him that Aikido's message is meant to be taken beyond the dojo into everyday and every walk of life, in order to make the world a better place for all human beings. 
 
Yet creating Aiki Extensions was a radical thing to do. Nothing stopped Don - not lesser rank, or refusals or rejections or general lack of acceptance within that other 'ae' / the 'aiki establishment' - nothing deterred him from knocking on dojo doors everywhere for practitioners to join AIki Extensions and broaden their training.
 
Where else but at a national AE Conference, or international gatherings literally in castles and camps, can you befriend other instructors and practitioners, to learn as well as inform how they link the non-violent principles of Aikido with their professional work as psychologists, doctors, lawyers, teachers, academics, mediators, business and leadership coaches, athletic trainers, counselors for veterans and PTSD recovery, growing boys into compassionate men and girls into empowered women? For all this we have Don to thank. 
 
That would be Dayenu, enough. 
 
But Don didn't stop there. As an Ethiopian scholar, he was instrumental in bringing the peaceful path of Aikido to war-torn Ethiopia, and training Tesfaye Tekelu as together they (with others here) built the Action for Youth & Community Changecampus and the AE Peace Dojo in Hawassa. 
 
That too would have been Dayenu, enough. But Don dared to unite even Arabs and Jews through The Martial Art of Peace; called on me as a dual American-Israeli citizen; brought in other key players; and together we cooked up the 'Salaam Shalom' Middle East Aikido Project. To his profound thrill and joy, the project launched in 2005 with our historic Training Across Borders Conference, in the UN Buffer Zone between Greek and Turkish Cyprus. Following Don's chutzpah-style leadership we managed to gather 100 Aiki 'warriors for peace' from Israel, Palestine, Iraq, Jordan, Greece, Turkey, Serbia, Bosnia, the Americas and Europe. And we are continuing to forge seemingly Impossible bridges through AE's peace-building projects and 10th Anniversary Training Across Borders Conference this fall in Athens, in dedication to Don Sensei.
 
Don Levine was my dearly beloved colleague, mentor, friend, and we loved calling each other Achi and Achoti ~ my brother and my sister. Working with him, I always loved the feeling of co-conspiratoring. Despite his greatness, and indeed as a part of it, he had no qualms calling me his sempai (senior in aikido rank) and at times even asked me about things. His vast smarts and knowledge came from always being humble enough, open enough, willing enough to be a lifelong student as much as he was our brilliant way-showing teacher.
 
To me Don will always be the dearest and greatest of souls. The man of great heart and wisdom, with a brilliant incisive mind, all blended with the youthful playful spirit of a wide-eyed child forever full of wonder and energy, always making new creations and seeking next frontiers of daring worthy adventures. Were it not for the nasty C-word, I know he would have gladly kept trailblazing ad me'ah v'esrim / to 120. 
 
When people ask the usual question of what is your home dojo, my answer has become 'Aiki Extensions.' I shall always carry Don in my every step and word. I am endlessly grateful to him for giving me my Aikido home, and enabling me to be in the most authentic and useful place I know of. For providing such incredible opportunities for us all to work with our Aiki brothers and sisters off as well as on the mat, so creatively, happily, meaningfully. For the great legacies he has left each one of us to fulfill daily, for as long as we walk this earth.  And I bless him for allowing me to be part of his magnificent, so gifted, and so loving family. 
 
Deep deep bows dearest Don. We know you are alive and well, and living on even more powerfully in the ever-expanding spheres of your remarkable influence.
 
As you would say: Gambatte! Kadima! Onwards! 
Salaam. Shalom. Domo arigato. Abrazos. 
 
Adieu achi, I love you.
 
Jamie Leno Zimron, April 7, 2015

Dear AE Friends, 
We have all lost a dear and irreplaceable friend, colleague, and leader in Don Levine's recent passing. I was grateful to be asked to share about Professor Don Sensei's aikido and AE work at the funeral last week. The service was a beautiful gathering and reflection of the loving communities Don created and nurtured so well. As people expressed their experiences with and appreciations for him, through words and stories and soul-stirring music, a tapestry of tribute was weaved that spoke and sung from the hearts of everyone who was graced by this great and wonderful man. 
In love and gratitude as together we keep on training and moving along the path.
Jamie
 
 
Professor Don Levine Sensei Celebration of Life
 
The founder of Aikido, Morihei Uyeshiba O'Sensei, saw his Martial Art of Peace as 'medicine for a sick world.' Tho Don didn't begin training until he was 48 years old, his whole being - mind, body, heart and soul - resonated immediately and completely with the great master's teachings. Don relished Aikido, both intellectually and interactively, every moment even to his dying days. 
 
Through his vast vision and tireless efforts, Don Levine has given what O'Sensei directly charged us with: infusing the world itself with more Aikido and Ai-Ki. He not only articulated but formed the actual not-for-profit organization - Aiki Extensions - to allow conscious application of Aikido principles and practices into every facet of life. We, his students and colleagues, all have him (and O'Sensei) to thank for perhaps the most meaningful part of our training and our lives.
 
Don himself was a divine extension of AiKi on earth. In his own inimitable ways, he was filled to overflowing with AI / love, and with KI, life-energy. Indeed he was the embodiment of living life & love. For this and so many reasons his absence leaves a huge hole. He will be sorely missed.
 
Assuming Don is hovering here to hear what we're all saying about him, I think he'd be nodding along that being a Sensei is a lot like being a rabbi on the mat, dressed up in Japanese dogi and hakama rather than talit and yarmulke, and sermonizing through somatics. Aiki Extensions is a complete embodiment of what were Don Sensei's Jewish social action genes and penchant for doing full-time Tikkun Olam - Repair of The World. 
 
Not only that. Don was a master of chutzpah! While many people scarcely dream, his visions were grand and he always took audacious action. It just seemed obvious to him that Aikido's message is meant to be taken beyond the dojo into everyday and every walk of life, in order to make the world a better place for all human beings. 
 
Yet creating Aiki Extensions was a radical thing to do. Nothing stopped Don - not lesser rank, or refusals or rejections or general lack of acceptance within that other 'ae' / the 'aiki establishment' - nothing deterred him from knocking on dojo doors everywhere for practitioners to join AIki Extensions and broaden their training.
 
Where else but at a national AE Conference, or international gatherings literally in castles and camps, can you befriend other instructors and practitioners, to learn as well as inform how they link the non-violent principles of Aikido with their professional work as psychologists, doctors, lawyers, teachers, academics, mediators, business and leadership coaches, athletic trainers, counselors for veterans and PTSD recovery, growing boys into compassionate men and girls into empowered women? For all this we have Don to thank. 
 
That would be Dayenu, enough. 
 
But Don didn't stop there. As an Ethiopian scholar, he was instrumental in bringing the peaceful path of Aikido to war-torn Ethiopia, and training Tesfaye Tekelu as together they (with others here) built the Action for Youth & Community Changecampus and the AE Peace Dojo in Hawassa. 
 
That too would have been Dayenu, enough. But Don dared to unite even Arabs and Jews through The Martial Art of Peace; called on me as a dual American-Israeli citizen; brought in other key players; and together we cooked up the 'Salaam Shalom' Middle East Aikido Project. To his profound thrill and joy, the project launched in 2005 with our historic Training Across Borders Conference, in the UN Buffer Zone between Greek and Turkish Cyprus. Following Don's chutzpah-style leadership we managed to gather 100 Aiki 'warriors for peace' from Israel, Palestine, Iraq, Jordan, Greece, Turkey, Serbia, Bosnia, the Americas and Europe. And we are continuing to forge seemingly Impossible bridges through AE's peace-building projects and 10th Anniversary Training Across Borders Conference this fall in Athens, in dedication to Don Sensei.
 
Don Levine was my dearly beloved colleague, mentor, friend, and we loved calling each other Achi and Achoti ~ my brother and my sister. Working with him, I always loved the feeling of co-conspiratoring. Despite his greatness, and indeed as a part of it, he had no qualms calling me his sempai (senior in aikido rank) and at times even asked me about things. His vast smarts and knowledge came from always being humble enough, open enough, willing enough to be a lifelong student as much as he was our brilliant way-showing teacher.
 
To me Don will always be the dearest and greatest of souls. The man of great heart and wisdom, with a brilliant incisive mind, all blended with the youthful playful spirit of a wide-eyed child forever full of wonder and energy, always making new creations and seeking next frontiers of daring worthy adventures. Were it not for the nasty C-word, I know he would have gladly kept trailblazing ad me'ah v'esrim / to 120. 
 
When people ask the usual question of what is your home dojo, my answer has become 'Aiki Extensions.' I shall always carry Don in my every step and word. I am endlessly grateful to him for giving me my Aikido home, and enabling me to be in the most authentic and useful place I know of. For providing such incredible opportunities for us all to work with our Aiki brothers and sisters off as well as on the mat, so creatively, happily, meaningfully. For the great legacies he has left each one of us to fulfill daily, for as long as we walk this earth.  And I bless him for allowing me to be part of his magnificent, so gifted, and so loving family. 
 
Deep deep bows dearest Don. We know you are alive and well, and living on even more powerfully in the ever-expanding spheres of your remarkable influence.
 
As you would say: Gambatte! Kadima! Onwards! 
Salaam. Shalom. Domo arigato. Abrazos. 
 
Adieu achi, I love you.
 
Jamie Leno Zimron, April 7, 2015

cards.name: Brandon Williamscraig accept PCTS Codron Prize for Huston Smith
cards.content:
Remarks for the Pacific Coast Theological Society on the occasion of accepting the Codron Prize for Huston Smith

 

{{Brandon Williamscraig accept PCTS Codron Prize for Huston Smith video}}

 

[[Huston Smith]]'s beloved, Kendra, asked that I accept this award for him, offer profound gratitidue for the long friendships he has known here, and report to this community that

He has been in hospice for more than a year, and very gradually weakens.  Right now he has a mild cold and laryngitis.  He coughs, but seems to forget that he has recently coughed.

Family members come to his bedside for a final visit, only to discover that he will stay a bit longer in our company before departing.

 

{{+image|size:large;float:right}}Professor Smith brought me in to this gathering of lovers of theological wisdom in 2007.  In 2009, we co-created and video recorded two community conversations about belief, mythology, and psychologies of contemporary culture. At the beginning, I asked about the assertion in his book Tales of Wonder that he is not, in fact, a scholar of religions. He jumped in to exclaim "I am a communicator!" and promptly shifted what could have been An Interview With A Superstar into a warm and participatory opportunity for shared inquiry. He brought the larger than life figure of Professor Smith into the room as Huston and illustrated his natural gift for helping us regard ourselves and our ideas of the divine with a healthy dose of modesty. Idolatry slunk away and the divine mystery alive in gathered people was celebrated.  He wielded ideas like a liberal and martial arts master devoted to nonviolence. The idolatry of Institutions seemed to gain no ground as he held forth on behalf of the often waivering spirits made vulnerable by belief and the trust that accompanies Faith.

 

I hope we will celebrate him tonight and hereafter not just because he became so widely known, but because his life work celebrated the way that Religion, imagined through the relational lens of mystery, makes us more humane and the world more likely to be a place of deep listening, empathy, amazement and learning than a place of war and destruction. Celebrate him because he provided a living example of this principle. Even as he sometimes does and sometimes doesn't wake up when I enter the room, or remember my name, he remains available to be deeply and warmly known by any person he meets, suggesting that we might all do the same, religiously. 

 

I am profoundly grateful to be asked to appear on behalf of and thereby be associated with Huston Smith. Ted Peters wrote in an email to me the words "old timers in PCTS know and revere Huston". May someone, someday, say something similar of each of us, perhaps as we are in the process of enjoying our last hours here before depating for The Hereafter.

 

{{+cuts|closed}}

It is a bit beyond the scope of tonight's festivities to put it in these terms, but I am a terribly small player in the world of Dalai Lamas and Hustons Smith. Before I had even earned a doctorate, he invited me to tea, disagreed with me with great tenacity and respect, brought me into your company, attended and wept at the funeral of my first-born, Aidan Paul, and was overjoyed about the arrival of my daughter, Rosalie Victoria. These days, my two year old son, Huston David, accompanies me to visit and sing for his namesake.

Aikido for Balance and Confidence is ready for you!

Please RSVP to (510) 697-1513

This Friday, January 17th, from 1-2pm at 1514 University Ave, I will offer a no-impact class which will provide immediately usable structural tools to honor your body's concerns while maintaining and improving balance and the ability to move with confidence.

Please wear flexible gym clothes that will allow reclining and moving on our comfortable floor mats. Bring any assistive devices you use on a daily basis. We have changing rooms for men and women. Please arrive up to ten minutes early if you would like to use them.

If you are already a student of aikido or Martial Nonviolence and not working with movement issues, you are most welcome to come, learn, and help demonstrate.

Hoping to see you,

Brandon

P.S. If you have not made payment arrangements or a special agreement already,

please contribute $20 or more on the day, or go to http://abcglobal.net and become a member of Association Building Community for whatever one-time or recurring donation you feel is appropriate.

1514 University is a "partial accessibility" public space. A wheeled personal transport device can access the entry area from University Ave, but a step-up of approximately 6 inches is required to enter and leave the mat and access the bathroom, which is not ADA ready.

It goes something like this:

Once upon a time there were brother and sister cities gathered around a Bay, all with a storied history of social justice work. The people who lived nearby knew that, even though water, food, clothing, and shelter are required to survive, not everybody gets them. Healthcare too, they realized as a basic human requirement, and education to be able to think and communicate so that group decisions for the good of all become more likely. Many people who worked to serve the needs of the most vulnerable did so because they wanted to help humanity become more humane, and had seen thirsty, hungry, exposed, or ill people fail to get help and then suffer and die. Many people who hadn't seen this in person yet had a hard time undetstanding how it could happen, and so despaired of being able to help despite truly wanting to reach out to their brothers and sisters in need. Even beyond basic survival, they couldn't see how public policy and bureaucracy could really be a matter of life or death, until they experienced personal losses due to systemic violence. Nonetheless, many people struggled to be free from fear and make the world better for their children and grandchildren.

Very few people realized that the survival challenges and policy fights could be transformed by re-shaping how we imagine conflict. This final major barrier between real everyday experience and a truly humane life was not even on the radar of most decision-makers. Few people knew, until somebody told them this story and put the problem clearly in these terms, that our survival as a species hinges on how we are and aren’t educated to welcome difference and work through conflict. After an argument seemed to be over, you could ask a participant "how did that go?" and many would grimace, shrug, and reply "Awful, but what can you expect from a fight?"

One day, a few workers in the middle of these cities began to insist that you can expect quite a bit. Just as some people study the liberal arts to have options when faced with a new idea, and some study a martial art to have options in the face of aggression, these people practice peace like a martial art in order to make better outcomes much more likely for everyone involved. They practice a [[Martial Nonviolence]] which combines aikido with language to deal with fear and physical violence and get the imagination and strategic mind working at the same time. Many of them learned to love improvisation, so that they could imagine and create "[[Conflict Done Well]]" together in response to real dilemmas. Through their [[Association Building Community]], they practiced facilitation skills to shift groups from win-lose habits into crafting best possible outcomes with no victims needed. They began to share the [[Peace Practices]] they had learned with children, adults, and families in Oakland, Richmond, and Berkeley, California.

An international foundation discovered these Peace Practices and gave this group enough support to become a daily part of two Montessori campuses in San Mateo and Emeryville. The learning about conflict there began to flourish in the classrooms and in the homes of the families who loved the school, until over two hundred more people of all ages had learned that Conflict Done Well was possible. But the workers practicing peace in so many places, while they knew how to help people learn to work through conflict, found themselves small and alone in the Wilderness of Fundraising and began to cry out. The stories told in the dark around the non-profit fires suggested that the survival of life-giving work depended on self-immolating executive heroes, or angel visitations, or dark and unsustainable practices which left no energy for the beloved work. Despite the modest support of many individuals, the financial lifeblood of this vital work continued to ebb, to the point that Peace Practices seemed unlikely to reach the people who and places that needed it most.

The next installment is for you to write.

This work for the survival of the planet out-performed all of our targets, with the one exception of fundraising. Are you a savvy philanthropist or social entrepreneur who can lead our fundraising taskforce through this wilderness?

 

 

 

I wish that the link between suffering and scarcity and conflict was clearer in the beginning. Perhaps just one sentence: Quickly, communities felt the need to defend against alternative views of the world, and conflict became a source of tension rising to violence.

The core theme of al martial arts is Readiness, created primarily by long term training combined with complete attention to current circumstances. Several sub-themes are universal in establishing readiness for conflict:

Balance

Balance is a verb which refers to a set of structural habits which are always in need of being reestablished. It is something you do, all the time, rather than a thing (noun) you have or lack.

Connection

Connection refers to the energy-transfer relationship through which intention not only becomes action but gets a result.

Change

Change is movement that is always in progress.

Results:

Dear dear Brandon. You are great. I don't want you to meet my expectations. I want you to be you. Hopefully you will like me and we can be comfortable together.

You seem to be an genuine, kind father who works to create peace and social justice.

An interesting 'exercise' . I warn you that people are not truly going to tell you what you should hear, seeing the commentary that was posted on this site, it appears people giving you nice frothy and complementary comments. I have known you for a number of years and although we have lost contact for a while and seeing your commentary it appears that little has changed. So here it goes:

There is usually two people have in one person, the person people see and the person they really are. Often these two are different. Like when a couple meet for the first time, they put their best foot forward but later after the dust settles, the other person sees that side they did not get to see often a darker side. That is the side that people have the most problems with and often will not want to face it. I suspect that you will ignore this post like you have done so in the past.

Who you want people to see:

1) Well spoken: often you talk in riddles and often are very verbose confusing you subject to appear well versed but basically comes off as inarticulate.

2) Weird: You wear strange clothing (or at least you did) with a 'kilt' and a fanny pack (seriously?). This is to make you appear quirky, but in fact you're very socially apt.

3) Educated: See number one

4) Have desire for social change: This one may be true or not, I do not know. It appears it is more like an idea that you have to prop yourself up, like having your own non profit, which does really nothing and has no really use.

5) Good nurtured: You want to appear that you laugh things off when in fact you get resentful when someone crosses you and have deep rooted anger and for no real reason (like most American males)

How you appear:

1) Arrogant: This is a trait that all American white males seem to carry to some degree but some seem to be more rude about it than others, you seem to fall in the latter category.

2) Socially apt: You are quite the social butterfly. Contrary to your odd garb, that some socially awkward person may wear, you are very good at socializing. As a result, you are quite normal and only pretending to be odd, like someone who tries to be weird because it is the 'cool' thing to be.

3) Mean: Yep, you are a bully. There were many times that I observed you rudely bully someone because you could and you even bragged about it to your friends, not cool. Often you would bully those who had a lower station than you that did someone that you disapproved of.

4) Condescending: I have experienced this myself. You tend to talk down to others, as if you are lecturing them than having a conversation

5) Shiftless: Except having your non-profit and a PhD program, it did appear that you were gainfully employed. I think in certain circles this is socially acceptable, but from where I stand it is definitely not plus,especially since you have ability this appeared to a wasted resource.

6) Angry: You have deep seated latent anger that seeps out at the right time. Even your idea “doing conflict right(LOL)” appears to try to correct this fault.

Congratulations! You are a typical American white male in a post industrial society. Yes you have some great flaws, but defiantly not ones that you will put in jail. Although I do not think you will look at this list or even care I thought you should know.
