cards.name: Mythological Studies with an Emphasis in Depth Psychology Degree
cards.content:
{{+Shannon Sloan-Spice Intro}}

[[Pacifica Graduate Institute]]’s Mythological Studies program, a unique interdisciplinary humanities program, is the only doctoral program in the United States that investigates mythologies and cultural traditions as systems through the lenses of religious studies, literature, and depth psychology. By discerning similarities in the world’s traditions, students uncover the common patterns in the history of ideas, systems, and structures, as well as the diverse ways human beings live and make meaning of their experience. Cultivation of the mythic imagination provides a capacity for self-understanding, as well as an understanding of cultures other than one's own. This cultivation becomes an interpretive and communicative art that thrives on paradox, ambiguity, and the shape-shifting ways in which symbol and metaphor inform and transform our lives and bring us back into authentic relationships with ourselves and other cultures. This approach is rigorously academic or historical, but is also much more: it asserts that myths mirror the patterns of human thought, can help map consciousness itself, and must be studied as important symbols and mysteries of human nature. Exploring the myths of various world traditions through the lens of depth psychology, graduates of this program also explore their relevance at the individual level. We look for experiences, dreams, and patterns in human activities and institutions like art, literature, pop culture, architecture, and education that explain our current attitudes and ideas and point the way to how we can contribute positively to the world.

 

The study of myth is interdisciplinary and multicultural. The program emphasizes the interpretive modes of depth psychology, and particularly the influences of Sigmund Freud, C.G. Jung, Marie Louise von Franz, James Hillman, and Joseph Campbell. It also integrates the world of great aesthetic and hermeneutic philosophical thinkers, from which depth psychology builds its foundation. The Mythological Studies Program is a doctoral program designed as an integrated M.A. / Ph.D. sequence with advanced coursework in four areas of study, resulting in over 18+ graduate credits in each discipline. Equipping graduates to teach in any one or more of these humanities disciplines, we are trained to expertly facilitate conversations about recurring mythic themes in classic and contemporary literature, theatre, art, and film, while recognizing the cultural and historical contexts.

 

A breakdown of a recent transcripts is as follows:

Mythological and Religious Traditions
Hindu Traditions: 2 credits, Ritual: 2 credits, African Diaspora: 2 credits, Native Myths: 2 credits, Buddhist Traditions: 2 credits, Christian Traditions: 2 credits, Islamic Traditions: 2 credits, Hebrew and Jewish Myths: 2 credits, Religious Approaches to Myth: 2 credits, Egyptian Mythology: 2 credits

= 20 Total Graduate Credits.

 

Myth and Literature
Greek and Roman Myths I: 2 credits, Sacred Traditions: 2 credits, Myths of the Underworld: 3 credits, Mythic Motifs in Cinema: 2 credits, Greek and Roman Myths II: 2 credits, Epic Imagination: 2 credits. Mythopoetic Images: 2 credits, Folk and Fairytales: 2 credits, Colloquium III: 1 credit

=18 Total Graduate Credits.

 

Psychology and Culture
Dreams, Visions and Myths: 2 credits, Metaphor, Myth and Culture: 2 credits, Jungian Depth Psychology: 2 credits, Colloquium II: 1 credit, Archetypal Theories: 3 credits, Cultural Myths: 2 credits, Myths of the Self: 3 credits

= 20 Total Graduate Credits.

 

Research

Approached to Myth: 2 credits, Myth and Philosophy: 2 credits, Integrative Studies: 1 credit, Research Strategies: 2 credits, Dissertation Formulation: 2 credits. Dissertation Writing: 15 credits

= 24 Total Graduate Credits.

By

Shannon Sloan-Spice
 

Hello Everyone, I am following up on a discussion we had some months ago about seeking employment teaching with our degree. This was around February, the post was started by Priscilla. I have been working with my dear friend Sharon Chapman in conjunction with the myth faculty in crafting a one-page equivalency statement--for those of us in the job search who have been asked to provide one when applying to teach at community colleges, especially. I previously shared one, but since bouncing ideas off of Dennis, have found a particularly effective way of crafting something that not only honors the coursework, but features our capabilities as alums of the program to the best possible degree: As many of you know, one is required to have 18 graduate credits to teach in any particular discipline. This statement is crafted to suggest that our PhD was like getting four master's degrees in the blended humanities. The trend more and more seems to be toward hiring people in departments who can teach across the disciplines. While looking at it, you can argue that the courses can belong to more than one category, which is true. The point is to give a minimum of 18 credits in each cornerstone category of our degree that Pacifca officially says are the foundations to our work so you can teach in each of those four disciplines. 


My aim, after that FB thread,( aside from finding employment) was to help find a way to offer everyone a cutting edge in their job search. The end result for me is after nine months, and countless rejections, I was offered to teach a class in world mythology at Oakton Community College in IL. Very grateful for a for a foot in the door as they offer 10 sections of world mythology classes! 


I am also grateful to Patrick for providing useful cover letter verbiage which I shared in that thread, and to beloved Dennis for helping me solidify what that cutting edge needed to be. I have added the equiv statement to my CV. You have permission from both the dept and myself to use this verbiage in whatever way helps you. Please keep me posted if it works! Definitely will want to celebrate your success! 


Please note that the dept has crafted their own equivalency statement as a result of my request, but did not assign 18 credits to each category and some of the coursework names have been changed from 2014 to 2015 according to their document. I took what the courses were called on my transcripts for this document. They have also crafted a very fine official dept document which may be helpful to crafting an equivalency statement that works for your needs. 
I hope these resources help. 
Many Blessings, 
Shannon

David Williams:

Word up dude... life is good. I just had a procedure yesterday. Now I can do things without any pain but my leg feels like it belongs to somebody else. I hope this goes away. But as we all know there is no free lunch. The nerve that was blocked, is just a sensory nerve. So, my leg now feels like it belongs to some other dude; however, there is no longer any pain. My ego is Raging. My initial diagnosis was correct! The next step is to find an orthopedic hip Doctor Who can discover why there's a trapped nerve in my pelvis. I am aware that this is a terrible old cliche, but getting old is not for the faint of heart. 

On to another unrelated topic. I'm starting to feel happy and productive again. That has to be a really great milestone. After one decides  that nobody really gives a shit what one does, one has to decide what one really wants to do. (God are there a lot of ones in that sentence). That is the problem. Well anyway, I'm now studying ancient history and Greek. Having  a lot of fun. Isn't it sad. There is just no shortcut to a great education. I think often of David Miller and James Hillman. Even if you only have two weeks to live there is just no way to cut corners.

Dadlio

 

Brandon:

Word to my father! I couldn't be happier to hear about all that excellent stuff. Amazing, isn't it, how the actual person experiencing the medical condition has important information to bring to the diagnostic process? I'm really glad to hear about the history and Greek too, by the way. The only problem with that in the past has been imagining that you needed to be a world-class professional scholar. That goal is harder than hell at the best of times, and shouldn't ever interfere with anyone's avocations. Life is too short to waste on whatever fails to feed the soul.

David:

Oh also, I'm checking out an amazing scholar named Thomas McEvilley. His book is the Shape of Ancient Thought. His 2000 page 53 pound book seeks to prove  that ancient Greece is not the Cradle of the Western intellectual philosophical tradition. He claims that they inherited this from India based on trade routes and in that they were both part of the Persian Empire.  Maybe I hurt my back lifting this book. Anyway, I'm on page 2 of the preface. I think I got a pretty good grasp on it. Anyway that should do it. You know what they say about too much of a good thing. Well time for a nap.

 

Brandon:

Appreciating you. A bit of Dad humor is precisely what this day required.

David:

When you have a moment, let me know what you're up to.

That's what the day needed a little Broski humor.

{{+image|size:large;float:right}} Here's to genetics! 

David:

Brace yourself. Here's the way it goes down. You're working 16 hour days without time to go to the bathroom and then overnight you're grazing In The weeds saying "what the hell happened?" It probably pays to have a plan.

Love that picture! I've still got my Kilt, but I can't afford to wear it and also pay for the divorce.

 

Brandon:

Or in my case: no savings, a six-figure debt, almost 50, doing essential work with lots box satisfaction but no pay, with two small children still to get all the way into college, so it's almost pointless to make a plan. This is the New Middle Class. Retirement is a fiction for us. There won't even be weeds left to graze in, unless our kids fix the system somehow. Sorry. True story, My Kilt was actually made for me by a bride who wanted me to be in her Celtic wedding. How could I say no? The funny thing is, there was a high wind that day and I came within an inch of being the best man.

That's my dad! Gotta go. More later.

You're probably right about the content and text messaging. However, let me say that working into old age is probably not a bad idea at all if you really enjoy what you're doing. I think having to adapt to the Work World Keeps you out of the death cue. But I'm not sure. Talk later.

cards.name: Aikido and Practicing Peace Like A Martial Art
cards.content:
Aikido is a Japanese martial art that was designed in the 20th century with a specific purpose in mind. It is unique in its dedication to a specific ethics that changes the way conflict works globally, rather than simply defeating adversaries. The ethics that accompanies aikido practice explicitly requires redirective responses which accompany and preserve an attacker through the conflict process, as well as the extension of these “aiki” principles into everyday life. 

In this way, the process of practicing aikido as a martial art is similar to the dialogical process of the liberal arts in which ideas and their advocates are entertained as guests, a process which may lead to the development of authentic citizenship. Both aikido and liberal studies have the opportunity to create an ongoing learning community which works by way of differences toward a deeper understanding of the tensions involved in thinking, moving, and being. Participation in this process frames human endeavor so that it may become more humane, committed to justice, and more subtle so that power is exercised wisely.

Donald N. Levine was the Peter B. Ritzma Professor Emeritus of Sociology and the dean of the College at the University of Chicago. At the time of his death in 2015, he was the most prominent in a group of academics and professional martial artists around the world who teach courses which integrate learning aikido with liberal education at the curricular and institutional level. This course is rooted in his scholarship.

My name is Brandon Williamscraig and I have been studying aikido since 1990. I am ranked a 5th degree black belt, and am Founder of Free Aiki Dojo and Chief Instructor of Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley. My Ph.D. and primary academic interest is in the relationship between psychology and mythology--the study of interpretation, imagination, and culture-making through belief narratives. Professor Levine recruited me in 2008 to join in the work of moving forward the theoretical and practical study of peace and conflict. With many others around the world, we created public programs, projects, conferences and an administration for an international NGO, called [[http://www.aikiextensions.org/about/governance/board-of-directors/|Aiki Extensions]], home of the [[http://tab2015.org|Training Across Borders]] initiative which gathers aikido leaders from peoples and countries in direct conflict so that they may train together and co-create peaceful relationships. I created the [[Martial Nonviolence]] ™ method and the [[http://peacepractices.org|Peace Practices]]™ project at [[http://abcglobal.net|Association Building Community]], and continue to be actively engaged in the work of which this course is a part.

 

Aikido & Practicing Peace Like A Martial Art

 

DRAFT Syllabus (proposal) for St. Mary’s College - January Term 2017

Brandon Williamscraig Ph.D., instructor

Julian Wilner, apprentice, course assistant

 

This course has three aims:

  1. to expand knowledge about conflict and ways of dealing with it responsibly;

  2. to explore themes and resources for cultivating character and understanding others;

  3. to introduce the Peace Practices of Martial Nonviolence (aikido, language, performance, and facilitation) as a means for dealing with conflict and the cultivation of citizenship.

I believe that this class offers a unique approach ideally suited for January Term, but requiring some explicit clarifications. Each week is a unit building on previous work, such that each learning outcome is required to be able to do well on whatever comes next. The fitness of students for a martial arts class should not be a major concern. While aikido techniques are used to offer a feast of nonviolent conflict resolution principles, combat of any kind will not be on the menu.

I. SOMATIC AWARENESS AND AIKIDO

Aikido the Connector (embodied ideas about sensation, feeling, mind, spirit, soul)

  • Mind > body (mental framing and emotional balance)

  • Body > feelings (postural structures and expression of affect)

  • Mind > body > energy (alignment of intention)

  • Body > perceptions > mind > spirit > soul (relaxation, connection, and systems)

These are modes of learning through aikido, attending to experience and collaborative inquiry with training partners.

Which conditions support intense bodymind learning--dedicated place (dojo), uniform (dogi, if available), attitude (shugyo) and disciplines of safety and respect: 1) for Place; 2) for self; 3) for partners; 4) for /experienceteachers; 5) for conversations; 6) for Truth?

The mat-dojo as a place for learning the martial Way (budo) Respect in the dojo (li / rei)

Elements of martial practice: Tai sabaki (body management). Stance (kamae; hanmi). Changing hanmi. Stepping and pivoting. Sitting (seiza). Turning falls into rolls, if mats are available. The dojo/training process as a place for learning about one’s self. Centering experiences. Testing for centering and ki extension.

Technique(s): Tai no henko (katatedori tenkan) “You’re wrong!” “I’m listening.”

“Why Aikido?” Context of study profoundly shapes learning results.

Announce plan for remainder of course - take questions on syllabus

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

II. INQUIRY INTO CONFLICT

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises based on Session One

Technique(s): Katatedori kokyunage (wrist-grab, breath-throw).“You’re wrong!” “Let’s sit.”

Broaching the study of anything. Is it? Why study it? How to define it? Why define it that way? (cf. “essentially contested concepts”) Why/How study it?

Broaching the study and redefining/normalizing conflict. Aikido practice as collaborative associative inquiry.

Attacking sincerely and falling safely (ukemi). Investigating conflict on the mat. Types of conjoint training. 

Seminar discussion of reading

Technique review

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

III. ELEMENTS OF AND TRAINING FOR CONFLICT

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Katatedori kotegaeshi “Me first!” “Let’s go together.”

Motives, means, and consequences in conflictual interaction

Three part model: basic, expanded, and immediate

Elements of martial engagement: Distance and timing (ma-ai)

Categorizing attacks and types of responses.

Seminar discussion of reading.

Technique review.

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

IV. ESCALATION / DE-ESCALATION: PERSONAL SOURCES

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Menuchi Iriminage “You!” “Tell Me More”  

Paradigms of escalation. Escalatory effects of different responses to attack Counter-attack. Acquiescence. Moving off the line. Taking a hit. Offline with connection.

Escalatory effects of different forms of aggressive expression Expressing antagonism in a relationship.

Seminar discussion of reading.

Technique review.

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

V. ESCALATION / DE-ESCALATION: SOCIO-CULTURAL SOURCES

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Shomenuchi Ikkyo Omote/Ura “You!” “Do you mean that/this?”

Social mechanisms for controlling escalation

Bodymind mechanisms for controlling dispositions to escalate Positive receptivity. Reframing and redirection. Embodied responsive techniques for controlling escalation

Seminar discussion of reading. REFRAMING ASSIGNMENT DISTRIBUTED

Technique review.

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

VI. VIOLENCE

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): TBA

Dimensions of violent engagement. Training for courage Entering the line of attack.

Staying centered under stress Multiple attacks (randori). Irimi waza.

Seminar discussion of reading.

Technique review.

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

VII. MARTIAL NONVIOLENCE

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): TBA

Conceptions of non-violent engagement

Training for Calm Control. Mushin. Reframing and redirection.

Leading the mind.

Seminar discussion of reading.

Technique review.

Reading assignment informed by this session and preparing for the next.

 

VIII. IMPROVISATION AND PERFORMANCE

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): TBA

Using imagination to connect real life with training. Framing all conflict as training.

 

IX. MEDIATION AND FACILITATION

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): TBA

Happo giri undo

Third parties in the management of conflict

Hovering awareness (zanshin).

Position and timing in mediating conflict. Conflicts with multiple parties

REFRAMING ASSIGNMENT DUE

 

X. PEACE PRACTICES AND CULTURE-MAKING

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): TBA

Review of Readings and Discussion of Final Paper

Bringing real life concerns and working with them on “the mat”

 

XI. LIBERAL, MARTIAL, AND PERFORMING ARTS - KINDRED DISCIPLINES

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Student choice

Bringing real life concerns and working with them on “the mat” across domains

 

XII. OTHER ASPECTS OF CONFLICT AND LEADERSHIP

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Student choice

Leadership consulting

Bringing real life concerns and working with them on “the mat”

 

XIII. THE AIKI WAY AND MYTHOLOGY AS PARADIGM

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Student choice

Classic formulations Ueshiba, The Spirit of Aikido

Quotations from Aikido Masters: Ueshiba, Saotome, Doran

Training as ritual and vice versa

 

XIV. PUTTING IT TO THE TEST - A

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Review

 

XV. PUTTING IT TO THE TEST - B

Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Technique(s): Review

 

XVI. ENDING

Demonstrations of Preparatory Stretching and Body Management exercises

Final papers due

Testing and Celebration

cards.name: Psychology on the Outside and Mythology On The Inside
cards.content:
Course Title:

Psychology on the Outside and Mythology On The Inside: An Archetypal Introduction to Depth Psychologies and Culture-making

Course ID:

JAN XXX

Instructors:

Brandon Williamscraig

Contact Email:

bdw1@stmarys-ca.edu

Course Description:

Human beings use and wander around in ideas big enough that they seem eternal and able to reproduce in endless variations. Some “archetypal” patterns have appeared in cultures around the world at least as long as there has been writing to memorialize the human experience. This course will surface personal and cultural narratives we develop and perpetuate in order to discover some of the ways we use the ideas we believe to make the world in which we live. Brother Camillus has agreed to visit lead us in meditations if he is available, but is not yet certain if he will be.

 

If we construct daily life based on the ideas we use, then our methods of interpreting and assigning meaning to experience are of profound importance and deserve careful study. At some point, an obligation arises for an adult to examine habits of thought, her own and then others’ relationships to cultural patterns and norms, and decide which beliefs and actions are best to repeat. This is the work to which the liberal arts are a prerequisite, and can lead to authentic citizenship through the practice of entertaining ideas as guests, relationships proposed by others.

 

We will pursue avenues of inquiry identified with C.G. Jung and several influenced by him, including Joseph Campbell, David Miller, Thomas Moore, and James Hillman, the founder of Archetypal Psychology. Each studies psychology and mythology as though one were a language for the other, a way of connecting the worlds imagined as inside and outside the individual, so that it is possible to make both personal and collective choices which make specific lives, communities, and the world as a whole more beautiful and sustainable.

 

Human beings are not only architects of the cultures which make the world and daily life. We are also shaped by the habits, rituals, and structures we live through every day. This course will introduce archetypal meditations alongside art, social media, and corporate products. In counterpoint with introductory texts on mythopoetic hermeneutics, we will begin to surface and engage contemporary forces that influence belief and motivate social action, drive trends, create norms and public policy, and set the stage for the ways we entertain, categorize and stereotype, violate, love, and abandon each other, constructing lives with and without future generations in mind. There will be both examination and play.

 

Division:

Lower Division

Prerequisites:

None

Reading List:

Texts In Hand

 

Bruno Bettelheim, Freud And Man's Soul, selections

Joseph Campbell, Myths to Live By

William G Doty, Myth: A Handbook

James Hillman (with Thomas Moore), A Blue Fire, selections, and Healing Fiction

C.G. Jung, Jung on Christianity, selections, and Memories, Dreams, Reflections (with Jaffé)

David L. Miller, Facing Apocalypse, selections

George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, Metaphors We Live By, selections



Articles, Essays, Exercises, Media, and Presentations

 

Articles and cartoons from the New Yorker, Atlantic, and other magazines

 

Brewster Y. Beach, "God as Trauma" presentation for the October 2002 Journey into Wholeness conference archived at http://www.cgjungpage.org/learn/articles/analytical-psychology/602-god-as-trauma

 

Brother Camillus Chavez FSC, audio meditations

http://www.brothercamillus.com/brcamillus/audio.php

Videos [San Francisco, California, USA] Kanopy Streaming, 2014

http://stmarysca.kanopystreaming.com.stmarys-ca.idm.oclc.org/video/james-hillman-archetypal-psychotherapy

http://stmarysca.kanopystreaming.com.stmarys-ca.idm.oclc.org/video/james-hillman-soulless-society?final=1

http://dlmiller.mysite.syr.edu/lectures.htm

http://www.myss.com/free-resources/sacred-contracts-and-your-archetypes/appendix-a-gallery-of-archtypes/

 

Basis for Final Grade:

Basis for Final Grade: one major 10-page paper or two minor papers, 5 pages each (40%); Quizzes (20%); Oral reports (20%); Engaged participation (20%)

Course Fee Per Student:

$10

Description of What the Course Fee Covers:

The course fee covers the production of readers.

Class Schedule:

Spaces reserved for freshmen:

7

 

Psychology on the Outside and Mythology On The Inside:

An Archetypal Introduction to Depth Psychologies and Culture-making

 

DRAFT Syllabus

St. Mary’s College - January Term 2017

Brandon Williamscraig Ph.D., instructor

 

Outcomes:

At the end of this course students will be able to

  1. Work critically with patterns often referred to as "archetypal" which recur across human cultural experience and are uniquely accessible to students of the liberal arts.

  2. Relate ideas associated with C.G. Jung, Joseph Campbell, William Doty, George Lakoff, and James Hillman having to do with the interrelationship of psychology and mythology.

  3. Have access to specific practices which connect critical thinking with "personal mythologies" and systemic value narratives.

  4. Deploy a mythopoetic social justice critique of contemporary culture vis–à–vis art, media, policy, and corporate products.

 

Core Curriculum Learning Goals

 

American Diversity

 

The student who connects critical thinking with "personal mythologies" and systemic value narratives must engage differences and note the generationally persistent dynamics which permeate belief narratives. In this course, ethnicity, race, class, and other categories often used to negatively discriminate are surfaced as roles and stereotypes, studied for the power they make available for both oppression and liberty, and included in strategies for encouraging the more humane treatment of self and other.

 

The reading, paper assignments, and examination requirements develop a critique of historical and fictional patterns at play specifically in the United States. The student cultivates diversity at the level of image, such that the social implications of an idea become sensible in the form of a rich, imaginal narrative. It becomes clearer what kind of story one is living in, and less problematic to figure out the ways in which this kind of story often plays out. In this way, the structures of power are laid bare and the effect of the beliefs behind the power-plays are easier to articulate. This articulation contributes to proposals that account for the social, role-based projections foisted upon both individual persons and the groups with which they are identified. Tropes like "Make America Great Again" cannot help but come under scrutiny.

 

Common Good

 

Critical work with archetypal patterns demands a perspective that is fundamentally communitarian, because making a case for ubiquity requires demonstrating recurrence across human cultures in the potentially fulfilling search for meaning. C.G. Jung, Joseph Campbell, William Doty, George Lakoff, and James Hillman all work at the intersection of psychology and mythography in order to propose thinking and actions that will forward a just social order, keeping in mind the abuses of narrative for political power that echo to this day. A mythopoetic critique of concrete social problems visible in contemporary media, policy, and corporate products allows for both the demonstration and evaluation of coherence analysis, and fruitful challenges to be offered as to the principles being practiced both in the choice of interpretive lense and in the formulation of conclusions.

cards.name: Conflict Done Well for the Cadets of the UC Berkeley ROTC program
cards.content:
{{GBA_20150831_2792|float:right;size:large; padding: 0px 20px 15px 10px}}I hope you will join me for training that will help you meet your educational and service goals. This page is both an orientation to the principles we will be testing, and the beginning of an argument, a case I will make for a particular kind of practice, conflict training I believe everyone needs in order to:

  1. Balance and deploy from a position of strength while under stress, including the stress of being a student and service member

  2. Plan strategically and execute tactically as part of a team striving to both meet requirements and excel

  3. Transition between roles and assignments in a way that makes sense, for instance, moving between command environments and civilian life.

Everyone has a limited amount of time. Some essential skills get enough training to make a good beginning. Many necessities get less attention than they deserve. In my experience, the one essential skill that gets the least training is how to do conflict well. To be a part of any team, especially in a conflict environment, you need to be able to engage in conflict on purpose, while under stress, staying relaxed, balanced, and ready to choose the options likely to work best for everyone involved. The only way to learn this is to practice it until you can embody it even under the worst circumstances.

{{GBA_20180205h_8795|float:left;size:large; padding: 0px 20px 15px 10px}}A martial art called aikido was created to make this training possible. It's purpose, from design to execution, is to use the physical self-defense techniques originally found in jujutsu to shift how conflict works - the rules of engagement. For instance, a well known aikido and leadership professional, a Marine named Richard Strozzi-Heckler, wrote "In Search of the Warrior Spirit: Teaching Awareness Disciples to the Military" after working with Special Forces for an extended period. They learned that conflict is somatic, involving the whole person as one system, which is very different from the idea that efficiency simply follows increasing control of the body by the mind. They learned that physical and psychological practices are distinct but inseparable ways of understanding and adjusting one whole, dynamic system, and incorporated more subtle exercises in their elite training to increase their individual effectiveness and coherence as a team.

After getting aikido started, my students move beyond the physical movement into real-time conflict practice that is also verbal and systemic so that they can apply these practices to their learning, leadership, and longevity. In this way, physical and psychological modes begin to work together. What before seemed separate is connected: body/mind/spirit/soul moves in concert to shift conflict's rules of engagement from habits of automatic fight/ flight/ freeze to responsive, natural movement toward solutions that work in the real world.

If you want to be truly ready when duty calls, to lead and follow well, get your balance back when you lose it, and do well in whatever you choose, then the way to get there is through practice. What you do with your limited time is, finally, up to you. Please train with us, so you can be ready to do conflict well.

Many thanks to the UC Berkeley ROTC leadership for this opportunity!

Brandon Williamscraig Ph.D., Aikido 5th dan

learn@conflictdonewell.com

 

{{brandon_kendogi_lateral|float:right;size:medium; padding: 0px 20px 15px 10px}}

{{+Lesson Plan|closed}}

Introduction

I’m here to offer you something you need because it will help you to be effective, admirable, and more likely to get back up when you fall. If you are like my other students, you will do what I do and test the principles over and over, returning again and again to train together and improve ourselves and each other. We challenge each other in ways that make us better than our earlier selves without making anyone a victim, without harming anyone in the process. We will warm-up, do some exercises, stop for questions pretty much any time, and then debrief. My reasons for being here are to introduce you to Conflict Done Well, and ask you to be a part of my training group.  

Warm Up

Falling Down well? and getting up easily and quickly

Somatic

[Ask what “somatic” means]

  1. Greek word for body as whole system. People say body and mind as though there were a separation, but there really is none.

  2. How you move reflects how you think, and vice versa, so training and education are both vital, because one shapes the other through repetition.

  3. Doing something over and over makes habits. The more you do and think in a certain way, the more you are likely to repeat the same kind of process and project it into the world as belief, choices, and behavior.

Don't let them pull you over the line.

Balance, Flexibility, and Response

What you need will change, and will always be influenced by but not always provided by others. As a result you must be able to operate as:

  1. An individual, on your own initiative Kihon

  2. A member of a team of two or more Ki no nagare

  3. An influence in a system Ki musubi

 

Balance allows one to deploy from a position of strength Structural Movement Litany

While under stress How To Be Annoyingly Helpful

Option Generation While Staying On Target Randori

Optional: Numbers, while moving, while being pushed, counting backward

 

Outcome of Ongoing Training - Habits That Work

Incorporate difference, failure, and conflict in your planning, so strategic choices stay relevant

Be in the habit of executing tactically as part of a team striving to both meet requirements and excel

Transition between roles and assignments in a way that makes sense, for instance, moving between command environments and civilian life.

cards.name: Goodbye California
cards.content:
The Short Version

{{Williamscraigs 20180506_9551|size:large;float:right}}I will be ending my work as an instructor of graduate students at Pacifica Graduate Institute and Communications Director at Ragged Wing Ensemble, so that we may move back to Texas. We will be moving back to Dallas at the first of August to be with my mother, who turns 80 this year. Lisa is very happy to begin teaching for [[White Rock Montessori School]], and we are in the midst of grieving, packing, spending time with friends, and feeling overwhelmed by logistics, endings, and the tremendous potential associated with this move. I am going back to the land of my birth, and plan to provide executive leadership, speak publicly, teach all ages of students, and write, as I devote more time to loving my family and taking in the beauty of being alive in the world.

Please contact me right away to schedule anything that needs to happen in June or July, including time together, so that I may attempt to follow up and make arrangements. There are many things with which we could use some help, given capacity and availability. If we don't make contact before August, I will also look forward to seeing you when next we meet, wherever that may be. If you’d like updates about [[Peace Practices]], [[Conflict Done Well]], and my other adventures in teamwork and social justice, please be sure to subscribe at http://abcglobal.net/Find_Us and follow https://www.facebook.com/brandonwilliamscraig/.

There is more to all of this, obviously. If you want to connect with me, move the work I do forward, or read more and deeply into what is happening now, I cannot ask sincerely enough that you stay within my circle of friends: 

  1. I'll be writing more at Culturesmith.com, with the more detailed and personal material protected by signing-in. Please request an account via http://culturesmith.com/account/signup or sign in, if you already have an account. I will approve and welcome you, after which you will also have access to all kinds of fascinating materials for cultural study, should that interest you.
  2. I will use the newsletter here ([[Subscribe to my newsletter]]) for communicating the ways that this transition connects our inner lives with the wider world. There will be various gatherings to say goodbye, and I'll use that list to let you know about them.

Please re/subscribe now, during this time of profound transition, so we may stay connected, even if at a distance.

Love,

B

Given time and interest, for the full version of this post please click here.

 

This probably won't surprise anybody...

http://www.kron4.com/news/bay-area/46-of-people-living-in-bay-area-plan-to-leave-in-next-few-years/1217518902

SAN FRANCISCO (KRON) - "Forty-six percent of people living in the Bay Area say they plan to leave it in the next few years,...according to a survey from the Bay Area Council. Last year, that number was 40 percent. People say housing costs and traffic are the reasons they want to leave...24 percent said they would move within California, and 61 percent said they would leave the state altogether."

{{Williamscraigs 20180506_9551|size:large;float:right}}We will be moving back to Texas in July to be ready for school to start there in August. The Chair of the Depth Psychology Somatics Department at Pacifica Graduate Institute let me know that Pacifica had instituted a hiring freeze, and would not employ me at the end of of my time teaching as a post-doc/adjunct. Immediately thereafter, my employer in Oakland, Ragged Wing Ensemble, eliminated my position to address their budget crisis. In Dallas, my 80 year old mother's house was robbed as she slept with her hearing aids out, and Lisa was recruited by a prominent Montessori School.

I came to California from Texas in 1995, leaving all my family and support networks behind to become a traditional, full time, live-in aikido apprentice, because my career in vocal music and the professional theater seemed to be only part of my calling. I became a professional aikido teacher, mediator, and group process facilitator. I organized, protested, and worked to forward social justice causes. I co-founded and lead nonprofits, became a leadership consultant, and earned a Ph.D. in psychology and mythology in order to speak the language of culture-making fluently. I served local and international organizations at an executive and board-level, working for peace through alternative dispute resolution while providing support and pay-what-you-can, no-barrier-to-entry [[Conflict Done Well]] training for colleagues of all ages and experience levels who identify as people of color, queer, disabled, transgendered, immigrant, displaced, and otherwise marginalized.

Individuals have recognized the value of the work outlined above, and subsidized our housing, made donations to keep us afloat in times of utmost distress, offered space for classes, and expressed appreciation in many different ways. With a partner school, I obtained international funding for the [[Peace Practices]] project, which vaporized after two of a promised three years, resulting in lay-offs, closure, and debt, despite paying myself a minimal salary.

In all this time, through the death of a child, a Great Recession, and thousands of hours of lead generation and searching for professional opportunities, no business model reached the point of sustainability in the San Francisco Bay Area, burdened with a once-deserved reputation for innovation, gentrification, and an ultra-high cost of living. With a large educational debt, no home that is ours, no savings or investment, and creeping up on 50 years of age, I have asked my family to pay a significant price for these years of determination to work No Matter What for a world that works for all. It is time to shift to a different pace and longer view, care more deeply for my family, raise funds, perform work with a much higher level of remuneration, and let go of the conviction that I know what is best or needs to be next. This ending represent a death, the closing of a chapter of the dream that carried me West. For this I have some grieving to do.

After stating the facts as clearly as possible, the initial problem in taking next steps has to do with genre. When one is deep in a time of trial, the world looks very grim indeed, and daily life feels thorny and inimical at its core. When one is enjoying the gifts of living, the biting wind seems merely a cooling breeze, the dark is more invitingly mysterious than terrible, and the customary messages that you don't really matter to other people seem more quirky than weaponized. If the path of the Williamscraig family leads to opportunity and discovery of unanticipated blessings, then this will have been a comedy. If the current dice-rolling is ill advised, for reasons within or out of the realm of control, then the cascade of failures to come will seem tragic...if we had only known...

How to figure out which kind of story we are in? After years of studying mythology and psychology together, I know for sure that, despite the story one has been taught to believe or would rather be living, what's really happening matters. When you ask for support and not enough people respond, or do and then disappear, then obvious consequences follow. What others see and do matters. They can push the framing of the story in a particular direction. How we tell the story matters. The work I do is essential, by all accounts, so I clearly lack something necessary in bringing the story of [[conflict done well]] to life for other people in a way that they find compelling. As belief is required to bring about change, a lack of the former denudes the latter. 

With that said, some things should be easy to change, like politicians who either serve the people or don't, and some things should be hard to change, like the institutions on which a vast majority of people depend for their care of each other. We live in a time of casual but vicious institutional destruction by people who should be as temporary as possible, and it is difficult to build a support institution in a time where disruption seems more attractive than cultivation. So, I gues, the final problem also has to do with genre. Contemporary people seem profoundly confused what kind of story they want for themselves and their children. We put gamblers in charge of banking, shamelessly public thieves and liars in charge of government, and watch our financial and civic systems burn, while allowing those who need nurture to fail and fall. 

Some understand that it is a time for bulding new infrastructures, and act. I ask that you join me in trying to be like those who are most admirable. Do the things you can do. Admire, click like, share, comment, and offer appreciation, but also contribute money, donate your time, and don't stop. The new thing you want to become the status quo will always require a mass of people to pass the appreciation phase and get all the way through to Don't Stop. Peace Practices, for instance, children and adults practicing [[Conflict Done Well]] continually and absolutely depend on your specific and continual support to have any kind of future.

Please contact me right away to schedule anything that needs to happen in June or July, including time together, so that I may attempt to follow up and make arrangements. There are many things with which we could use some help, given capacity and availability. If we don't make contact before August, I will also look forward to seeing you when next we meet, wherever that may be. If you’d like updates about Peace Practices, Conflict Done Well, and my other adventures in teamwork and social justice, please be sure to subscribe at http://abcglobal.net/Find_Us and follow  https://www.facebook.com/brandonwilliamscraig/.

Also, I must learn to let go of relationships that are not reciprocal. If you want to connect with me, move the work I do forward, or read more and deeply into what is happening now, I cannot ask sincerely enough that you stay within my circle of friends: 

  1. I'll be writing more at Culturesmith.com, with the more detailed and personal material protected by signing-in. Please request an account via http://culturesmith.com/account/signup or sign in, if you already have an account. I will approve and welcome you, after which you will also have access to all kinds of fascinating materials for cultural study, should that interest you.
  2. I will use the newsletter here ([[subscribe to my newsletter]]) for communicating the ways that this transition connects our inner lives with the wider world. There will be various gatherings to say goodbye, and I'll use that list to let you know about them.

Please re/subscribe now, during this time of profound transition, so we may stay connected, even if at a distance.

Love,

B

Through a Postdoctoral Fellowship at Pacifica Graduate Institute (Carpinteria, CA), I served as an Adjunct Faculty member in the Somatics Specialization of the Department of Depth Psychology.

Classes Taught:

DPS 955 Frontiers of Somatic Depth Psychology Winter 2018 III

Frontiers of Somatic Depth Psychology is a foundational “bookend” course for those completing their graduate coursework, about to launch through the dissertation into the world. I was asked to design it to revisit and build out from the cornerstones laid in earlier classes in a way that frames individual, group, and archetypal contribution to depth psychology, and takes up the social justice, peace, and conflict-related studies implied by Pacifica’s orientation--to tend soul in and of the world. We connected core texts and recent innovation with student-chosen articles and direct experience in order to support their identity as colleagues contributing to a growing and essential field. We explored the humanistic and qualitative perspective, describing, proposing, and demonstrating an operative archetypal sense of body-centeredness from which communitarian narratives and conflict-transformative practices arise, thereby making a practical planetary peace possible.

DPS 851 Relational Embodiment Fall 2017 III

This course took final-year graduate students through the ways embodiment is learned, located, and lived as a relational orientation.  It moved in three themed phases: 1) self, and the sense of evolving born of a developmental narrative, 2) other, and the adult sense of connection--the use of power that is supported/challenged through the dyadic encounter, and 3) system, the holistic sense that is supported/challenged through group and community experience. In-class exercises, reaching through the body as an interpretive process, integrated practices that make room for discoveries about difference, conflict, trauma, and healing, while connecting the theoretical metaphors in the reading and class discussion with the felt sense of lived experience.

DPS 792 Integrative Seminar Winter 2018 I

Integrative Seminar offered first-year graduate students a structured and facilitated opportunity to integrate varied course material into a cohesive theoretical framework, and to practice applying their developing knowledge and skills to a range of professional issues and contexts. Embodied learning, critical thinking, divergent perspectives, and intergroup relations were key areas of focus, and led each week to participation in a professionally facilitated Council process.

DPS 899 Summer Fieldwork Proposal 2018 II

Students developed and submitted successful fieldwork proposals in preparation for DPS 906 - Summer Fieldwork II. I mentored each through the proposal development process as one of three Fieldwork Advisors working with a sub-set of second year students.

DPS 932 Dissertation Development Winter 2018 III - co-taught with Kesha Fikes Ph.D.

In this course, final-year students mastered the elements of a research concept paper and its relationship to the proposal and final draft of a dissertation. This sequence resulted in every third year student completing a viable and approved dissertation concept paper.

Time Slicing draws into the same frame of reference how much you can notice and how you notice it, and asks that you increase the former by changing the latter.

An example: challenging circumstances tend to narrow focus to the highest energy components. If someone is going to hit you in the face perhaps you are distracted by the look in their eyes or the incoming fist. There is a feel that you have changed your relationship to time when you focus on their posture in order to notice how they are striking, thereby making it more difficult for them to land their blow. You've done more in the same stretch of time based on how you use your attention.

 

So you would respond to a psychological attack in the same way: don't focus on the fact that it is happening and is unfair, scary, mean, ect. instead focus on how it is happening? How do you know what is important to notice?

--[[dena burd]].....2018-12-19 01:34:51 UTC

cards.name: Conflict Done Well Aikido Training at SSUMC
cards.content:
This is history! Conflict Done Well is no longer taught in person at St. Stephen United Methodist Church, as we now gather at [[Aikido Oak Cliff]]. Please come join us!

Below you will find the words we used to describe our work together.

[[Conflict Done Well]] begins with martial arts and yoga-based exercises, then aikido movement and concepts, which are then used to learn nonviolent self-defense. To the movements and principles we add language and practice improvisation in order to apply techniques in daily conflicts of all kinds so that restorative justice leadership results. We will be forming a volunteer social justice action team in which you may want to participate. All adult persons of any description, ability, and misgivings are most welcome to join. Teens are warmly invited to ask for parental permission and to join as well.

Please wear clothes in which you can comfortably stretch to your full range of movement and learn at your own pace to keep your balance under stress and rise easily from the floor. If you are able, a sustainability donation is requested after beginning regular attendance, but none is required to begin or continue training. A portion of the donation will go to the St. Stephen community.

{{Automatic_Billing}}

Conflict Done Well includes [[Martial Nonviolence]] (MNv) training with [[Brandon WilliamsCraig]] Ph.D. - 5th dan Aikikai. When the MNv curriculum is adapted for and adopted by a particular community, that is called [[Peace Practices]] (PxPx). Here is a video with more information.

cards.name: Conflict Done Well method
cards.content:
{{CDW Ai2 MNv PxPx logo 20211025aSm 500x422|size:full}}Conflict Done WellTM is based on principles from the martial "Art of Peace", called aikido, professional theater techniques, and somatic psychological research on long-term teamwork and leadership. We have received international funding, been deployed by families, in schools, and by leaders across many professional domains, and CDW has proven helpful to both children and adults giving and receiving assistance while working through conflict exacerbated by behavioral challenges.
We use movement and language sequences to develop conflict habits which are directly applicable to the difficulties that are part of daily life. Learn at your own pace the full range of options available to respond creatively in conflict. Keep your balance under stress and recover more easily from difficult experiences.
CDW is ideal for first responders and other service providers who must weigh their need for life-balance and personal safety on the same scale as the needs of clients who experience escalating levels of stress. We achieve results by creating an ongoing learning environment, rather than offering tempting but insufficient one-off solutions, and co-creating a practice of conscious conflict as though learning an art form. Results of working on your conflict skills include increased quality of life, positive family, team, and community connections, and courage to take tools in hand with which it is possible to craft a satisfying future.

Conflict Done Well involves the next itteration of aikido, called [[Aikido_2|Aikido 2.0]], to which improvisation and facilitation skills are added to make the [[Martial Nonviolence]] (MNv)TM method. When the MNv curriculum is adapted for and adopted by a particular community, that is called [[Peace Practices]] (PxPx)TM. All training offered at this time is with the founder, [[Brandon WilliamsCraig]] Ph.D. and 5th degree blackbelt.

cards.name: Three of a Crime game rules
cards.content:
Game play is very simple. The game has seven suspects – Humpty Bumpty, Loose-Eye Lenny, Jonny Cortex, Kid Cassidy, Louie St. Louis, Pencil Top, and No Neck Nick. Thirty-five cards, showing every combination of three of these suspects is shuffled, and one player is chosen to go first.

This player takes one of the cards and secretly looks at it; this player is the “eyewitness” of that round. Starting with the next player (detective), each player takes the top card from the deck and displays it face up on the table. The eyewitness then takes a cardboard token numbered “0”, “1”, or “2” and places it next to the card, denoting how many of the suspects on the card match the one hidden by the eyewitness. This continues, with the next player placing a card, etc.

At any point, any player may shout out Accusation!, pausing the game. They then indicate the three suspects they believe are on the eyewitness’ card. If they are incorrect, the guessing player is out of that round, and play continues. If everyone has guessed incorrectly, the eyewitness wins the card. However, if the player has guessed correctly, they win the suspect card. The player to the left of the eyewitness becomes the new eyewitness, and another round begins. This continues until one player wins three suspect cards – at which point they are declared the winner!

About

I am ready to serve on your management team! I have provided C-level collaborative leadership, executive consulting, communications planning and messaging implementation, team development, conflict management facilitator training, and alternative dispute resolution since I began offering mediation services in 1999. As CEO of Association Building Community and principle consultant at Culturesmith, I created the Peace Practices curriculum and internationally funded project, which delivers my Martial Nonviolence method in K-12 schools, universities, and other institutions. I originated and offer Conflict Done Well (TM) at the enterprise level to evolve next-level leadership and teamwork through somatic (whole living-systems), conflict-based, mindfulness training for wellness and increased productivity.

I also teach at the university level. For more information, please visit my academic profile at https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Brandon_Williamscraig

Specialties: Transforming businesses and groups into high-yield/lower stress professional communities through "conflict done well" and dynamic communication; third-party-neutral ADR and facilitation of non-adversarial resolution through both mediation and negotiation; agile and sustainable administration, ensemble creation, and team building; communications and performance; supervision and management.

cards.name: School Bus Stop Arm Safety Program
cards.content:
Doug Yates, Captain 

Criminal Investigations Bureau
Mesquite Police Department

Captain Yates,

My name is Brandon Williamscraig, and I am happy to be a new resident of Mesquite, having moved our family here last year. The purpose of this letter is to notify you of a potential fraud being committed in the name of a "Mesquite Marshal's Office" and the Mesquite Independent School District pursuant to a "School Bus Stop Arm Safety Program" (SBSASP ?) and the website ViolationInfo dot com. If it is not appropriate to involve you in this, I hope you will forward this information to any representatives of the city or school district who can put an end to the practices described herein, and that you will reply to me by email to brandon@williamscraig.com with a confirmation of receipt and any suggestions I may follow to protect my family. The amount they are attempting to extract from us would leave us without groceries, and so exceeds what they probably calculate they can expect from people who don't want to spend time investigating or just want to make an inconvenient intrusion go away. We are educators, and it represents way more than an inconvenience to us.

I have the following information due to a postal mail item I received November 7, 2019. The parties who are behind the SBSASP and ViolationInfo website served me with a "Delinquent Notice", of which I first became aware on that day, saying:

"Dear Sir/Madame:

If you have already paid the Notice of Violation, please disregard this Notice. You have failed to respond in a timely manner to the Notice of Violation listed above, issued to the vehicle registered in your name and a late fee has been assessed. Failure to respond may cause a registration hold be placed on your vehicle with accordance to applicable state laws. It is in your best interest to pay this immediately. Please see the reverse side for payment instructions."

I have attached a copy of the notice. Drawing parallels to widely published mail fraud tactics, I conclude that extortion at the national level may be taking place for at least the following reasons:

  1. I am also a professional driver, attentive and scrupulously law-abiding behind the wheel, and have no recollection of disregarding a school bus at any time.
  2. When I first heard of the matter on November 7th, I had allegedly already "failed to respond in a timely manner to the Notice of Violation". As "the time to contest this violation has passed", the amount demanded has increased to $325 and is due 12/4/2019.
  3. The "Mesquite Marshal's Office" appears to have no concrete/physical connection to or location in Mesquite. When I search on the internet for the various names and specific phrases used in the message, it does not appear to be real. Furthermore, it uses the PO Box 22091 in Tempe, AZ 85285-2091 for its "School Bus Stop Arm Safety Program" (SBSASP).
  4. Payment by check or money orders should be payable to "Mesquite ISD" but are to be mailed to another PO Box 742629 in Cincinnati, OH 45274-2629 where, it is reasonable to be certain, the Mesquite Independent School District is not located.
  5. The "Mesquite Marshal's Office" prints on its postal mail an apparently fabricated shield resembling law enforcement badges, in general.
  6. The location of the alleged offense is given only as a set of coordinates, entirely absent more commonly understandable terms such as street names or locations.

Should I notify Mesquite ISD that their name is being used in this way? If so, do you know with whom I should communicate? 

Is there any chance that SBSASP operatives can extort our family, either through a "registration hold" or in any other way that can be made to appear to be legal? In the unlikely event that this is possible, I ask that you take this matter seriously and reply as soon as possible, as we have little recourse if public systems are leveraged to extort us.

With appreciation for your service to the community,

Brandon, Lisa, Rosalie, and Huston Williamscraig

3733 Strayhorn Dr., Mesquite TX 75150

I'm by no means well-educated on either conflict, but as we prepare finally to withdraw from Afghanistan, one big parallel with Vietnam looms clear-once again the U.S. was trying to win a military conflict that was always, in fact, a political conflict, and in the end what will happen is that Afghanistan, like Vietnam before it, will have paid a terrible price to form the exact government they would have formed before the war...the Taliban will institute their "Islamist" system, as the Viet Cong instituted their "Communist" system, and in hindsight/history, it will be hard to understand fully why we were there...

Brandon WilliamsCraig
It doesn't seem to me very hard to understand fully why we were there. The real difficulty, the betrayal, and the reason for so extensive a cover-up, in both cases, is the lies that lead us in. The stated reason for being there was not the actual reason, which leads to cognitive dissonance (Gosh, I Don't Understand How This Could Be Happening) and decades of alleged soul searching because the truth is so hard to accept. Tens of thousands of ours and theirs died because a tiny elite wants to be more powerful/wealthy and places no value on the lives of less powerful people.

Don Olander
I don't entirely agree. There's always that crowd of course, but we always have the real policy people and the true believers and those that are really trying to do good as they see it. Communism = bad, then Islamist = bad. When they make the formula that simple, it gets too easy to go on for a while. But the real reason for how long it went on is that the administrations and military continued to treat it like a military conflict, that we just had to beat enough of them (kill enough of them), where for them defeat was never an acceptable alternative to any kind of cost and horror...

Brandon WilliamsCraig
An admittedly too simple description of the order I see might look something like this: In a given war, Believers (Just War) and Betrayers (Blood Money) both get things rolling. Betrayers work at all times toward a system that makes war easy and more likely to continue when it can be started, whereas Believers turn their attention to other things when the war machine is not the most direct path to the ends they prefer, thereby surrendering the System to the Betrayers. Both like formulas that are too simple, because that makes it easy to go on killing for long enough to secure The Goal. Then the Too Simple runs its course and both Don't Understand How This Could Be Happening, but with differing degrees of self-awareness and cynicism. The Believers are very ready to Not Think About It Anymore. Lots of people with less power/wealth die, we return to some version of the status quo, some very few people make a ton of money and accrete a bunch more power, the workers then spend their lives during "peace" to rebuild the infrastructure on which the wealthy depend, and the cycle gets ready to repeat when the next ideological &/or financial plumb is ripe for the picking. There are sub-narratives (tactics) which advance the greater strategy, like "we just have to kill enough of them to win their hearts and minds" (get our adherents into power). These are usually specious at the outset but Good Enough To Get The Ball Rolling for everyone on board the project as a whole.

cards.name: Toby Threadgill - Carolyn Enas Threadgill 1932-2020
cards.content:
Carolyn Enas Threadgill (1932-2020729)

My mother passed away yesterday in Georgetown, Texas from severe respiratory distress. It has not yet been confirmed as COVID19 but in the last two weeks 10 new cases of the virus have been confirmed in her nursing facility, including infections among staff members. My mother was one day away from celebrating her 88th birthday.

Piano was my mother’s passion. As a child, Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini or some other classical masterpiece was my alarm clock each morning. She got her degree in Music Performance/Piano from Texas Christian University, the host of the Van Cliburn International Piano Competition. She counted Van Cliburn among her friends in the early days of his fame and was an avid supporter of the Van Cliburn Foundation. It was her talents as a pianist that captivated Edwin Threadgill in 1957 during a party at his girlfriend’s house. My father, a very eligible bachelor, zooming around town in a new Jaguar XK-120, was considered quite dashing, and my grandmother, a local socialite, had big plans for her only son. So, imagine the surprise that flowed through the room when a divorcee with a young son, named Carolyn Enas sat down at the piano and ripped out a flawless rendition of Chopin’s Fantaisie Impromptu that totally bewitched my father. He once told me, that at that moment, all the other women in the room disappeared, including his girlfriend Kitty, and everyone noticed. My mother and father were married two weeks later in a private ceremony at the home of HC & Gwen Enas. Hilariously, my parents didn't even spend their wedding night together because my father was afraid to tell his own mother. Apparently there was a lot of growling and gnashing of teeth by my socialite grandmother over the revelation that she had instantly become a mother-in-law and stepgrandmother to a woman and little boy she’d never even met. Eventually it all worked out and Kitty forgave her two friends, providing a kitten named gidget to the couple as a wedding present so she wouldn’t be totally forgotten.

In the early 1960s, piano playing took a hiatus while my mother tried to manage raising three sons, the two youngest of which, me and Tommy, were double trouble. One story my mother loved to tell explained why she temporarily ceased volunteering for the Van Cliburn Foundation. Somehow, during a visit by female foundation members, her two toddlers attempted to flush some unguarded and very expensive hats down a toilet. Another story she loved to entertain friends with was how my brother Tom and I stuck a garden hose in the sunroof of our Volkswagen Beetle, filling it to the top. She would physically act out a scene reminiscent of a Three Stooges comedy skit, where she opened the car door and was washed into the gutter by the tsunami of water that burst forth. Laughing, she mentioned that Tommy and I just stood there watching the event unfold like we were innocent bystanders.

In time my half-brother Mike was old enough to corral his two younger brothers and maintain some sense of domestic harmony. With this my mother jumped back into her passion of playing music and started giving piano lessons at our house. She would go on to become quite popular and respected as a piano teacher, but to me she was just mom. I never realized she was so well-regarded as a teacher until many years later when at a party some members of the Van Cliburn Foundation came up to me and asked me my name. Jeanne Graham Frick, who had attended high school and college with my mother, pointed me out to them. After confirming my identity, accolades were heaped on my mother for her ability to identify students with exceptional talent, instill strong basics into their playing, and then send them on to more advanced teachers. One woman explained that my mother’s ego never entered into her teaching, and that as soon as a student learned everything she could teach them, she without hesitation sent them off to another teacher for more advanced instruction. She added that without this kind of selfless dedication to the pursuit of excellence, many students with extraordinary talent had been held back too long by a teacher’s ego and consequently never enjoyed the chance to realize their full potential.

In the late 1970s, following the death of my father who tragically died of a heart attack at only 45, my mother dove back into music, again pursuing her own skills as a pianist. She developed a fascination with Béla Bartók’s music thanks to Lili Kraus, the famed artist-in-residence, at TCU from 1967-1983. I can remember my mother’s frustration at trying to play Bartók’s Mikrokosmos, a series of increasingly difficult etudes, totally different from anything she ever attempted. Lili told mom that she should try to master some of Bartók’s etudes to broaden the scope of her repertoire and improve her keyboard dexterity. In the end, it worked out fine but in the interim she was frustrated as hell. Bartók’s modern style with its syncopated rhythms and occasional dissonance just weren’t her style. Mom really preferred the compositions of the romantics, particularly the Russians, but that said, she could go into an impressive pyrotechnical display on the keyboard when she really needed to. Her rendition of Scarlatti’s Sonata in G Major L 286, that I recorded around 1982, proved that Lili Kraus’ advice had paid off. It remains mesmerizing to me that with her hands starting to suffer from arthritis, she could still perform with such a dizzying display of dexterity. In the mid-1980s two 7-foot grand pianos, a Steinway and a Yamaha graced her living room. The Steinway Model B was her preferred piano for its robust lower register, but the Yamaha C7, with its lighter and more precise keyboard touch ultimately became her favorite due in part to the increasing limitations created by her arthritis. She just couldn't bang away on the big Steinway anymore.

In the mid-1980s, emptying out old boxes that had belonged to my father, I found a stack of reel-to-reel tape recordings of my mother playing. They were dated 1957 and 1959. Among the recordings, I was shocked to hear Satie’s Gnossiennes, Scarlatti’s Sonata in G Major and Handel’s Harmonious Blacksmith. These compositions were recorded when my mom was in her mid-20s and she was really on the mark. She had Satie’s subtle phrasing down to perfection as well as the escalating elegance of Handel’s Blacksmith. To this day, tears well up when I hear the recordings of her playing the Handel and Satie compositions. It takes me back to the magical days of my childhood, to times when everything around me was new, exciting and grand. Like a movie soundtrack, behind every experience of my youth was this wondrous music played by my mother. Looking back, I realize how incredibly lucky I was. I had two parents who were supportive, present, involved, and thoughtful, who always encouraged me to cultivate passions and pursue my dreams. My mother was never curt, critical or manipulative in any way. I was never pressured to pursue something I didn't have a yearning for. I can only think of one instance when she tried to nudge me to do something she hoped I would enjoy, which was of course, playing the piano. Well, it was not to be. Despite my love of music, I was not interested in the piano, and once she realized this fact, never again did she try to push me to play. She knew to really play well, there had to be a zeal that welled up from inside the soul, and with me that zeal was photography.

My mother struggled with clinical depression during her life, particularly following the tragic death of my father, and then again, following the equally tragic death of my older brother, Mike. His death in a plane crash caught us all off balance. Those were some very dark days and her grief compelled her to compose some of the most melancholy music I have ever heard. For years it seemed like sadness and tragedy poured from her fingertips every time I visited. My father was everything to my mother, her only true love, while my older brother Mike was a kind and sensitive soul she emotionally connected to in a way she simply did not with me or Tommy. In a real sense she never completely recovered from their absence in her life. Although she did remarry a man named David King, who shared her love of music and the piano, they were really just friends. It was more like they both needed someone with whom to fill the tedium of day to day life. They finally divorced after a few years, but continued living in the house together on separate floors from one another. Mom once told me they were perfect roommates, but terrible spouses.

Mom eventually moved to Albuquerque, NM and then Georgetown, TX to be near my brother Tommy and her grandchildren, Lauren and Austin. She was also fortunate to be visited there by Mike’s wife Karen and her other granddaughter Jaclyn. Mom continued playing and composing music until about a year before her death. The arthritis in her hands had finally made her once precise keyboard magic impossible, but that didn't stop her from singing the tunes floating around in her mind when I visited every few months from Colorado. I like to think that as she drifted away, the music that accompanied her throughout her life drifted with her keeping her company on the voyage to wherever she is now.

Thanks for the patience, the love, the hugs, kindness and of course, the music……….

Toby

Presentated at the United States Association for Body Psychotherapy 2018 Conference held at Pacifica Graduate Institute

[[Brandon WilliamsCraig]] Ph.D.     

brandon at culturesmith dot com

 

Embody Nonviolence: Peace Practices and the Embodiment of Social Justice Learning

 

Abstract

 

There is an urgent need for a lifelong education, both explicit and implicit, that is humane and humanizing. Learning processes and other social systems which habituate humanity must both incorporate, which is to say "embody", the richest portions of human experience, and provide resources to moderate the trauma that lives on in soma as testament to necessary and unnecessary suffering. Habit forming systems must encourage the development of ways of maturing which explicitly eschew strategies that disempower participants in favor of those which foster the kind of meaning-making that leads to wisdom and conscious power-sharing. Wisdom is defined here as the kind of cultivated understanding that critically explores the past, lives creatively in a vivid present, and leads directly to and is embodied in ethical decision-making, direct individual action which reflects an understanding of and ability to participate compassionately in systemic change. Wisdom suggests a demonstrable balance in the midst of complexity which acknowledges and plans for individual needs, the needs of strangers and nourishment of the body politic, the negotiations of special interest groups, and the unique living ecologies from which and in which humanity emerges.

 

Lifelong education that humanizes is conceived as embodied (somatic), rooted in relationship with unconscious and archetypal realities (depth psychological), and conscious of the working of systems by way of the study of mythologies, which is to say the narrative and interpretive nature of consciousness--worldviews becoming belief becoming behavior becoming polity. This lifelong education is also known as The Humanities, a discipline which appears to be getting the worst of a schoolyard battle over resources that has re-framed education as basic training and lost the sense that learning is a making of truthful relationship with the unknown, a becoming uncoupled for a time from urgent efficiencies, standardization, and other outcomes dear to the mechanical heart of globalized industrialized societies. This uncoupling makes it possible to couple more consciously, to become civilized, which is to say: sanguine about one's own and others' inconvenient motivations, transpartisan and dedicated to nonviolence with a martial intensity, determined to co-create outcomes that transform the natural antagonisms of conflicting interests into a learning process, peace practices through which everyone has serial opportunities to become more humane.

 

In order to illustrate the assertions above by giving evidence, a theoretical article follows this abstract, but it is best paired with an experiential session introducing the Martial Nonviolence™ method and Peace Practices project, a program that enjoyed international funding, and an example of somatic psychology’s timely contribution to peace and conflict learning. Participants in this learning will practice the normalization of the human need for conflict in a way that goes beyond symptom reduction and repairs the bodymind connection such that the experienced self and body work in concert. To place the work in context, the article offers a brief orientation to Rae Johnson’s new book, Embodied Social Justice, and then offers one creative response to her research and call to experiential understanding--a way of practicing peace as though it were a martial art, through re-patterning, recovery from trauma, and ongoing co-creative training for responsiveness to social justice concerns. Participants may discover that somatic peace-building is an already growing field of study, is ready to take a leap forward, and that the world could thereby experience seasons of true nourishment, rich harvests of budding work by professionals working together at the junction of somatics, depth psychology, and guardianship of peace, dedicated to a humanity growing ever more humane.

 

Presenter Biography

 

Brandon WilliamsCraig, Ph.D. is co-founder and CEO of the San Francisco Bay Area nonprofit Association Building Community, or ABC (ABCglobal.net). He is a post-doctoral fellow, fieldwork supervisor, and instructor for all levels of graduate students at Pacifica Graduate Institute in the Depth Psychology Somatics Specialization, as well as Communications Director for the Ragged Wing Ensemble theater company and The Flight Deck in Downtown Oakland, CA. He has extensive experience with private and public institutions, accepts executive positions corp-to-corp and as a contractor or employee, offers leadership and facilitation training, and has worked in the study of peace and conflict since 1998, as well as providing curriculum development, conflict education, and community mediation services. His academic teaching and research focus on the embodied (somatic) psychology of belief, the narrative (mythological) construction of culture, and The Myth of Peace.


Brandon Sensei is a 5th degree black belt in aikido and Founder/Chief Instructor of Free Aiki Dojo and Golden Bears Aikido at UC Berkeley. His students learn to Embody Nonviolence through somatic conflict resolution, a pairing of traditional aikido, professional theater techniques, and real-time facilitation that results in Conflict Done Well. His body-based facilitation method, called Martial Nonviolence, is the heart of the internationally funded Peace Practices curriculum being offered by ABC and practiced by students from 4 to 84 years of age in schools and Fortune 100 companies. Brandon resides in California and consults nationally and internationally.
